concepts.label: Decoder transformer pipeline
concepts.definition: The end-to-end path from context to next token: tokenize, embed, pass through the decoder stacks, produce probabilities, pick a token. The same basic architecture sits under Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini.

concepts.label: Tokenization
concepts.definition: Splitting text into tokens drawn from a fixed vocabulary and replacing each with its token ID (a number).

concepts.label: Token
concepts.definition: The unit a model reads and writes: a whole word, a piece of a word, or a symbol. Models predict tokens, not words.

concepts.label: Token embedding
concepts.definition: The learned vector (a long list of numbers) that a token ID is mapped to before the decoder stacks. One fixed embedding per token, whatever the sentence.

concepts.label: Semantic space
concepts.definition: The high-dimensional space embeddings live in, where location is meaning: related tokens sit near each other and directions can carry relationships (king - man + woman lands near queen).

concepts.label: Attention
concepts.definition: The part of each decoder stack that lets a token gather information from the other tokens in the context, moving its representation toward its meaning in this particular sentence.

concepts.label: MLP (multi-layer perceptron)
concepts.definition: The feed-forward part of each decoder stack. Its learned weights hold a compressed, lossy picture of the world (the "fuzzy JPEG") that it applies to each token's representation.

concepts.label: Decoder stack
concepts.definition: One block of attention followed by an MLP. A model runs many stacks in sequence, each refining the representation further.

concepts.label: Activation space
concepts.definition: The changing internal representations (activations) of tokens as they move through the stacks. Unlike the fixed token embedding, these depend on the context.

concepts.label: Recurrent depth (looping)
concepts.definition: Running the same decoder stack or block more than once so a representation gets another pass ("a second bite of the apple"), adding computation without adding parameters.

concepts.label: Probability distribution over tokens
concepts.definition: The model's output at each step: a probability for every token in its vocabulary (the softmax at the end of the pipeline).

concepts.label: Next-token prediction
concepts.definition: The single job a language model is trained to do and does at run time: predict what token comes next given the context.

concepts.label: Sampling and temperature
concepts.definition: How one token is chosen from the probability distribution. Temperature reshapes the distribution: higher means more varied, lower means more predictable.

concepts.label: Autoregression
concepts.definition: Generating one token at a time and feeding each chosen token back into the context for the next step, so every choice shapes what follows.

concepts.label: Parameter
concepts.definition: A single learned number (weight) in the model. The parameter count is how many there are; they are fixed once training ends.

concepts.label: Model size
concepts.definition: How big a model is (parameter count, width of the embedding space, number of decoder stacks) and what bigger does and does not buy you.

concepts.label: Learned knowledge
concepts.definition: What a model knows from training and how it is stored: compressed and approximate, not a searchable database of facts or a copy of its sources.

concepts.label: Hallucination
concepts.definition: Fluent output that is wrong. The model always produces the likely-sounding continuation; sometimes likely-sounding is not true.

concepts.label: Context
concepts.definition: Everything the model sees for a given step: system instructions, the conversation so far, uploaded files, tool results and its own output so far. The most important lever you have.

concepts.label: Context length
concepts.definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can hold in its context at once (the context window), and what happens as you approach it.

concepts.label: Grounding with documents
concepts.definition: Putting the relevant source material into the context so the answer draws on it rather than on the model's lossy memory, and why irrelevant material does not help.

concepts.label: Pre-training
concepts.definition: The first, largest training stage: next-token prediction over a huge body of text (and sometimes images), producing a base model.

concepts.label: Self-supervised learning
concepts.definition: Training where the answer key comes from the data itself, such as hiding the next token and asking the model to guess it.

concepts.label: Post-training
concepts.definition: Training after pre-training that turns a base model into an assistant: supervised fine-tuning on example responses, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and similar methods.

concepts.label: Alignment
concepts.definition: Work to make a model's behavior helpful, honest and safe, such as refusing harmful requests, and why that behavior is never perfectly reliable.

concepts.label: Training vs. inference
concepts.definition: Training changes the weights; inference (using the model) does not. A model can respond differently to new context without learning anything.

concepts.label: Thinking / reasoning
concepts.definition: A model generating hidden tokens that work through a problem before its visible answer. Same architecture and same next-token mechanism, just more tokens spent first.

concepts.label: Thinking budget and effort
concepts.definition: The limit on how many thinking tokens a model may spend (the effort setting in Claude), and matching that budget to the task.

concepts.label: Choosing a model
concepts.definition: Picking a model tier (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, Fable, or another vendor's equivalents): the smallest model that does the job correctly.

concepts.label: Inference speed and hardware
concepts.definition: How fast tokens are produced (GPUs, specialized chips, local laptops) and why taking in a prompt is faster than writing an answer.

concepts.label: KV cache
concepts.definition: The stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed, so each new token does not recompute the whole context.

concepts.label: Cost, usage and footprint
concepts.definition: Usage limits and credits, and the energy and environmental cost of bigger models and bigger budgets.

concepts.label: Multimodality
concepts.definition: Models that work with images, audio or video as well as text, whether trained jointly (native) or given a separate adapter.

concepts.label: History of AI
concepts.definition: The eras of AI (problem solvers, expert systems, machine learning, deep learning) and where transformers, generative AI and agents fit.

concepts.label: AGI (artificial general intelligence)
concepts.definition: What AGI has been taken to mean, how definitions and levels frameworks differ, and the argument about whether a milestone has passed.

concepts.label: Agent
concepts.definition: A model plus tools plus autonomy: a system that can take actions in a loop toward a goal, not just reply once.

concepts.label: Chat vs. agent
concepts.definition: The difference between a plain chat and an agent surface (Cowork, Claude Code): same model, different access, tools and ability to act.

concepts.label: Harness
concepts.definition: The software around the model that manages context, carries out tool calls, enforces permissions and returns results. The model proposes; the harness executes.

concepts.label: Tool
concepts.definition: A capability the harness can run on the model's behalf, such as reading a file, running a command or searching, with the result returned into context.

concepts.label: Connector (MCP)
concepts.definition: An add-on that gives an agent access to an outside system, often through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

concepts.label: File system
concepts.definition: The folders and files an agent can read and write, and why working through files lets an agent handle projects bigger than its context.

concepts.label: Memory
concepts.definition: How information persists beyond one context window: notes, working records, remembered preferences and project files, and keeping them accurate.

concepts.label: Context management
concepts.definition: Keeping a long task's context useful: compaction and summaries, starting fresh chats, and keeping original evidence available.

concepts.label: Subagent
concepts.definition: A fresh agent given a focused assignment and just the background it needs, so it starts with a clean context.

concepts.label: Permissions and safety
concepts.definition: What an agent is allowed to do (access controls, sandboxes, approvals) and judging whether shared code or broad access is safe.

concepts.label: Computer use
concepts.definition: Agents that operate a computer's screen, mouse and keyboard, and why that remains hard.

concepts.label: Directing an agent
concepts.definition: Telling an agent what you need: stating the problem and goal (a "North Star"), constraints and acceptance criteria rather than step-by-step instructions.

concepts.label: Verification
concepts.definition: Checking that work actually happened and is correct (reading back the result, inspecting the file) rather than trusting a claim that it did.

concepts.label: Agent skill
concepts.definition: A folder of reusable instructions (and optionally scripts and references) that an agent loads when a task calls for it.

concepts.label: Skill structure
concepts.definition: What goes in a skill folder: SKILL.md with its name and description, references/, scripts/, assets/, and what stays loaded versus loaded on demand.

concepts.label: Skill selection
concepts.definition: How an agent decides which skill to use from its name and description, and how vague, overlapping or conflicting skills go wrong.

concepts.label: Skill scope
concepts.definition: Where a skill lives and who can use it: a personal skill that follows you across projects versus a project skill tied to one project's conventions.

concepts.label: Skill Creator
concepts.definition: The skill for building, improving and testing other skills.

concepts.label: Evaluating a skill
concepts.definition: Testing whether a skill helps: comparing runs with and without it on the same inputs, criteria set in advance, varied test cases, the cheaper model it will run on.

concepts.label: Sharing skills
concepts.definition: Moving skills between people and hosts: repositories, READMEs, portability across providers, and what breaks when a skill is copied.

concepts.label: Classification and decision models
concepts.definition: Choosing among fixed options (labels) rather than writing open-ended text, and when a specialized decision model fits better.

concepts.label: Calibration
concepts.definition: Whether stated probabilities match how often things actually happen: of events given 80%, about 80% should occur.

concepts.label: Decisions under risk
concepts.definition: Combining probabilities with costs (false alarms, misses, what each outcome costs) to choose an action, not just the most likely outcome.

concepts.label: Feedback and rubrics
concepts.definition: Grading against a rubric and writing feedback that names what was missed and how to fix it.

concepts.label: Data privacy
concepts.definition: Keeping personal and student data out of code, prompts and repositories, and building tools that look it up only when needed.

concepts.label: Class demonstration
concepts.definition: Questions about a specific in-class demonstration or case study (for example seat-minder or the grading demo) rather than a general concept.

concepts.label: Course logistics
concepts.definition: How this course runs: quizzes, appeals, labs and exercises.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In the lecture's tour of what "AI" (artificial intelligence) has meant over the decades, which approach came first?

options.text: General problem solvers
options.feedback: The timeline opened in the 1950s with programs meant to reason through problems in general, before anyone had tried expert systems or learning from data. Each later era redefined the word rather than replacing the goal.

options.text: Expert systems
options.feedback: Expert systems, hand-built rules gathered from human specialists, were the next chapter, along with the first neural nets. They came after the general problem solvers, not before.

options.text: Machine learning, such as random forests
options.feedback: Random forests and logistic regression belong to the machine learning era, when the field shifted to fitting models to data. That is two chapters in, not the beginning.

options.text: Deep learning
options.feedback: Deep learning is the current era and the one this course lives in. It is easy to assume it is where AI started because it is where the word is loudest now, but it arrived last.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Logistic regression and random forests were given in the lecture as examples of which era of AI (artificial intelligence)?

options.text: Expert systems
options.feedback: Expert systems encode rules written by human specialists, while logistic regression and random forests fit themselves to data. Both come before deep learning, which is why they are easy to blur together.

options.text: Machine learning
options.feedback: These are classic machine learning methods: instead of hand-writing rules, you hand the algorithm data and let it fit a model. The lecture placed them in the era just before deep learning.

options.text: Deep learning
options.feedback: Deep learning means many-layered neural networks such as convolutional and recurrent nets. Random forests and logistic regression learn from data too, but they are not neural networks, and the lecture kept them in the earlier era.

options.text: General problem solvers
options.feedback: General problem solvers were the earliest idea of AI, programs that tried to reason through any problem. They did not learn from data at all, which is exactly what logistic regression and random forests do.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The transformer was introduced in 2017. How does that architecture relate to the chat models you use today?

options.text: It has been replaced by a newer architecture designed for chat
options.feedback: It feels as though something so much better must have replaced a 2017 design, but the lecture's point was the opposite: the architecture has not changed. What changed is how big it is and how much text it is trained on.

options.text: It survives only as the part of the model that handles grammar
options.feedback: The transformer is the whole model, not one component inside it. The pipeline you saw, from context to next token, is the transformer end to end.

options.text: It is the same architecture, scaled up
options.feedback: Today's models are the 2017 design made much bigger and trained on trillions of words instead of a million. That is why one pipeline diagram describes Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini alike.

options.text: It is the same architecture, retrained yearly on the same amount of text
options.feedback: The architecture is indeed the same, but the scale is not. The lecture stressed that training went from about a million words to trillions, and the models themselves grew along with it.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: On the lecture's timeline, where do generative AI (artificial intelligence) and AI agents sit?

options.text: In a new era that began after deep learning ended
options.feedback: It is tempting to give generative AI its own box, but the lecture did not. Deep learning has not ended; generative models and agents are its newest chapter, built from the same kind of neural networks.

options.text: In the machine learning era, alongside random forests
options.feedback: Generative models do learn from data, which is why this sounds right. But they are deep neural networks, which puts them in the deep learning era rather than the earlier one of random forests and logistic regression.

options.text: In the expert systems era, because they follow written rules
options.feedback: A chat model can look as if it follows rules, but nobody wrote any rules for it. Expert systems were hand-built from human knowledge; a transformer learns everything from text.

options.text: At the leading edge of the deep learning era
options.feedback: Generative AI and agents are the red arrow at the far end of deep learning: the same kind of neural network, pushed further. That is the era this course lives in.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A friend tells you that ChatGPT must run on a brand-new architecture invented in the 2020s, since chatbots did not work well before then. Which point from the lecture answers this?

options.text: Chatbots became useful once expert-system rules were finally written well enough
options.feedback: Expert systems belong to an earlier era, and nothing in a modern chat model is hand-written rules. The improvement came from scale, not from better rule-writing.

options.text: The architecture dates from 2017 and has been scaled up rather than replaced
options.feedback: The transformer of 2017 is still the design in use. What made chatbots work well was training that same architecture on trillions of words instead of a million, and making the model much larger.

options.text: Deep learning itself only began in the 2020s, so nothing older could have worked
options.feedback: Deep learning dates from around 2010 on the lecture's timeline, with convolutional and recurrent networks. The transformer came in 2017, so both are older than your friend thinks.

options.text: The architecture is the same but was rewritten to run on much faster computers
options.feedback: Faster hardware helps, but the lecture attributed the leap to scale: bigger models and vastly more training text. Same design, more of it.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Reading the decoder transformer pipeline from left to right, what is the correct order of the stages?

options.text: Context, token encodings, token embeddings, decoder stacks, token probabilities, next word prediction
options.feedback: Text goes in as context, becomes numbers, becomes locations in semantic space, passes through the stacks, comes out as a probability for every token, and one token is chosen. Every stage feeds the next.

options.text: Context, token embeddings, token encodings, decoder stacks, token probabilities, next word prediction
options.feedback: Encoding and embedding are easy to swap because both turn tokens into numbers. But a token has to be given its vocabulary number (encoding) before that number can be mapped to a location in semantic space (embedding).

options.text: Context, decoder stacks, token encodings, token embeddings, token probabilities, next word prediction
options.feedback: The decoder stacks are the heart of the model, so it is tempting to put them right after the input. But they can only work on numbers, so the text must be encoded and embedded first.

options.text: Context, token encodings, token embeddings, token probabilities, decoder stacks, next word prediction
options.feedback: Probabilities are the output of the decoder stacks, not the input to them. The stacks refine the embeddings; only after the last stack does the model produce a probability for every token.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In a chat with a model such as Claude, what makes up the context?

options.text: The message you just typed, without the earlier turns
options.feedback: Your latest message is part of the context, but the earlier turns go in with it. If they did not, the model would lose the thread every time you replied.

options.text: Your typed prompt, with any attachments handled separately
options.feedback: There is no separate system for attachments. An uploaded document is turned into tokens and placed in the context alongside your typed prompt, which is how the model can draw on it.

options.text: Your prompt, anything you attached, and the conversation so far
options.feedback: Everything you put in front of the model counts as context: the prompt, uploaded documents, and every earlier turn of the conversation. All of it goes in together at the left of the pipeline.

options.text: Everything the model read while it was being trained
options.feedback: Training text shaped the model's parameters, but it is not sitting in front of the model when you chat. Context is what you supply for this request, which is why it is the lever you control.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What happens at the token encoding stage of the pipeline?

options.text: Each token is placed at a location in a high-dimensional semantic space
options.feedback: That is the token embedding stage, which comes next. Encoding happens first and is simpler: it only assigns each token an id number from the vocabulary.

options.text: The text is scrambled so that the company running the model cannot read it
options.feedback: The word 'encoding' sounds like encryption, but it is not about secrecy. It is bookkeeping: each token is swapped for its number in a fixed vocabulary so the model has numbers to work with.

options.text: The model computes a probability for each possible next token
options.feedback: Probabilities appear at the far right of the pipeline, after the decoder stacks. Encoding is the very first step after the context, before the model has done any thinking at all.

options.text: The text is cut into tokens, each with a vocabulary id number
options.feedback: Deep learning models handle numbers and nothing else, so the first thing done to your text is to break it into tokens and look each one up in a fixed vocabulary. What comes out is a list of id numbers; meaning enters one step later, at the embedding stage.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What does the token embedding stage produce for each token?

options.text: The token's id number from the vocabulary
options.feedback: The id number is what the encoding stage produces, one step earlier. An id number is arbitrary and carries no meaning; the embedding is where meaning enters.

options.text: A vector: the token's location in a high-dimensional space of meanings
options.feedback: An embedding is a list of thousands of numbers that place the token in a space where nearby tokens have similar meanings. Location is meaning, which is what lets the model work with what a word means.

options.text: A probability that the token is the correct next word
options.feedback: Probabilities come out at the end of the pipeline, after the decoder stacks. The embedding stage is at the beginning and is about representing the tokens already in the context.

options.text: A list of the token's dictionary definitions
options.feedback: There are no dictionary entries anywhere in the model; it only handles numbers. The embedding captures meaning as a position in space, not as text.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are made by three different companies. What does the lecture's single pipeline picture claim about all three?

options.text: Each one adds its own extra stage, which is why their answers differ
options.feedback: The differences you notice come from size, training, and the product built around the model. The stages themselves, from context through to one chosen token, are the same in each.

options.text: They can share one picture because they were trained on the same text
options.feedback: Training text differs from company to company, and it is not what the picture is about. What the three share is the architecture: each is a decoder transformer.

options.text: All three are decoder transformers, so one picture describes each of them
options.feedback: The decoder transformer is the architecture behind every modern chat model. Read the pipeline once and you have read all of them; what differs is scale, training, and the product wrapped around the model.

options.text: Only Claude matches the picture, since the lecture drew its examples from it
options.feedback: Claude turns up in the examples, but the picture was offered as the shape of a generative model in general. Every current chat model is built this way.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Why does your text have to be turned into numbers before the model can work on it?

options.text: Because numbers take up less storage space than letters
options.feedback: Storage is not the issue. Even if text were cheaper to store, the model could not use it: the arithmetic inside a neural network needs numeric input.

options.text: Because the model reads numbers faster than it reads words
options.feedback: Speed is not the reason either. A deep learning model cannot read words at all, quickly or slowly. Numbers are the only thing it can take in.

options.text: Because deep learning models can only ever deal with numbers
options.feedback: A neural network is arithmetic on numbers, nothing else. So text has to become numbers, first as vocabulary ids and then as embeddings, before any of the machinery can touch it.

options.text: Because numbers hide the content of your prompt from other users
options.feedback: Turning text into vocabulary numbers is not encryption; anyone with the vocabulary can turn them back. The conversion exists because the model needs numbers, not because of privacy.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture opened the pipeline with a fact it called counterintuitive. After all of the context goes into the model, how much comes out?

options.text: One complete sentence
options.feedback: A sentence is what you see on screen, so it is natural to assume that is the unit of output. It is not: a sentence is assembled from many separate runs of the model.

options.text: The whole response at once
options.feedback: The response you read was never produced in one piece. The entire context is processed for every single token of it.

options.text: One token for every token in the context
options.feedback: The input and output are not matched one to one. However long the context is, the model's job on each run is to produce just the next token.

options.text: Exactly one token
options.feedback: All of that input, your prompt, attachments, and conversation, is processed to produce a single next token. That is the whole job of one pass through the model.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture called context the single most important lever you have. Why does context deserve that title?

options.text: Because everything the model works from arrives through it
options.feedback: Your prompt, your attachments, and the conversation so far all enter at the left of the pipeline, and the model's parameters do not change from one request to the next. So the context is the one thing that varies between requests, and you are the one who decides what is in it.

options.text: Because a longer context always makes the model produce a longer answer
options.feedback: Context length does not set answer length; the model still produces one token at a time. Context matters for what the model can draw on, not for how much it says.

options.text: Because context changes the model's parameters a little with every message
options.feedback: Nothing you type alters the model's weights. Context is read, not learned from, which is exactly why it is the lever you can pull without retraining anything.

options.text: Because the numbers assigned to tokens depend on how much context there is
options.feedback: A token's vocabulary number is fixed regardless of what surrounds it. Context matters because the model responds to what is in it, not because it changes the encoding.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Token encodings and token embeddings are both ways of turning a token into numbers. What is the difference between them?

options.text: Encodings are used for common words and embeddings for rare ones
options.feedback: Both stages apply to every token; there is no split by word frequency. Each token is first encoded, then embedded.

options.text: An encoding is an arbitrary id from the vocabulary; an embedding is a location whose position carries meaning
options.feedback: The encoding is just a lookup number, like a seat number in a theater. The embedding places the token in a semantic space where nearby tokens mean similar things, so its position says something about what the token means.

options.text: An encoding carries the token's meaning; an embedding is just a shorter code for it
options.feedback: This has the two stages backwards. The encoding comes first and is meaningless on its own; the embedding is the larger object, thousands of numbers, and it is where meaning lives.

options.text: Encodings are computed by the decoder stacks; embeddings arrive already in the context
options.feedback: Neither is produced by the stacks and neither arrives in the context. Both are early stages that prepare the text for the stacks to work on.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: You upload a PDF (portable document format) file to a chat and ask a question about it. At which stage of the pipeline does that file enter?

options.text: Token embeddings
options.feedback: The document will eventually be embedded, but so will everything else. Embedding is a transformation applied to the context, not a place where the document lives.

options.text: Decoder stacks
options.feedback: The stacks process whatever is in the context; they do not hold the document. Your file has to enter at the left of the pipeline to reach them at all.

options.text: Context
options.feedback: An attachment is part of what you put in front of the model, together with your prompt and the conversation so far. It enters at the far left and flows through every stage after that.

options.text: Token probabilities
options.feedback: Probabilities are what the model produces at the end, not something you supply. Nothing you upload goes in at that stage.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Ten messages into a conversation, the model correctly refers back to something you mentioned at the start. What explains this?

options.text: The token encodings remember earlier turns of the chat
options.feedback: Encoding is a stateless lookup that turns a token into a number. It has no memory of what came before.

options.text: The model saved its token probabilities from the earlier messages
options.feedback: Probabilities are computed fresh on each run and are not stored between messages. The model does not carry them forward.

options.text: Attention kept your earlier remark in memory between the turns
options.feedback: Attention has no memory of its own; on each run it works only over the tokens in front of the model. Your remark is available because the whole conversation is sent again as context, not because anything was held over.

options.text: The conversation so far is part of the context sent to the model
options.feedback: Context is not just your latest message; it includes the whole conversation to that point. Your earlier remark went into the model along with the newest message, so the model could work from it.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: You type "Hello, world" into a chat. At which stage of the pipeline is that text first replaced by numbers?

options.text: Token encodings
options.feedback: Encoding is the first thing that happens to the context: the text is split into tokens and each token is swapped for its vocabulary number. From that point on the model handles numbers only.

options.text: Context
options.feedback: Context is your text as you wrote it, together with anything attached and the conversation so far. It is the input, still in words, before any conversion has happened.

options.text: Token embeddings
options.feedback: By the time embeddings are made, the text is already numbers. Embedding turns each vocabulary id into a location in semantic space, which is a second numeric step, not the first.

options.text: Decoder stacks
options.feedback: The stacks work on embeddings that are already numeric. If words reached the stacks, the model could do nothing with them.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The class played the model's game with the opening line of Zora Neale Hurston's novel: "Ships at a distance have every man's wish on ____." Which three kinds of knowledge did the lecture say you needed just to play?

options.text: Spelling, punctuation, and a large vocabulary
options.feedback: None of these were the point. You could have guessed a noun with a modest vocabulary; what mattered was knowing what kind of word fits, what the sentence is about, and how a writer like Hurston would finish it.

options.text: Syntax, semantics, and style with world knowledge
options.feedback: You knew the slot needed a noun (syntax), that the noun should concern ships and wishing (semantics), and that 'board' is the poetic choice a novelist would make (style and world knowledge). A model has to learn all three to guess well.

options.text: The author's biography, the novel's title, and its publication year
options.feedback: Knowing about Hurston helps with the last step, but the game was not trivia. Nobody needed the title or the year to know that a noun about ships belonged there.

options.text: Syntax, semantics, and a memory of having read the novel
options.feedback: The first two are right, and the third is the tempting swap. You did not need to have read Hurston to play; you needed a sense of how writers choose words and of the world the sentence describes, which is the third thing the model has to learn.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Training a language model by hiding the next word and having the model guess it is called self-supervised learning. What makes it "self-supervised"?

options.text: The model checks each guess against a database of facts
options.feedback: There is no database in training or in the model. The only thing a guess is compared with is the word that was actually there.

options.text: People label every training sentence as good or bad for the model
options.feedback: That would be ordinary supervised learning with human labels, and it could never scale to trillions of examples. Nobody labels the training text at all.

options.text: The text itself supplies the answer, because the hidden word is right there
options.feedback: The next word in the text is the correct answer, so the training data grades the model's guesses on its own. No human has to write anything down, which is why training can run on trillions of words.

options.text: The model writes its own rules of grammar and then follows them
options.feedback: Nobody writes grammar rules, not even the model. It learns grammatical structure as a side effect of guessing well, without ever stating a rule.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: According to the lecture, how is a language model trained?

options.text: Engineers write rules of grammar and lists of facts and load them into the model
options.feedback: That is how expert systems were built, and it is not how this works. No rules or fact lists are written down; the model has to pick them up on its own in order to guess well.

options.text: The model reads a dictionary and a grammar book before it sees any other text
options.feedback: There is no dictionary stage. Meaning and grammar are learned from the same next-word guessing as everything else.

options.text: The model memorizes the training text so that it can look passages up later
options.feedback: The model has no stored text to consult. Training adjusts parameters after each guess; it does not file the text away.

options.text: The model guesses each hidden next word and is adjusted when it is wrong
options.feedback: That loop is the whole recipe, run trillions of times: guess, compare with the word that was actually there, nudge the parameters, move on. Everything the model knows about grammar, meaning, and the world comes out of doing that at enormous scale.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In the Hurston exercise, every guess called out in the room was a noun. Why?

options.text: The word follows "on," and the structure of the sentence demands a noun there
options.feedback: You applied syntax without thinking about it: after a preposition like 'on' comes a noun. A model has to learn that same structure, and it does so simply because guessing a verb there would be wrong every time.

options.text: Nouns are the most common words in English, so they are the safest guess
options.feedback: Frequency alone would not stop someone guessing 'the' or 'is,' which are far more common than 'board.' It was the sentence's grammar, not word frequency, that ruled those out.

options.text: Hurston's writing style leans heavily on nouns
options.feedback: Style did come into the game, but at the last step, in choosing 'board' over 'deck.' Knowing the slot needed a noun at all came from grammar, before style entered.

options.text: The slide showed a list of nouns to choose from
options.feedback: No list was shown; the blank was open. Everyone converged on nouns from their own knowledge of how sentences work.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A classmate says: "The model never makes grammar mistakes, so someone must have programmed the rules of grammar into it." Which idea from the lecture corrects this?

options.text: Engineers add a grammar-checking step after the model produces its text
options.feedback: There is no separate grammar checker. The pipeline ends with a token being chosen from probabilities; nothing edits it afterward.

options.text: A grammar textbook in the training data is where the rules come from
options.feedback: Even if a grammar book were in the training text, it would be treated like any other text: more next words to guess. The model does not read rules and apply them.

options.text: Grammar was learned, not programmed, because guessing well required it
options.feedback: To predict the next word you have to know which kinds of word can go where, so grammatical structure falls out of the training itself. Nobody supplied a single rule, just as nobody in the room needed a stated rule to know a noun follows 'on'.

options.text: The model copies grammatical sentences from its training text
options.feedback: The model does not store or copy sentences; it has no text inside it. It produces each token from probabilities shaped by training, which is why it can write sentences that never appeared anywhere.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture pointed out what the next-word game was and was not asking of you. What was it asking for?

options.text: The one true statement about ships
options.feedback: Nothing in the exercise checked whether the completed sentence was true. It was a line of fiction, and a good guess did not need to be a fact about ships at all.

options.text: A plausible continuation of the sentence
options.feedback: You were rewarded for a guess that fits, and 'deck' would have been a fine one even though Hurston wrote 'board'. That is the same deal the model is trained on, which is why what it produces is always plausible and never guaranteed to be correct.

options.text: The most common English word that can follow "on"
options.feedback: Common words like 'the' can follow 'on,' but nobody guessed them, because the game rewards a good fit, not a frequent word.

options.text: The exact word from the novel, or nothing
options.feedback: Landing on 'board' was satisfying, but the exercise counted every sensible noun as playing the game well. It was about guessing, not about matching.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Hurston's actual word was "board." Why did the lecture single out that guess as demanding more than the others?

options.text: Because "board" is the only noun that fits grammatically after "on"
options.feedback: Syntax allows 'deck,' 'shore,' and 'star' just as well. What set 'board' apart was not grammar but the kind of knowledge it took to reach it.

options.text: Because "board" has more meanings than any of the other guesses
options.feedback: How many meanings a word has was not the point. 'Board' stood out for being the choice a particular writer would make, not for being ambiguous.

options.text: Because "board" was the only guess that had anything to do with ships
options.feedback: Every guess was about ships or wishing: deck, shore, sail, star. Semantics got everyone that far; it did not separate 'board' from the rest.

options.text: Because reaching "board" takes a sense of style and world knowledge
options.feedback: 'Board' is the more poetic choice, and it fits Hurston. To land on it you need to know something about how authors write and about the world, the third kind of knowledge a model has to learn.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A physicist trains the same next-item guessing architecture on gravity-wave readings instead of English text. Based on the lecture, what should she expect?

options.text: The model learns the structure of gravity-wave data the way it learns English
options.feedback: The learner is general-purpose: hide the next item, guess, adjust. Feed it English and it learns English; feed it gravity-wave data and it learns about gravity waves. Nothing in the method is specific to language.

options.text: The model fails, because the architecture was designed around words
options.feedback: The architecture is not built around words; it is built around predicting the next item in a sequence, whatever the items are. Words are just one kind of sequence.

options.text: The model needs a rulebook of physics loaded in before it can start
options.feedback: No rules are written down for English either. The whole point of self-supervised learning is that the data provides its own answer, so physics would be learned the same way.

options.text: The model translates the readings into English sentences before learning from them
options.feedback: Nothing gets translated. The readings become numbers the model predicts directly; there is no English step in between.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A decoder transformer produces exactly one token each time it runs. How does a chat model use that to write a whole paragraph?

options.text: The new token is added to the end of the context, and the full model runs again on that longer context
options.feedback: The output token becomes part of everything that came before, and that slightly longer context goes back through the whole pipeline to produce the next token. A paragraph is that loop repeated a few hundred times.

options.text: The whole paragraph is produced in a single pass and then revealed a token at a time so it is easier to read
options.feedback: The word-by-word display is not a presentation trick. Each new token really is the result of a fresh run of the model, which is why there is nothing to reveal until that run finishes.

options.text: A full sentence is predicted at a time, and then the model starts on the next sentence
options.feedback: It is tempting to think the unit of output is a sentence, since that is how we plan speech. But the model has no notion of a sentence as a unit; it produces one token, feeds it back, and produces the next.

options.text: A separate copy of the model runs for each sentence, and the results are joined together
options.feedback: There is only one model, and it runs many times in sequence rather than as several copies side by side. Each run sees everything produced so far, which is what keeps the paragraph coherent.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What is the name for generating a response one token at a time, feeding each new token back into the context before producing the next?

options.text: Self-supervised learning
options.feedback: Self-supervised learning is how the model was trained: hide the next word, guess it, adjust. The token-by-token loop at response time is a different idea with its own name.

options.text: Autoregressive generation
options.feedback: The "auto" is the model feeding on its own output: each token it produces becomes part of the context that shapes the token after it. That loop is what turns a one-token machine into a paragraph writer.

options.text: Token encoding
options.feedback: Token encoding is the step where text is chopped into tokens and each is replaced by its vocabulary number. It happens on the way into the model, not in the loop that produces the response.

options.text: Attention
options.feedback: Attention is a mechanism inside each decoder stack, working on the tokens already in the context. It is not the name for the outer loop that appends each new token and runs the model again.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What causes a model to stop producing tokens and end its response?

options.text: The app enforces a fixed number of words per reply
options.feedback: Apps can cap a reply, but that is not how a response normally ends. The model itself decides when it is done, using a token reserved for exactly that purpose.

options.text: Every token's probability drops too low for one to be chosen
options.feedback: The model always produces a full probability distribution over the vocabulary, so there is always a token to choose. Stopping is a positive choice the model makes, not a failure to find anything.

options.text: One of the tokens in the vocabulary means "stop," and the model chooses it
options.feedback: This is the end-of-sequence token, and picking it is a prediction like any other -- the model works out that it is finished the same way it works out any next word. That is why a reply can be one line or several paragraphs, depending only on the context.

options.text: The response is cut off once it reaches the length of the prompt
options.feedback: Prompt length and response length are unrelated. A short question can get a long answer and vice versa, because the model chooses the stopping point itself with a dedicated token.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A model produces a paragraph with a clear beginning, middle, and end. Given that it only ever chooses one token per run, where does that structure come from?

options.text: The model wrote an outline first and then filled each section in
options.feedback: Planning ahead is how you would write a paragraph, so it is the natural guess. There is no outline stage in the pipeline: every run produces exactly one token, and nothing is kept between runs except the context itself.

options.text: The model produced the ending first and then worked backwards to reach it
options.feedback: Generation only ever moves forward. Once a token is chosen it becomes part of the context and the next one is chosen from there, so there is no ending sitting in place to write toward.

options.text: The app split the request into sections and asked the model for each one
options.feedback: Nothing splits the request up. One run yields one token, and the paragraph is that single loop repeated, not several separate answers stitched together.

options.text: It emerges as the paragraph is written, since each token is chosen from everything written so far
options.feedback: Every run reads the whole context, including the part of the answer already produced, so a sentence that has opened a topic makes the tokens that close it more likely. Shape comes out of the loop rather than out of a plan.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture deliberately stops saying a model predicts the next "word" and starts saying it predicts the next "token." Why does that distinction matter?

options.text: "Token" is simply the technical word for "word" inside a neural network
options.feedback: If tokens and words were the same thing, the change would be cosmetic. It is not: a token can be a whole word or a fragment of one, and that difference matters for limits, costs, and unfamiliar words.

options.text: The unit the model works in is the token, a whole word or a piece of one
options.feedback: Common words get a token to themselves, and rarer words are broken into pieces shared across many words. Everything the model does, including what it charges for, is counted in those units.

options.text: "Token" is the unit companies bill you in, while the model itself still reads words
options.feedback: Tokens really are what you are billed for, which is what makes this sound right. But the billing follows the mechanism rather than replacing it: tokens are the units the model reads and writes, and the price is just counting them.

options.text: The model reads one character at a time, and "token" is the name for a character
options.feedback: Tokens are larger than characters. A common word is one token, and a rare word is a handful of pieces, not a string of individual letters.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: How does a model's vocabulary handle common words differently from rare ones?

options.text: Frequent words get one token each; rarer words are built from pieces shared with other words
options.feedback: Frequent words earn a dedicated token because they show up so often. Rare words are built from shared pieces, which is also what lets the model piece together a word it has never met.

options.text: Frequent words are dropped as filler, and only rarer words are given tokens of their own
options.feedback: Dropping common words is a habit from older keyword search, not from language models. The model needs "the" and "on" as much as any other token, because grammar lives in them.

options.text: Every word gets exactly one token of its own, whether it is common or rare
options.feedback: A one-token-per-word scheme would need a vocabulary entry for every possible word, including misspellings and new coinages. Splitting rare words into shared pieces avoids that.

options.text: Rarer words are swapped for a common synonym before the model ever sees them
options.feedback: There is no synonym lookup. The rare word is kept, just broken into fragments the vocabulary already contains, so its exact spelling still reaches the model.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Why can a language model make sense of a word that never appeared anywhere in its training data?

options.text: It looks the word up online before responding
options.feedback: Nothing leaves the model between tokens. The ability to handle a new word comes from how the text was chopped up on the way in, not from any outside lookup.

options.text: Its vocabulary is large enough to contain every possible word
options.feedback: No fixed vocabulary can hold every word people will ever coin or misspell. The model gets around that by not needing one entry per word.

options.text: The word is split into pieces that also occur inside other words
options.feedback: Rare and unseen words are tokenized as fragments shared across many familiar words. The model has meaning for the pieces, so it can assemble a reasonable reading of the whole.

options.text: It ignores the unfamiliar word and works from the rest of the sentence
options.feedback: Surrounding words help, but the new word is not skipped. Its fragments carry meaning of their own, which is why a made-up word can still be understood rather than dropped.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student writes to a chat model, "My roommate's cooking is dangerously Vanderbiltian," and the reply treats the invented word as a joke about Vanderbilt. Which idea from the lecture best explains why the model coped?

options.text: The model has a token for every proper noun, including newly coined ones
options.feedback: A vocabulary with an entry for every coinage would have to be infinite. The model manages without one by building unfamiliar words from parts.

options.text: The model autocorrected the word to the nearest real word before reading it
options.feedback: Autocorrect lives in your keyboard, not in the model. The invented word reaches the model intact, just split into pieces.

options.text: The model memorized the word from a Vanderbilt web page in its training data
options.feedback: The word was invented on the spot, so it could not have been memorized. What the model does have is meaning for the fragments "Vanderbilt" and "-ian" from other words.

options.text: Tokenization split the word into familiar pieces the model already knows
options.feedback: A rare or unseen word is broken into sub-word fragments that occur in many other words. The model can make sense of the parts, and so of the whole, even though it never saw the combination.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student sees that a chat model has a "200k limit" on how much it can hold in one conversation and asks what that number is counting. What is the answer?

options.text: Words, so roughly 200,000 words of prompt and conversation
options.feedback: Words are the natural guess, but the model never sees words as such. Many words become more than one token, so 200,000 tokens holds fewer than 200,000 words.

options.text: Characters, including spaces and punctuation
options.feedback: Characters are too fine a unit. The model's tokens are whole common words or multi-letter fragments, so a character count would overstate what fits.

options.text: Tokens, the word and sub-word pieces the model works in
options.feedback: Token limits and token costs both count the same unit the model reads and produces. That is why the same text can cost more or less depending on how many pieces it breaks into.

options.text: Times the model can be run before the conversation resets
options.feedback: The limit is about how much text the context can hold, not how many turns you get. Every run counts the tokens in the whole context, not the number of runs.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student watches a chat model pause for a second and then produce its answer a word or two at a time. She concludes her internet connection is slow. What is the better explanation?

options.text: The full answer was finished before anything appeared and is shown gradually to feel conversational
options.feedback: There is no finished answer waiting. Each fragment appears only when a fresh run of the model has produced it, so the trickle reflects real work happening.

options.text: Each piece of text is the model completing a full run and producing one more token
options.feedback: The pause and the trickle are the model itself running, once per token. Every visible fragment means the whole pipeline just executed again on a slightly longer context.

options.text: The server is holding her request in a queue behind other users
options.feedback: Queuing can add delay before the first word, but it does not explain the steady word-by-word arrival afterward. That rhythm is the model generating one token per run.

options.text: Her browser is rendering the text more slowly than it received it
options.feedback: Browsers render text far faster than it arrives here. The pacing is set upstream, by how long each run of the model takes to produce the next token.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Partway through an answer, a model picks a slightly unusual word. Why does that one choice matter for everything the model writes afterward?

options.text: The word joins the context, so every later token is predicted with it in view
options.feedback: Nothing the model produces is thrown away. Each chosen token is appended and fed back, so an unusual word early on tilts every prediction that follows it.

options.text: It does not matter, because each token is predicted from the original prompt alone
options.feedback: If tokens were predicted from the prompt alone, the response could not stay coherent with itself. The model sees its own earlier output every time it runs, which is what autoregression means.

options.text: The model goes back and revises the earlier word if later tokens do not fit it
options.feedback: There is no going back. Once a token is produced it is part of the context for good, so the model has to make the rest of the response fit the word, not the other way round.

options.text: The model restarts from the prompt whenever it produces a word it did not expect
options.feedback: The model does not judge its own output as expected or unexpected. It simply appends whatever it chose and keeps walking from there.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A model's reply comes to about 300 tokens. Roughly how many times did the whole model run to produce it?

options.text: Once, because a single pass produces the entire reply
options.feedback: A single pass produces a single token, not a reply. Getting 300 tokens out of a one-token machine takes the loop of appending and re-running.

options.text: Twice, once to read the prompt and once to write the reply
options.feedback: Reading and writing are not separate phases. Every run reads the whole context, including the prompt, and writes exactly one token.

options.text: About a dozen times, roughly once per sentence
options.feedback: Sentences are not the model's unit of work. Each run yields one token, so the count of runs tracks tokens, not sentences.

options.text: About 300 times, once for each token
options.feedback: The model runs once per token, and each run takes the whole context, now one token longer. That is why a long reply takes noticeably longer than a short one.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A large language model (LLM) has bigger MLPs (multi-layer perceptrons) and more decoder stacks than a small one. According to the lecture, what do those extra parameters buy you?

options.text: Room to hold a longer conversation before the context fills up
options.feedback: Context length is a separate matter, and the lecture treats it as the other half of the picture. Extra parameters do not lengthen what the model can read in one go.

options.text: Room for a sharper, more detailed picture of the world
options.feedback: More parameters mean more room to hold what training taught the model, so fewer topics sit in the blurry part of the picture. That is why the largest models are steadier on obscure subjects.

options.text: A larger vocabulary, so fewer words have to be split into pieces
options.feedback: Vocabulary size is settled when the tokenizer is built, not by the parameter count. A small model and a large one can split words in exactly the same way.

options.text: A checking step that catches wrong answers before they are shown
options.feedback: No model of any size has such a step; the pipeline ends with a token chosen from probabilities. A larger model is wrong less often on well-covered topics, but nothing verifies what it says.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture sums up token embeddings with the phrase "location is meaning." What does that phrase claim?

options.text: Where a token sits in the embedding space is what it means to the model
options.feedback: The model has no dictionary. A token's meaning is entirely its position: tokens with similar meanings are placed near each other, and moving through the space moves through meaning.

options.text: Where a word sits in a sentence determines what it means
options.feedback: Word order does matter later, when the surrounding words act on a token. But "location" here refers to position in the semantic space, not position in the sentence.

options.text: A word's meaning depends on where in the document it first appeared
options.feedback: Position in the document is not the location in question. The embedding places the token in an abstract space of meanings, regardless of where it showed up on the page.

options.text: The model stores each word's meaning at a fixed address in memory
options.feedback: That would be a database, and the embedding space is not one. Nothing is stored at the location; the coordinates themselves are the meaning.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In the model's embedding space, which tokens would you expect to find in the neighborhood of "king"?

options.text: Words that rhyme with it, such as "ring" and "sing"
options.feedback: Sound is not what organizes the space. The dimensions capture meaning, so a rhyme with nothing in common semantically sits far away.

options.text: Words that commonly follow it, such as "of" and "me"
options.feedback: Next-word probability is produced at the end of the pipeline, not encoded in the embedding's location. Neighbors in the space share meaning, not sentence position.

options.text: Words with related meanings, such as "queen" and "monarch"
options.feedback: The space is arranged so that similar meanings sit near each other. "Ruler," "crown," "royalty," and "tsar" are all in the same region, which is what makes arithmetic on meaning possible.

options.text: Words that begin with the same letter, such as "kitchen" and "kite"
options.feedback: Spelling plays no part in where a token lands. "Kitchen" and "king" share a first letter and nothing else, so they sit in unrelated parts of the space.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Starting from the embedding for "king," you subtract the embedding for "man" and add the embedding for "woman." Where do you land?

options.text: Near "queen"
options.feedback: Taking away the male component and adding the female one moves the location to the female royal, which is what "location is meaning" predicts. Arithmetic on positions is arithmetic on meaning.

options.text: Back near "man"
options.feedback: Subtracting "man" removes that direction rather than returning to it. What is left is royalty, and adding "woman" then moves it to the female royal.

options.text: Near a genderless "sovereign" or "ruler"
options.feedback: That is where you land after subtracting "man" alone. Adding "woman" takes one more step, from the genderless ruler to the female one.

options.text: Near "princess"
options.feedback: A princess is royal and female but is not the counterpart to a king. The arithmetic swaps gender and keeps rank, and the same-rank female royal is a queen.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Why does subtracting the embedding for "man" from the embedding for "king" produce something near a genderless "sovereign" or "ruler"?

options.text: Because the model has a rule written into it that "king" equals "man" plus "ruler"
options.feedback: No such rule is written down anywhere. The relationship falls out of where the tokens were placed during training, not from a formula someone entered.

options.text: Because "man" and "king" are stored in the same database record
options.feedback: There are no records. Each token is just a point in the space, and the result comes from the geometry of those points.

options.text: Because the two tokens' vocabulary id numbers are subtracted, leaving the id for "ruler"
options.feedback: Vocabulary ids are arbitrary labels, and subtracting one from another lands on nothing in particular. The arithmetic is done on the embedding vectors, where each direction through the space carries some aspect of meaning.

options.text: Because meaning is position, so removing the "man" direction leaves royalty
options.feedback: Since location is meaning, each direction in the space corresponds to some aspect of meaning. Subtracting "man" strips out the male aspect, and what remains sits among rulers and crowns.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Mathematically, what kind of object is a token embedding?

options.text: A single whole number that identifies the token
options.feedback: A single number is the token encoding, the vocabulary id. The embedding replaces that id with something much richer.

options.text: A probability between 0 and 1
options.feedback: Probabilities are what the model produces at the end, one per vocabulary token. The embedding is an input to the stacks, not an output.

options.text: A vector, a list of thousands of numbers
options.feedback: A location in a space with thousands of dimensions is specified by one number per dimension, and a list of numbers like that is a vector. That is what the decoder stacks read and refine.

options.text: A table that maps the token to its related words
options.feedback: Relationships between tokens are not tabulated. They are implied by distance: nearby vectors mean similar things, with no table needed.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Two prompts contain the same number of words, but one is everyday English and the other is dense chemistry vocabulary. The chemistry prompt is billed for many more tokens. What explains the difference?

options.text: Longer words cost more, because billing counts letters
options.feedback: Nothing is priced by the letter. The unit being counted is the token, so the question is how many tokens each word turns into.

options.text: Technical prompts are routed to a larger model, which charges a higher rate
options.feedback: The count does not depend on which model reads the text. The same passage breaks into the same pieces either way, and it is those pieces that are counted.

options.text: Unfamiliar words take the model longer to read, and cost follows time
options.feedback: Cost is counted in tokens, not seconds. A rare word is not read slowly; it simply arrives as several pieces instead of one.

options.text: Rare words are split into several sub-word pieces, and each piece is a token
options.feedback: Common words get a token to themselves, while rare ones are assembled from fragments shared with other words. The same number of words can be a very different number of tokens, and tokens are what limits and costs count.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: When a model answers your question, there are only two places its answer can draw on. What are they?

options.text: What you put in the context, and what training left in its weights
options.feedback: Attention reaches everything in front of the model right now, and the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) supplies what training compressed into the weights. There is no third source, which is why the context is the lever you have.

options.text: What you put in the context, and whatever it can look up while answering
options.feedback: Looking something up would need a search step, and the model as described has none: context in, one token out. Anything not in the context has to come from the weights.

options.text: Its weights, and a record of the conversations you have had with it before
options.feedback: Nothing from an earlier conversation reaches the model unless it is in this context. The weights do not change while you chat, and no transcript is kept inside the model.

options.text: The training text kept inside it, and the prompt you just typed
options.feedback: The training text is not kept. It was compressed into weights, lossy like a JPEG image, so there is nothing to reread. And your prompt is only one part of the context.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: To build intuition for embeddings, the lecture asked how you would specify where you are standing in the classroom: distance from one wall, distance from another, and height. How does that picture scale up to a token embedding?

options.text: The token gets thousands of coordinates rather than three
options.feedback: Three numbers pin down one spot in a room. A token embedding pins down one spot in a space with thousands of dimensions, and that spot is what the token means.

options.text: The three numbers become the token's id, length, and frequency
options.feedback: Those are facts about the token, not coordinates of meaning. The embedding's numbers are coordinates, and it takes thousands of them to place a word among its neighbors.

options.text: Each token gets three numbers, for grammar, meaning, and style
options.feedback: Three labeled dimensions would be far too few, and the dimensions are not hand-labeled. The space has thousands of dimensions, learned during training.

options.text: Each number records the distance to one specific other token
options.feedback: Dimensions are not distances to particular words. They are coordinates, like distance from a wall; distances between tokens are computed from those coordinates afterward.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Nobody sat down and decided that "queen" should sit near "king." So how did the embedding space come to be arranged by meaning?

options.text: Linguists supplied a map of which words mean similar things, and the space was built from it
options.feedback: Hand-built resources like that do exist, but a model does not use one. Nobody writes anything down for it: it has to work out what words mean in order to guess the next one well.

options.text: The positions were copied out of a dictionary, one entry at a time
options.feedback: A dictionary explains words with other words, which is no use to a network that can only take numbers. The positions have to be numbers that already carry meaning.

options.text: The model arranged it during training, because grouping similar words made its guesses better
options.feedback: Training is nothing but hide the next word, guess, adjust. Words that behave alike have to end up in the same region for those guesses to improve, so the arrangement is a by-product of the guessing rather than a design.

options.text: The words start at random positions, and attention spreads them out during the response
options.feedback: Attention does move a token's meaning, but only within one sentence and only after the embedding is in place. "King" starts among monarchs every time, which it could not do if the positions were random.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The token "king" has one embedding whether it appears in "the king of France" or in "King me." What does that tell you about what the embedding can and cannot capture?

options.text: It captures everything about the word, so both sentences are read the same way
options.feedback: The sentences are not read the same way in the end, or the model could never handle the checkers sense. The embedding is where reading starts, not where it ends.

options.text: It captures the sentence's grammar but not the word's meaning
options.feedback: It is the reverse: the embedding is all about the word's usual meaning and knows nothing about the sentence it landed in.

options.text: It captures nothing useful until the other words have been considered
options.feedback: It captures plenty: "king" starts among monarchs, which is right most of the time. What it cannot do is tell when this particular sentence is the exception.

options.text: It captures the word's usual meaning but not its meaning in this sentence
options.feedback: The embedding is a location chosen without looking at neighboring words, so it holds the typical meaning. Working out the meaning in context is the job of the decoder stacks that follow.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student notices that in one model's vocabulary, "king" is token number 4,127 and "queen" is token number 4,128, and concludes that the model must know the two words are related. What is wrong with that reasoning?

options.text: Nothing; consecutive numbers are how the model records related words
options.feedback: Ids are handed out by the tokenizer without any regard for meaning. Two words could be neighbors by id and unrelated, or related and thousands of ids apart.

options.text: Ids carry no meaning; relatedness shows up as nearby embeddings
options.feedback: The number is just a label used to look up the embedding. Meaning only appears once the id is mapped to a location in the semantic space, and there "king" and "queen" really are close.

options.text: The model never uses those id numbers, so nothing can follow from them
options.feedback: The id does get used: it is the label the embedding is fetched by, so it is not idle. What it cannot do is carry meaning, which is why two neighboring ids tell you nothing about the two words.

options.text: "King" and "queen" are not related in the model, so the conclusion is false
options.feedback: The conclusion happens to be true -- "queen" sits right beside "king", along with "monarch" and "crown". It is the evidence that fails, because relatedness cannot be read off the id numbers.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student reads "She looked across the board and said, triumphantly, 'King me'" and says the embedding for "king" must already encode the checkers meaning, since the model gets the sentence right. Which idea from the lecture corrects this?

options.text: The embedding for "king" holds every possible sense, and the app selects the right one
options.feedback: An embedding is one location, not a bundle of senses. And no app does the selecting; the shift toward the checkers meaning happens inside the model, after the embedding.

options.text: The tokenizer gives "king" a different token when it is used as a verb
options.feedback: Tokenization works on spelling, not on grammatical role. "King" is the same token in both sentences, and so it starts with the same embedding.

options.text: The embedding is only a first guess, fixed before the surrounding words have any effect
options.feedback: On its own, "king" lands among monarchs and crowns, and that is where the embedding puts it in this sentence too. Getting to the checkers meaning takes the rest of the model, working from the surrounding words.

options.text: The model looked up "king me" in a stored list of idioms
options.feedback: There is no list of idioms. Meaning is a location, and the model gets to the checkers reading by moving that location, not by matching a phrase against a table.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: According to the lecture, what are the two components found inside every decoder stack?

options.text: A token encoder and a table of token embeddings
options.feedback: Encoding and embedding happen before the stacks, turning text into numbers and numbers into locations in semantic space. The stacks take those embeddings as input and work on them.

options.text: An attention layer and an MLP (multi-layer perceptron)
options.feedback: Attention uses the surrounding words to move each token's meaning into context, and the MLP then nudges it further using what the model learned about the world. Every stack has both, and a model has many stacks in a row.

options.text: An attention layer and a temperature setting
options.feedback: Temperature is the noise added at the very end, when one token is picked from the probabilities; it does not live inside the stacks. The second half of each stack is the MLP (multi-layer perceptron), which carries world knowledge.

options.text: An embedding layer and a next-token probability layer
options.feedback: Embeddings come in at the front of the pipeline and probabilities come out the back, so it is tempting to put them inside the stacks. What actually sits in each stack is attention plus an MLP (multi-layer perceptron).

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: For a single token, what does the attention layer actually compute?

options.text: A lookup of the token's meaning in the knowledge the model stored during training
options.feedback: Stored knowledge is the job of the MLP (multi-layer perceptron), and even there nothing is looked up. Attention does not consult knowledge at all; it works with the embeddings of the words already in the context.

options.text: A copy of the embedding of the single earlier word that is most closely related to it
options.feedback: Attention does not pick one word and copy it. It blends every earlier token, giving more weight to the ones that matter, so "board" and "triumphantly" both pull on "king" at once.

options.text: A weighted average of every earlier token's embedding, weighting the ones that matter
options.feedback: That average is what lets the surrounding words move a token's meaning: "board" and "triumphantly" get heavy weight and drag "king" toward board games. The lecture's phrase for it is averaging the information to get you in about the right place.

options.text: A small amount of random noise so the same prompt can give different answers
options.feedback: Noise is added once, at the end, when a token is chosen from the probabilities, and it is controlled by temperature. Attention is deterministic: the same context always produces the same weighted average.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In "She looked across the board and said, triumphantly, 'King me,'" which earlier words does attention weight most heavily when it moves the meaning of "king"?

options.text: "board" and "triumphantly"
options.feedback: Those two words are the ones that tell you this is a game and someone is winning, so attention gives them the most weight in the average it builds for "king". The result lands "king" among board games rather than monarchs.

options.text: "She" and "said"
options.feedback: The subject and the speech verb tell you someone is talking, but nothing about what kind of "king" this is. Attention weights words by how much they matter to the token in question, and these matter little.

options.text: "me", the word that follows
options.feedback: "me" does help settle the meaning once you read the whole sentence, but attention for "king" looks back over the tokens before it, not after. It has to do its work with "board" and "triumphantly", which is enough.
