options.text: "looked" and "across"
options.feedback: These sit right next to "board" and it is easy to lump them together, but on their own they could describe looking across a room or a street. The word that carries the game meaning is "board", and the word that carries the winning is "triumphantly".

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Why does the meaning of "king" need to be moved at all when the model reads "King me"?

options.text: Because the embedding for "king" is random until attention assigns it a meaning of its own
options.feedback: The embedding is not random; it is a learned location in semantic space, and for "king" that location sits among queen, monarch, and crown. The problem is that this location is a first guess made without looking at any other word.

options.text: Because the model has never seen this exact sentence in its training text
options.feedback: The model does not need to have met a sentence before; it works out meaning from the words that are present. What makes the move necessary is that the embedding for "king" was fixed before any of those words were read.

options.text: Because the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) has not yet had a chance to see the word
options.feedback: The MLP acts after attention, using what it learned in training, so it is not what makes the initial embedding a poor fit here. The embedding is off because it was chosen before any context was read.

options.text: Because the embedding is a first guess, made with no context, and that guess is royalty
options.feedback: The token embedding places "king" among monarchs and crowns, since that is what "king" usually means. Attention exists precisely to correct first guesses like this one using the words around it.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture summarized attention as "averaging the information to get you in about the right place." What is the "place" in that description?

options.text: The token's position in the sequence of words that make up the sentence
options.feedback: Word order does matter to attention, but the place being described is not a position in the text. It is a location in semantic space, the same space where king - man + woman lands near queen.

options.text: A location in semantic space near the word's meaning in this context
options.feedback: The averaged embedding is a new location, moved from where the token started toward where the context says it belongs. It is only "about" the right place because later layers, including the MLP (multi-layer perceptron), refine it further.

options.text: The entry for the word in the model's fixed vocabulary list
options.feedback: The vocabulary maps a token to a number, and that number never changes. Attention works on the embedding, a location in a space with thousands of dimensions, not on the vocabulary index.

options.text: The single most probable next token in the vocabulary
options.feedback: Probabilities over the next token come out at the very end, after all the stacks. Attention happens inside each stack and produces a refined embedding, not a prediction.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Besides which earlier words matter most, what else is the attention layer sensitive to when it builds its weighted average?

options.text: How often each word appeared in training
options.feedback: Training frequency shapes what the model knows, which lives in the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) and the embeddings, but it is not something attention weighs in the moment. Attention responds to the words in the context and how they are arranged.

options.text: How many times each word is repeated in the context
options.feedback: Repetition is not what the weighting measures. Attention weights a word by how much it matters to the token being resolved, and a word that appears once can matter far more than one that appears five times.

options.text: The order the words came in
options.feedback: The same words in a different order can mean something different, and the grammatical slot "king" sits in is part of what told the room it was a verb. Attention keeps track of order as it averages.

options.text: How many decoder stacks the model has
options.feedback: The number of stacks is what makes a model large or small, and it changes how much refining happens overall. It is not an input to any single attention layer.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: How far can attention reach when it gathers information to shape a token's meaning?

options.text: Over everything in front of the model, including documents you pasted in
options.feedback: Attention looks back across the whole context, so a document you attach or a fact you stated earlier in the conversation can pull on the meaning of a word later on. That is why what you put in front of the model can override what it learned in training.

options.text: Over the sentence the token belongs to, stopping at the period
options.feedback: It is natural to think of disambiguation as a sentence-level job, but attention is not fenced in by punctuation. The whole context, including earlier turns and attachments, is available to it.

options.text: Over the handful of words immediately before the token in question
options.feedback: Nearby words often matter most and get heavy weight, which makes this tempting. But attention takes its weighted average over every earlier token, however far back it sits.

options.text: Over what the model absorbed about the world during training
options.feedback: What was absorbed in training is the territory of the MLP (multi-layer perceptron). Attention does the opposite job: it draws on what is in front of the model right now.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Consider: "After the storm, the river rose so fast that water spilled over the bank and flooded the road." To move "bank" away from its money meaning, which words would attention weight most heavily?

options.text: "After" and "so"
options.feedback: These connect the clauses but carry nothing about rivers or money. Attention gives weight in proportion to how much a word matters to the one being resolved, and function words like these get little.

options.text: "spilled" alone, because verbs matter most
options.feedback: The verb helps, but attention does not privilege one part of speech. It averages across all the earlier words, and the nouns "river" and "water" are the ones that pin down this "bank".

options.text: Every earlier word equally
options.feedback: An equal average would let "After", "the", and "so" dilute the signal from "river" and "water". The whole point of the weighting is that some words count for much more than others.

options.text: "river" and "water"
options.feedback: Those words put the sentence firmly by a river, and their embeddings, averaged in with heavy weight, drag "bank" out of finance and toward riverbanks. This is the same move that took "king" from monarchs to checkers.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Nobody loaded a list of facts into the model, yet it can tell you the capital of Australia. Why does training on next-word guessing alone leave the model knowing things about the world?

options.text: Because a fact sheet is assembled from the training text and stored alongside the weights
options.feedback: No fact sheet is built at any point. Training only ever compares a guess with the word that was actually there and adjusts the parameters.

options.text: Because the model was given a reference work to read before its ordinary training began
options.feedback: There is no reading list and no first stage of that kind. Every sentence in training is handled the same way: hide the next word, guess, adjust.

options.text: Because you cannot guess the next word well without absorbing what the text is about
options.feedback: Text about Australia can only be continued sensibly by something that has picked up what is said about Australia. Facts, grammar, and style are all learned as a side effect of being scored on the next word.

options.text: Because the model keeps the sentences it guessed correctly and reuses them later
options.feedback: Nothing is kept. A correct guess produces no record and no stored sentence, only a set of parameters that were already good enough to leave alone.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A model reads "She finished her sales pitch and waited" in one conversation and "After a week of rain, the muddy pitch was unplayable" in another, and handles "pitch" correctly both times. Which idea from the lecture explains this?

options.text: The model has two separate tokens, one for each of the two meanings of "pitch"
options.feedback: A token is just a number for a string of characters, so both sentences hand the model the same token. The difference arises afterwards, when the embedding is moved by context.

options.text: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) stores a definition for each meaning and selects one
options.feedback: The MLP holds no definitions and does no selecting; it is weight matrices that nudge an embedding along. The sentence-by-sentence difference comes from attention, which reads the surrounding words.

options.text: Attention lets the surrounding words move "pitch" to a different place in each sentence
options.feedback: Attention averages in the tokens that came before, so "sales" pulls the embedding toward persuasion while "rain" and "muddy" pull it toward a playing field. Same starting embedding, different weighted average, different meaning.

options.text: The model memorized both sentences during training
options.feedback: Training teaches the model to guess the next word, not to store sentences. Even for a sentence it has never seen, attention can use the words present to settle what "pitch" means.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Suppose a model had no attention layers at all. What would happen to the meaning of "king" in "She looked across the board and said, triumphantly, 'King me'"?

options.text: It would stay where the embedding put it, among monarchs, whatever the surrounding words said
options.feedback: The embedding is a first guess made in isolation, and attention is the only mechanism that lets the other words move it. Without attention, "board" and "triumphantly" would have no way to reach "king".

options.text: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) would use the surrounding words to move it toward checkers instead
options.feedback: The MLP works only on the embedding it is handed and applies what it learned in training; it does not read the other words in the context. Gathering from the context is attention's job, and nothing else does it.

options.text: The token encoding would switch to the verb form of "king" to compensate
options.feedback: Token encoding assigns the same number to "king" regardless of sense, and it happens before any meaning is worked out. It cannot respond to context.

options.text: The model would be unable to produce a next token for the sentence
options.feedback: The pipeline would still run and still produce probabilities; it would just do so with a poor sense of what each word means here. The failure would be a worse guess, not no guess.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The model is working on the word "crane" in "Wading through the marsh, the tall gray crane stretched its neck." Which words can attention draw on for that token?

options.text: Every word in the sentence, since the model takes the sentence in as a whole
options.feedback: The whole sentence is in the context, but attention for a given token averages over the tokens that came before it. "Neck" has not been reached yet when "crane" is being resolved.

options.text: Only the words that come before it in the context
options.feedback: Attention looks back: for each token it takes a weighted average of the tokens already in front of it. That is why "wading", "marsh", and "gray" can move "crane" toward the bird and "neck" cannot.

options.text: Only the handful of words sitting closest to it
options.feedback: Nearby words often carry the most weight, but nothing fences attention into a window. It reaches back over the whole context, including a document you attached earlier.

options.text: Only the words the model has produced so far in its own reply
options.feedback: The model's own output does join the context as it goes, but so does everything you supplied. For a token in your sentence, attention draws on the earlier words of that sentence.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What does the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) in a decoder stack contribute?

options.text: What the model learned about the world during training
options.feedback: The MLP is where world knowledge lives: it is what knows that you king someone in checkers, not chess, and that "king me" is said when winning. It applies that knowledge by nudging the embedding attention handed it.

options.text: A weighted average of the earlier words in the context
options.feedback: That is attention, the first half of the stack. The MLP takes attention's output and adds what the model already knew before it read this context.

options.text: The random noise that varies the model's answers
options.feedback: Noise enters once, at the end, when one token is picked from the probabilities, and it is set by temperature. The MLP is deterministic and runs inside every stack.

options.text: The number assigned to each token in the vocabulary
options.feedback: Assigning numbers is token encoding, which happens before anything else. The MLP works far downstream, on embeddings that attention has already shaped.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Which of these best describes what the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) is made of?

options.text: A table of words paired with their definitions and usages
options.feedback: A table would let the model look meanings up, but the lecture is emphatic that there are no words stored in the MLP and nothing to look up. What it holds is numeric, learned in training.

options.text: A search index over the text the model was trained on
options.feedback: If training text were indexed, the model could quote it back exactly, and it cannot. Training text is compressed into weights, lossy like a JPEG, not stored for retrieval.

options.text: Numeric weights, learned in training, that shift an embedding along
options.feedback: Given the embedding attention just produced, those numbers push it further toward what the model picked up in training. Nothing is looked up; the knowledge is baked into the numbers themselves.

options.text: A list of grammar rules the model was given before training
options.feedback: Nobody hands the model rules; it learns grammar along with everything else by guessing the next word. And what it learns is stored as weights, not as a list.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Where does the knowledge in the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) come from?

options.text: From the documents you paste into the context
options.feedback: What you paste is read through attention, not stored in the MLP. The MLP's contents were fixed when training ended, before you ever typed a prompt.

options.text: From what the model absorbed during training
options.feedback: The MLP's weights were set by trillions of next-word guesses over an enormous body of text. Everything it knows about checkers, or anything else, was picked up that way.

options.text: From an internet search the model runs while answering
options.feedback: The model as described in the lecture does not search anything; it takes a context and produces one token. Knowledge that is not in the context has to come from the weights.

options.text: From the token embeddings, which already hold the facts
options.feedback: An embedding is a first guess at a single word's meaning, a location in semantic space. Knowing which game you say "king me" in is far more than a word's location, and that lives in the MLP.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture called the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) "a fuzzy JPEG of the world." What is the point of that comparison?

options.text: Pictures of the things the model read about in its training text
options.feedback: The comparison is about compression, not images. A JPEG stands in for any lossy copy: it keeps the gist and loses detail, which is what happens to training text on its way into the weights.

options.text: An exact, uncompressed copy of the training text, ready to be reproduced on demand
options.feedback: An exact copy is what a JPEG is not. The whole reason to reach for the metaphor is that the MLP loses information, keeping some parts sharp and letting others blur.

options.text: A picture the model consults whenever it needs to check a fact
options.feedback: Consulting would be a lookup, and the MLP does not do lookups. The JPEG image is about what the weights are like, a compressed and imperfect picture, not about how they are used.

options.text: A compressed, lossy picture of the world, sharp in places and blurry in others
options.feedback: Like a JPEG, the MLP compresses an enormous amount of information and loses some of it. Topics heavily represented in training stay sharp; rare details blur.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) was described as a picture that is sharp in some places and blurry in others. According to the lecture, what decides which parts are sharp?

options.text: How heavily a topic appeared in the training text
options.feedback: Topics the model saw again and again during training end up sharply rendered in the weights; topics it saw rarely end up fuzzy. The rules of checkers are sharp; the details of one historical checkers match are not.

options.text: How recently the topic appeared in the news or online
options.feedback: Recency does not enter the picture; what matters is how much of the training text was about the topic. A very old but much-discussed subject can be sharp while a recent obscure one is blurry.

options.text: How long and detailed the user's prompt is
options.feedback: The prompt is read through attention and can add detail the MLP lacks, but it does not change what is in the MLP. Sharp and blurry describe the weights fixed at training time.

options.text: How confidently the model words its answer on that topic
options.feedback: Fluent, confident wording is what the model produces everywhere, blurry regions included, so it tells you nothing about how much it holds. Sharpness is set by how much of the training text covered the topic.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A model explains the rules of checkers accurately but gets the details of a specific nineteenth-century championship match wrong. Which idea from the lecture explains this?

options.text: Attention failed to weight the right words in the prompt
options.feedback: If the match details were in the prompt, attention would pull them in. The trouble here is that they were never in the context, so the model had to fall back on what its weights hold, and for this match that is not much.

options.text: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) is lossy: common topics sharp, rare details blurry
options.feedback: The rules of checkers appear all over the training text, so they are rendered sharply in the weights. One old match barely appears, so the weights hold only a blur, and the model fills it in plausibly rather than accurately.

options.text: The entry for that match in the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) was corrupted or lost
options.feedback: There are no entries in the MLP to corrupt; it is not a database with a row per fact. The detail was never stored crisply in the first place, because it was too rare in training to leave a sharp trace.

options.text: The temperature was set too high for factual questions
options.feedback: Temperature adds a little noise to the final choice, but it cannot invent knowledge that is not there or destroy knowledge that is. The gap here is in what the weights hold.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A classmate says, "When I asked for the capital of Australia, the model looked it up in its memory." What is wrong with that picture of the MLP (multi-layer perceptron)?

options.text: Nothing; that is exactly how the MLP works when it answers
options.feedback: Looking up implies a stored record to find, and the MLP has none. Its weights nudge an embedding toward "Canberra" because training text about Australia shaped them that way, which is a very different thing from retrieval.

options.text: It was attention, not the MLP, that did the lookup in memory
options.feedback: Attention draws on what is in the context, and the capital was not in the prompt. But attention does not look things up either; nothing in the model does. The answer came from the MLP's compressed picture of the world.

options.text: There is nothing to look up: the MLP is weights, not stored facts
options.feedback: The MLP is a set of weight matrices, and the fact emerges from them as a nudge on the embedding, not as a record read back. That is why the answer is reliable for well-covered facts and shaky for rare ones.

options.text: The fact lives in the token embeddings rather than in the MLP
options.feedback: An embedding is one word's location in semantic space, a first guess at meaning. Connecting a country to its capital is world knowledge, and that is what the MLP holds.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A model has dozens of decoder stacks in sequence. What does that sequence accomplish that a single stack could not?

options.text: Each stack handles a different word, so more stacks means the model can read longer prompts
options.feedback: Every stack processes every token; the stacks are layers, not slots. How much text you can put in front of the model is a matter of token limits, not of how many stacks it has.

options.text: The first stack does all the real work and the later ones only check it for errors
options.feedback: No stack is a checker. Each one applies attention and its MLP (multi-layer perceptron) to the embedding it receives, moving it a bit further, and none of them can see the whole job.

options.text: Each stack stores a different subject area, like the chapters of an encyclopedia
options.feedback: Knowledge is not filed by stack; it is spread across the weights of many MLPs (multi-layer perceptrons). Stacks differ by how far along the refinement they sit, not by topic.

options.text: Each stack refines the embedding a bit; many in a row turn a rough guess into a rich meaning
options.feedback: One stack moves a token's meaning only part of the way. Attention and the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) repeat, stack after stack, until "king" is not just a verb in a game but a checkers move made by someone who is winning.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Within a decoder stack, attention runs first and the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) second. Why does that order make sense?

options.text: The MLP works on what attention hands it, so the meaning in context has to be settled first
options.feedback: The MLP nudges whatever embedding it is handed. If "king" still sat among monarchs, the MLP would push it toward royal facts; once attention has moved it toward board games, the MLP can add that the game is checkers.

options.text: Attention needs the MLP's facts to decide which words matter, so the MLP has to be ready
options.feedback: Attention weights words using their embeddings and positions, not stored facts. It works out that "board" and "triumphantly" matter without knowing anything about checkers.

options.text: The order does not matter, since both layers do the same kind of averaging over the context
options.feedback: They do different things: attention averages across the context, and the MLP applies weights learned in training to one embedding. Feeding the MLP an uncorrected first guess would send its nudge in the wrong direction.

options.text: The MLP picks the word's meaning and attention then confirms it against the context
options.feedback: This has the roles backwards. Attention is what reads the context; the MLP cannot see the other words at all, so it could not choose a meaning for "king" on its own.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture asked whether JPEG is the format you would choose for archiving a photograph, and answered no. What does that answer imply about the MLP (multi-layer perceptron)?

options.text: It should be replaced by a proper database as models improve
options.feedback: The lossy, compressed form is not a defect to be engineered away; it is how a neural network holds what it learned. Larger models make the picture sharper, but it stays a picture, not a database.

options.text: You should not expect it to preserve every detail it was trained on exactly
options.feedback: Archiving demands a lossless copy, and a JPEG throws detail away to save space. The MLP does the same with training text, which is why it can be confidently vague on specifics.

options.text: It compresses your prompt before reading it, losing some of what you wrote
options.feedback: Your prompt is not compressed; attention can draw on all of it. The compression happened long before, when training text was squeezed into the weights.

options.text: It keeps a low-resolution copy of each conversation it has had
options.feedback: The MLP does not change between conversations, and it stores nothing from them. What is low-resolution is its picture of the training data, fixed once training ended.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Making the model bigger was the field's whole strategy for several years. Why does a much larger model still produce confidently wrong answers?

options.text: Because the extra decoder stacks introduce small errors that build up
options.feedback: Stacks do not accumulate error that way; each one refines the representation a little further. Size changes how much the model knows, not how carefully it computes.

options.text: Because a bigger model is trained on less text, so its coverage is thinner
options.feedback: The bigger models were trained on far more text, not less. Parameters and training text grew together, which is how the picture got sharper at all.

options.text: Because a bigger picture of the world is still a lossy one, and nothing checks for truth
options.feedback: Scaling adds resolution, so fewer topics sit in the blurry region. It adds no step that tests an answer, so the model is still producing the most probable continuation, and probable is not the same as true.

options.text: Because larger models lean on the context and ignore what they learned in training
options.feedback: Both sizes use both sources: attention reads the context and the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) supplies what training left behind. A larger model has more of the second, not less.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In "She looked across the board and said, triumphantly, 'King me,'" the model works out that this is a checkers move made by someone who is winning. Which part of that came from the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) rather than from attention?

options.text: That "board" is an earlier word worth weighting heavily in the average
options.feedback: Deciding which earlier words matter is attention's job; it is the weighting that builds the average. The MLP never sees the other words at all.

options.text: That "king" is being used as a verb in a game
options.feedback: This is what attention establishes by averaging in "board", "triumphantly", and the grammatical slot. It gets you into board-game territory without yet knowing which game.

options.text: That "king" sits near "queen" and "monarch"
options.feedback: That neighborhood is the token embedding's first guess, made before any context is read. It is where "king" starts, not something either layer of the stack adds.

options.text: That the game is checkers and you say "king me" when winning
options.feedback: Nothing in the sentence names the game, so this cannot come from the context. It has to come from what the model absorbed in training, and that is what the MLP holds.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A friend says a model must have a copy of Wikipedia stored inside it, since it can answer so many of the questions Wikipedia answers. Based on the lecture, what is the more accurate picture?

options.text: It compressed everything it read into weights: a lossy picture, not stored text
options.feedback: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) holds no articles, only weights shaped by training. That is why the model is sharp on widely covered subjects and blurry on obscure ones, which a stored copy would never be.

options.text: It contains the text, but zipped, so it can be unpacked exactly whenever it is needed
options.feedback: A zip file is lossless, and the lecture's metaphor is deliberately a JPEG, which is not. If the model could unpack its training text exactly, it would never be fuzzy on rare details, and it is.

options.text: It stores only the articles people ask about most often
options.feedback: Nothing is stored article by article, and the model keeps no record of what it was asked. What varies is how sharply a topic is rendered in the weights, set by how much training text covered it.

options.text: It fetches the relevant article through attention each time it is asked a question
options.feedback: Attention reaches only what is in the context in front of the model. Unless you paste the article in, it is not there to fetch, and the answer comes from the weights instead.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: After the embeddings have passed through the final decoder stack, what does the model produce from the last position?

options.text: The one correct next word, looked up from the vocabulary
options.feedback: Nothing in the model looks a word up, and nothing in it knows which word is correct. The output is a spread of probabilities across the whole vocabulary, and choosing one token is a separate step that comes afterward.

options.text: A probability for every token in the vocabulary
options.feedback: The rich, contextualized representation at the last position is turned into a probability for each token the model knows, tens of thousands of them. Only after that spread exists does anything choose the next token, which is where temperature comes in.

options.text: A probability for only the tokens that fit the grammar
options.feedback: Grammar does shape the probabilities, which is why a noun after "on" scores well. But the model does not first filter the vocabulary; it assigns every token a probability, and the ungrammatical ones simply get numbers near zero.

options.text: A ranked list of its ten best candidate words
options.feedback: Some chat tools display a short list of alternatives, which makes this tempting. The model itself does not stop at ten; it produces a probability for every token in the vocabulary, and a top-ten view is just a slice of that.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: For the context "She looked across the board and said triumphantly, 'King ...'", which description of the resulting token probabilities is right?

options.text: "me" gets the highest probability and "cat" gets a moderate one, since it is a common noun
options.feedback: Overall word frequency is not what decides the probabilities at this point. By the last stack the representation carries that "king" is a verb in checkers with a winner speaking, and "cat" fits none of that, so its probability is essentially zero, however common a word it is.

options.text: "checkers" gets the highest probability and "cat" gets zero
options.feedback: The model has worked out that the game is checkers, but that is not the same as predicting the word "checkers" next. "King" here is a transitive verb that needs an object, and the winner says "King me," so "me" is the token that wins.

options.text: "me" gets the highest probability and "cat" is dropped from the vocabulary
options.feedback: The vocabulary is fixed; no token is ever removed from it during generation. "Cat" stays in the vocabulary and receives a probability like every other token; that probability is just essentially zero here.

options.text: "me" gets the highest probability and "cat" gets essentially zero
options.feedback: By the last position the representation knows the verb is transitive, the game is checkers, and the speaker is winning, so "me" dominates. "Cat" is still in the vocabulary and still gets a number, but that number is as close to zero as makes no difference.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture says that all the transformer does is produce a probability distribution over the tokens. What does that tell you about how the actual next word gets picked?

options.text: Picking a token is a separate step that happens after the transformer has finished
options.feedback: The transformer's job ends at the distribution. Choosing one token from it, with a little noise added, is a step outside the transformer, and that separation is what makes temperature a setting you can change without touching the model.

options.text: The transformer picks the word and then reports how confident it was
options.feedback: It is easy to imagine the choice coming first and the probability being a confidence score attached to it. The order is the reverse: the probabilities come out of the transformer, and only then does something choose a token from them.

options.text: The transformer writes several candidate sentences and keeps the best one
options.feedback: The model generates one token at a time, not whole sentences to compare. What it produces at each step is a spread of probabilities over single tokens, and one is chosen before the next step begins.

options.text: The transformer checks the distribution against a table of facts before choosing
options.feedback: There is no table of facts anywhere in the pipeline. The distribution is the end of the transformer's work, and nothing downstream checks it for truth, which is exactly why a plausible answer and a correct one can differ.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Given the context "She looked across the board and said triumphantly, 'King ...'", why does the model give "me" far more probability than "cat"?

options.text: Because "me" is a more frequent word than "cat" in English as a whole
options.feedback: Raw frequency is what the model would fall back on with no context at all. Here the context has done its work: by the last stack the representation has been moved to a place where a winner in checkers is speaking, and that, not frequency, is what lifts "me."

options.text: Because the model stores "King me" as a fixed phrase and retrieves it
options.feedback: That is the database picture, and the lecture rules it out. Nothing is stored as words to be retrieved; the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) is a fuzzy JPEG that nudges an embedding, and the probabilities are computed fresh from the contextualized representation.

options.text: Because the representation now carries that this is a checkers verb spoken by a winner
options.feedback: Attention moved "king" out of monarch-space using "board" and "triumphantly," and the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) added that this is checkers and a winner speaks. The probability for "me" is what that fully contextualized representation yields.

options.text: Because "cat" is not one of the tokens in the model's vocabulary
options.feedback: "Cat" is certainly in the vocabulary of any model trained on English. It receives a probability like every token; the point is that the probability is essentially zero, not that the token is missing.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In the lecture, what is the temperature setting?

options.text: A little noise added before the next token is chosen from the probabilities
options.feedback: Temperature is the small nudge applied at the very end, when one token is picked from the distribution. It is what lets the model take a slightly different path through the same probabilities each time.

options.text: A filter that removes implausible tokens before the choice is made
options.feedback: Implausible tokens already have probabilities near zero, so nothing needs to filter them out. Temperature does the opposite of narrowing: it adds noise so that a less-than-top token sometimes gets chosen.

options.text: A dial that changes how much of the context attention reads
options.feedback: Attention always looks back over the whole context, and no setting shortens that. Temperature acts after every stack has finished, at the moment of choosing a token, not while meaning is being computed.

options.text: A setting for how many decoder stacks the embedding passes through
options.feedback: The number of decoder stacks is fixed by the model's architecture, and it is part of what makes a model large or small. Temperature touches none of that; it only affects the final choice of a token.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Up to the point where the token probabilities are produced, how does the model behave from one run to the next?

options.text: Randomly, because the embeddings start from a fresh position each run
options.feedback: Embeddings are learned during training and then fixed; a token lands in the same location every time. Nothing before the probabilities is random, which is why the variation has to be added on purpose at the end.

options.text: Randomly, because attention samples which earlier tokens to look at
options.feedback: Attention computes a weighted average over every earlier token; it does not sample a subset. The whole path from context to probabilities is a fixed computation with no dice in it.

options.text: Deterministically, so a repeated context produces the identical spread of probabilities
options.feedback: Everything from token encoding through the last decoder stack is a fixed calculation, so identical context gives identical probabilities. The variety you see in answers is introduced afterward, when noise is added at the choice step.

options.text: Deterministically, but only when no noise is added at the choice step
options.feedback: Noise is added after the probabilities exist, so it cannot reach back and change them. The stages before the choice compute the same way whether or not noise is applied later; only which token gets picked varies.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Why would a model that always took the single most likely token tend to produce flat, repetitive text?

options.text: Because the most likely token is usually the wrong one
options.feedback: The most likely token is a perfectly good guess most of the time; that is what makes it the most likely. The problem is not accuracy but monotony: always taking the top choice never explores the many other reasonable continuations.

options.text: Because the model would soon run out of tokens in its vocabulary
options.feedback: The vocabulary never runs out; every token stays available at every step. The trouble with always taking the top choice is that the same well-worn words would keep winning, not that anything is used up.

options.text: Because the probabilities would drift and the model would lose the context
options.feedback: The probabilities do not drift; the same context gives the same probabilities every time. Repetition comes from the choice rule, not from any loss of context.

options.text: Because the same common words and phrasings would keep coming out on top
options.feedback: People repeat themselves, so the most ordinary wording sits at the top of the distribution again and again. Adding a little noise before choosing lets the model take a different path and explore, which is the whole reason for temperature.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: How can a small amount of noise at the moment of choosing a token lead to two whole answers that differ, rather than one word here and there?

options.text: The noise is added to every embedding, so the meaning of the prompt itself shifts
options.feedback: The embeddings and everything up to the probabilities are fixed; the noise enters only at the choice step. What makes it spread is not a changed prompt but the fact that each choice is fed back into the context.

options.text: Each chosen token joins the context, so one different choice steers every choice after it
options.feedback: Generation is autoregressive: the token just chosen is appended to the context and the whole model runs again. A slightly different word early on changes the context for the next word, and the paths diverge from there.

options.text: The model drafts the entire answer several times and returns a different draft each time
options.feedback: The model never holds several finished drafts; it produces one token at a time. The divergence builds up token by token because each choice shapes the next, not because whole answers are swapped.

options.text: The noise changes which stored answer the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) retrieves
options.feedback: The MLP stores no answers to retrieve; it is a fuzzy JPEG that nudges embeddings, and it runs the same way every time. The noise acts after the MLP, at the choice, and it spreads because chosen tokens become context.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student pastes a report into a chat and gets accurate answers about it. The next day she opens a fresh chat, asks about the same report without pasting it, and the answers are wrong. What explains the change?

options.text: The report was in the context the first time and is not in the context now
options.feedback: Everything the model works from has to be in front of it on this run. Attention could read the report while it sat in the context; in a new chat there is nothing there to read, so the model falls back on its fuzzy picture of the world.

options.text: The model forgot the report because too much time passed between the chats
options.feedback: Time has nothing to do with it. Nothing from the first chat was ever held, so there was nothing to fade; the context is assembled fresh for every request.

options.text: The model learned the report on the first day and then unlearned it
options.feedback: Nothing you paste changes the model's parameters, so there was no learning to undo. The document mattered only while it sat in the context.

options.text: The second chat was served by a smaller model with fewer parameters
options.feedback: The largest model available would do the same. Without the report in the context, no number of parameters supplies a document the model has never been shown.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student is using a model to fill in a standard form letter and wants the output to be as predictable and repeatable as possible. What should they do with the temperature?

options.text: Raise it, so the model is more confident in each choice
options.feedback: Temperature does not change the model's confidence; the probabilities are fixed before it acts. Raising it adds more noise to the choice, which makes the output wander more, the opposite of what this student wants.

options.text: Lower it, so less noise is added and the top token wins more often
options.feedback: Noise at the choice step is what lets the model walk a different path through the same probabilities. With less of it the top token wins nearly every time and the model retraces its route, so the flat, repetitive output the lecture describes is exactly what a form letter wants.

options.text: Leave it alone, since the same prompt already produces the same text every run
options.feedback: The probabilities are the same every run, but the choice is not: noise is added before a token is picked, so the same prompt normally gives differently worded answers. That is the variation this student is trying to reduce.

options.text: Lower it, so the model spends longer checking each answer
options.feedback: Nothing in the pipeline checks an answer, and temperature does not change how long the model runs; each token takes a full pass through the stacks either way. Lowering it changes which token wins the choice, not how carefully anything is done.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student asks a chatbot the same question in two fresh chats and gets different answers. They conclude that the model must be broken, or else remembering them from the first chat. What is actually going on?

options.text: The model is comparing the two chats and deliberately varying its wording
options.feedback: Fresh chats share nothing; the second run sees only its own context. The variation is not a deliberate comparison but the ordinary effect of noise at each token choice.

options.text: Noise at each token choice sends the model down a different path each time
options.feedback: Up to the probabilities the model is deterministic, and then temperature adds a little noise before choosing. That is intended, so that output is not flat and repetitive, and it means two runs of the same prompt normally differ.

options.text: The model's parameters shifted slightly as it learned from the first chat
options.feedback: The parameters are fixed once training ends; a chat does not teach the model anything that survives into the next one. What differs between the two runs is the path taken through the same probabilities, not the model itself.

options.text: A glitch in the decoder stacks produced slightly different probabilities
options.feedback: The decoder stacks give the same probabilities for the same context every time; there is no glitch to find there. The difference enters after the stacks, at the moment a token is chosen with a little noise.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What does the decoder transformer's mechanism actually select for when it produces its output?

options.text: Output that has been checked against a store of verified facts
options.feedback: There is no store of facts to check against; the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) is a fuzzy JPEG, not a database. No step in the pipeline verifies anything, which is why plausible and correct can come apart.

options.text: Output that matches its training documents word for word
options.feedback: Training taught the model to guess the next token well, not to reproduce any document. Its output is a fresh continuation drawn from probabilities, and it can produce sentences that appear nowhere in the training text.

options.text: Output that is the most cautious answer available
options.feedback: Nothing in the mechanism prefers caution; a confident-sounding wrong answer and a hedged right one are both just continuations. What is selected is the probable next token, whatever tone that carries.

options.text: Output that is a probable continuation of the context
options.feedback: The model was trained to guess the next token well, and that is the only thing it ever does. Nothing in the mechanism selects for true, which is why the lecture insists on plausible rather than correct.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: How does the lecture reframe what people call a hallucination?

options.text: As the model doing exactly what it always does, in a case where the context did not contain the answer
options.feedback: The same process produces every answer, right or wrong: a probable continuation drawn from the context and the fuzzy JPEG. When the context lacks the answer, the JPEG fills in something plausible, and that is what gets labeled a hallucination.

options.text: As a rare fault in the decoder stacks that better engineering will eventually remove
options.feedback: That treats hallucination as a bug, which is what the lecture pushes back on. The stacks are working normally when the model is wrong; they are producing a plausible continuation, and no fix to the mechanism changes what it selects for.

options.text: As what happens when the model's fact database returns the wrong entry
options.feedback: There is no fact database to return anything. The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) is a lossy JPEG of the world, and a wrong answer is the blurry part of that picture being read off as if it were sharp.

options.text: As a sign that the model was trained on false information
options.feedback: A model can be wrong about something its training text got right, because the JPEG is fuzzy where a topic was rare. The wrongness comes from the mechanism producing something plausible without the answer in context, not from bad training data.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: The lecture says the bad news about hallucination is that hallucinating is all the model ever does. What point is being made?

options.text: That the model cannot be trusted for any task and should not be used
options.feedback: The line is not a warning against using models; the rest of the course is about using them well. It is a description of the mechanism: the output is always a plausible continuation, so getting truth out of it depends on what you put in.

options.text: That the model hallucinates far more often than most people notice
options.feedback: The claim is not about frequency at all. It is that there is no second mode the model switches into when it is right; the process that produces a wrong answer is the same one that produces a right one.

options.text: That a right answer and a wrong one come from the identical process, with no truth mode
options.feedback: The model always produces a probable continuation; that is its whole job. A correct answer is the case where the plausible thing happened to be true, usually because the context or a sharp part of the JPEG supplied it.

options.text: That the model produces random text and only sometimes lands on sense
options.feedback: The output is far from random; it is the most probable continuation with a little noise added. The point is that probable is not the same as true, not that the model is guessing blindly.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Why can a document placed in the context override what the model learned in training?

options.text: Because the context is written into the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) alongside the training data
options.feedback: The MLP is fixed after training and nothing you type is written into it. The context enters through attention, which is a different path, and that path can carry evidence the MLP's fuzzy picture does not have.

options.text: Because attention reads the context, which can outweigh a blurry memory in the weights
options.feedback: Attention looks back over every token in the context, so a document you paste is directly available when the representation is built. The MLP then nudges from a lossy picture of the world, and sharp evidence in context can override a blurry memory.

options.text: Because the model briefly retrains itself on any document you upload
options.feedback: No training happens during a chat; the parameters do not move. The document works because attention reads it as part of the context, not because the model has learned it.

options.text: Because documents in the context are checked for accuracy before the model reads them
options.feedback: Nothing checks the context for truth; a wrong document in the context can override a right memory just as easily. What matters is that context is the evidence attention can draw on, whatever its accuracy.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student asks a model for sources on a niche topic and it returns a paper with a convincing title, authors, and journal that turns out not to exist. Which idea from the lecture explains this?

options.text: The model's citation database was out of date
options.feedback: There is no citation database; the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) stores no papers to look up. What the model has is a fuzzy picture of what citations on that topic look like, and it produced one that fits the picture.

options.text: The model glitched under a hard question and produced garbage
options.feedback: The output was not garbage; it was a well-formed, plausible citation, which is precisely the model working as designed. A hard question exposes the blurry part of the JPEG, but nothing malfunctioned.

options.text: The model found a real paper but mis-copied its details
options.feedback: The model does not find and copy; it generates a probable continuation token by token. On a niche topic the sharp parts of its picture run out, and it fills in a citation-shaped answer from the blur.

options.text: The model produced a citation-shaped answer from its fuzzy JPEG
options.feedback: A citation is a highly patterned kind of text, so the model can produce one that looks right without any real paper behind it. With no source in the context, the fuzzy JPEG supplied something probable, and nothing in the mechanism checks that it exists.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student asks a model for ten slogan ideas, runs the same prompt several times, and keeps getting nearly the same list. Based on the lecture, what would give more variety between runs?

options.text: Start each attempt in a new chat, so the model has a clean slate
options.feedback: A fresh chat changes what is in the context, which can change the answer, but from the same prompt the model would still take much the same path. What varies a run is the noise added when each token is chosen.

options.text: Lower the temperature, so the model weighs more options before choosing
options.feedback: Lower temperature does the opposite: with less noise the top token wins nearly every time and the model retraces the same path. That is what you want for a form letter, not for brainstorming.

options.text: Raise the temperature, so more noise is added when each token is chosen
options.feedback: With more noise at the choice step, a token that was not quite the top choice sometimes wins, and because each chosen token becomes context, the paths diverge from there. That is the exploring the lecture described.

options.text: Ask for fifty slogans instead of ten, so the model has to reach further
options.feedback: A longer list does push past the most obvious ideas within one answer, but nothing in the mechanism changes. How much the model wanders between runs is set by the noise at the choice step.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student asks a model about a company's refund policy and gets a wrong answer. They paste the policy document into the chat, ask again, and the answer is now right. Which idea explains the change?

options.text: The model learned the policy and updated its parameters
options.feedback: The parameters never change during a chat. The document made a difference because it was in the context for attention to read, and it will be forgotten as soon as it leaves the context.

options.text: The second attempt happened to run at a lower temperature
options.feedback: Temperature only decides which of the model's plausible paths gets taken, so it changes wording between runs. It cannot supply a fact the model never had, and no setting on the choice step would turn a made-up policy into the real one.

options.text: The policy was in the context, where attention could draw on it directly
options.feedback: The first time, the model filled in a probable-sounding policy from its lossy picture of the world. The second time, the real policy was in the context, attention could draw on it directly, and that evidence won out over the blur in the MLP (multi-layer perceptron).

options.text: The model recognized the document as official and switched into lookup mode
options.feedback: There is no lookup mode; the model runs the same pipeline either way. The document helped not because it was recognized as official but because it was in the context, where attention could use it to shape the representation.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: A student gets an answer that sounds right but turns out to be wrong. According to the lecture, what should they try first?

options.text: Switch to a larger model, since more parameters is what fixes wrong answers
options.feedback: The lecture does list a model that is not strong enough as one of the two possible causes, but calls it the far less likely one. Before changing models, check whether you gave the model any evidence to work from.

options.text: Put more evidence into the context, such as the relevant document
options.feedback: A wrong-but-plausible answer usually means the model was drawing on its fuzzy JPEG because the answer was not in the context. Attention can draw on anything you put there, and what is in the context can override what the model half-remembers.

options.text: Ask the model whether it is sure, so that it can check its facts
options.feedback: The model has no facts to check and no way to verify its own output; asking again produces another plausible continuation. The remedy is to give it the evidence, not to ask it to look inward.

options.text: Turn the temperature down so the model stops guessing
options.feedback: Temperature only affects which plausible path is taken; every path is a guess in the sense that matters. A lower temperature makes the same wrong answer more repeatable, not more correct.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What does the word "large" literally refer to in "large language model"?

options.text: A larger and more carefully checked collection of training facts
options.feedback: Large describes the model, not a curated set of facts; there is no fact collection inside it. The size is in the parameters: bigger MLPs (multi-layer perceptrons) and more decoder stacks.

options.text: A longer context window than a small model has
options.feedback: Context length is a separate matter, and the lecture treats context as the other half of the picture, not as what large means. The slide shows only one change for a large model: the boxes get taller.

options.text: Bigger MLPs (multi-layer perceptrons) and more decoder stacks
options.feedback: That is the whole difference between the small-model slide and the large-model one: taller boxes and more of them. More parameters means more room for a sharper JPEG of the world, up to hundreds of billions of parameters in the largest models.

options.text: A more advanced architecture than a small model uses
options.feedback: Small and large models use the identical architecture. The transformer introduced in 2017 is still the one in use; what changed is the scale, not the design.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: How does a small language model relate to a large one, according to the lecture?

options.text: The same architecture throughout, with fewer stacks and smaller layers inside them
options.feedback: A small model has the same attention-plus-MLP (multi-layer perceptron) stacks, just fewer of them and smaller. Its JPEG of the world is blurrier, and the trade is that it fits on hardware you carry, such as a laptop or a phone.

options.text: A simpler architecture that leaves out the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) layers to save space
options.feedback: Dropping the MLP would drop the model's world knowledge entirely, and no model does that. Small models keep every part of the architecture; each part is just smaller.

options.text: The same model with its vocabulary cut down to the most common words
options.feedback: The vocabulary is not where the size lives. What shrinks in a small model is the parameter count in the MLPs (multi-layer perceptrons) and the number of decoder stacks.

options.text: A large model with most of its decoder stacks skipped at run time to save memory
options.feedback: A small model is built and trained small; it is not a large one with parts switched off mid-run. It has fewer stacks and smaller MLPs (multi-layer perceptrons) from the start.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: Making the model bigger was the field's whole strategy for several years, and the lecture says that is only half of it. What does it point to as the other half?

options.text: Faster hardware, so the models can run more stacks in less time
options.feedback: Speed is not what the lecture points to; a faster model with the same fuzzy JPEG still produces the same plausible answers. The missing piece is what you give the model to work with.

options.text: Training only on facts that have been checked for accuracy
options.feedback: Better training data would still leave a lossy compression that is blurry wherever a topic was rare. The lecture's remedy for wrong answers is not cleaner training but evidence placed in front of the model.

options.text: Adding more noise at the choice step so the models explore further
options.feedback: Temperature gives variety between runs; it cannot supply anything the model does not know. The rest of the picture is about knowledge the model can draw on, not about the choice rule.

options.text: The context you give it, which attention can draw on directly
options.feedback: Scaling took the field from GPT-3 to the first Claude models, but a bigger JPEG is still fuzzy somewhere. Attention can draw on anything in the context, so getting the right material there is where the course goes next.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: What is the one-line definition of an agent given at the close of the session?

options.text: A model plus a much bigger context window
options.feedback: A large context helps, but it is only part of what the agent's context holds. The definition hinges on what the model can do, not on how much it can read.

options.text: Tools plus autonomy
options.feedback: An agent is a model that can call tools and has the freedom to keep looping until the job is done. Everything else in the picture, the working space, documents, memory, and skills, is the harness that supports that.

options.text: A large model and a small model working together
options.feedback: The size of the model is not what makes something an agent; a single model of any size can be one. What matters is that it can act through tools and decide to keep going.

options.text: Memory plus a task list
options.feedback: Memory and task lists are parts of the harness around the model, not the definition. They support an agent, but the defining pair is tools and autonomy.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In an agent product such as Claude Code, what role does the decoder transformer play relative to everything else in the product?

options.text: It is the whole product, and everything else is a chat window drawn around it
options.feedback: That is a fair description of a plain chat app, where the model really is nearly all there is. An agent product puts much more around the same model, while the model itself still does only what it always did: context in, one token out.

options.text: It has been replaced by a newer architecture designed for agents
options.feedback: The transformer from 2017 is still the model at the center, in an agent as much as in a chat. What is new around it is the harness, not the architecture inside.

options.text: It holds the working space, memory, and task lists inside its own weights
options.feedback: The weights are a fuzzy JPEG of the world and cannot hold your files or your task list. Those live outside the model, on disk, and reach it only when pulled into the context.

options.text: It is the small piece in the middle, with a harness built around it
options.feedback: The transformer still only does what it always does: context in, one token out. The harness gives it a place to work, documents to read, memory to keep, tasks to track, and a library of skills to load into its context.

questions.source: Quiz 1 - Sessions 1-2: The Decoder Transformer
questions.question: In the phrase "tools plus autonomy equals an agent," what does autonomy mean?

options.text: The model decides for itself which tools it is given
options.feedback: The tools come from the harness built around the model; the model chooses which of them to call, not which exist. Autonomy is about being allowed to keep working, not about supplying its own tools.

options.text: The model can decline tasks it decides are inappropriate
options.feedback: Refusing is a separate matter from autonomy in the lecture's sense. Autonomy here is the freedom to keep going, not the freedom to say no.

options.text: The model has the freedom to loop until the job is done
options.feedback: A chat model produces one response and stops; an agent can think, write code, call a tool, look at the result, and go again as many times as the task needs. That loop, combined with tools to act through, is what makes it an agent.

options.text: The model runs without any context supplied by the user
options.feedback: Agents depend on context more than chats do: a problem statement, requirements, papers, and guidance all go in. Autonomy is not the absence of instructions but the freedom to keep looping on them until the job is done.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Claude's four model tiers, listed from the smallest to the largest, are:

options.text: Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5, Opus 5, Fable 5.1
options.feedback: Sonnet is the tier you land on by default, and a default feels like a starting point -- but being the default is not the same as being the smallest. Haiku is the tier built for speed, which is what puts it at the bottom.

options.text: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Fable 5.1
options.feedback: The ladder runs from the quick, small tier up to the enormous one. Haiku is sold on speed, Sonnet is the everyday default, Opus takes complex work, and Fable sits on top behind usage credits.

options.text: Haiku 4.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Fable 5.1
options.feedback: Opus and Sonnet are swapped here. Opus is the tier offered for complex tasks, so it sits above the everyday default rather than just above the fastest one.

options.text: Fable 5.1, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5
options.feedback: This is the ladder upside down. Fable is the enormous tier that eats usage credits, so it belongs at the top, and the fast little tier belongs at the bottom.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In the Claude model picker, which tier is presented as the fastest choice for quick answers?

options.text: Haiku 4.5
options.feedback: Haiku is the smallest tier, and small means quick -- there are fewer numbers to push each token through, so the answer comes back sooner. The picker sells it on exactly that.

options.text: Sonnet 5
options.feedback: Sonnet is the everyday default, described as efficient rather than quick. Efficient is a claim about balance -- enough capability for most work without paying for more -- and that balance is bought by being bigger than the bottom rung, which costs time on every token.

options.text: Opus 5
options.feedback: Opus is offered for complex tasks. A larger model spends more computation on every token, so speed is part of what you give up to get that capability.

options.text: Fable 5.1
options.feedback: Fable is the largest tier, kept for the toughest problems and gated behind usage credits. Running something that big is the opposite of quick.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Which Claude tier is the default you get without changing anything, described in the picker as the efficient choice for everyday tasks?

options.text: Haiku 4.5
options.feedback: Haiku is the tier below the default, and the picker sells it on speed for quick answers. Fast is not the same claim as efficient for everyday work.

options.text: Opus 5
options.feedback: Opus is positioned for complex tasks, which is a step above ordinary use. Making it the default would mean spending its capability on work that does not need it.

options.text: Sonnet 5
options.feedback: Sonnet sits in the middle of the ladder, which is why it is the sensible thing to hand someone who has not chosen. It is capable enough for most work without the cost of the tiers above it.

options.text: Fable 5.1
options.feedback: Fable requires usage credits and is reserved for the hardest problems. Nothing that expensive would be handed to you as a default.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Which Claude tier does the picker flag as requiring usage credits, and offer for the toughest challenges?

options.text: Haiku 4.5
options.feedback: Haiku is the smallest and quickest tier. Being cheap to run is the whole point of it, so it is not the one behind a credit gate.

options.text: Sonnet 5
options.feedback: Sonnet is the everyday default. A default cannot sit behind an extra payment, or most people would never reach a working model at all.

options.text: Opus 5
options.feedback: Opus is where cost starts to be something you have to manage, which is why the take-home guidance was to keep its effort setting at High or below. A credit gate is a stronger measure than that, and the picker puts it only where a single answer costs a great deal more compute than Opus does.

options.text: Fable 5.1
options.feedback: Fable is enormous, and every answer it produces costs a great deal of compute. The credit requirement is the interface making that cost visible before you spend it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A model tier is the same architecture built bigger. What is bigger inside the larger tier?

options.text: A wider MLP (multi-layer perceptron), a wider embedding space, more stacks
options.feedback: Those are the three things you can widen, and each one is more numbers: bigger weight matrices in the multi-layer perceptron, more dimensions for a token's meaning to sit in, and more copies of all of it stacked up. That is why a bigger tier has more parameters and costs more compute on every token.

options.text: A larger vocabulary of tokens, so it has more words to choose between
options.feedback: The vocabulary is the list of tokens the model can produce, and nothing ties its length to tier -- the probability distribution at the end covers the whole vocabulary either way. Growing a model means enlarging the parts that do the work, not lengthening that list.

options.text: A longer conversation, so you can hand it more text in one sitting
options.feedback: How much you can put in front of a model is a property of the conversation, not of the model's size, and the two are set separately. Size is about the model's own numbers, which are fixed once training has finished.

options.text: A richer set of tools and features built around the model itself
options.feedback: Tooling is the part that mostly carries over when you drop a tier, which is why going smaller costs less than people expect. What a larger tier buys is more numbers inside the model itself.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: When you move from a larger Claude tier down to a smaller one, what largely carries over with you?

options.text: Most of the tooling the larger tier had
options.feedback: Size mostly buys knowledge and reasoning, not access. The smaller tier still reaches the same kinds of tools, which is why dropping a tier usually costs less than students expect.

options.text: Most of the world knowledge the larger tier had
options.feedback: World knowledge is one of the two things named as lost when you go smaller. A smaller model holds the world in fewer numbers, so the gaps show up here first.

options.text: Most of the reasoning quality on hard problems
options.feedback: Reasoning quality is usually the other casualty of going smaller. Some tasks will not survive the drop, which is why you test rather than assume.

options.text: Most of the wording of the answers it gave
options.feedback: Different tiers are different models, so they will not phrase things the same way even on an easy task. What carries across is the surrounding tooling, not the text.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Dropping to a smaller model tier costs you something. According to the lecture, what do you give up?

options.text: Access to the tools and features that surround the model
options.feedback: Tooling is the part that mostly survives a drop in tier. A smaller model still reaches the same kinds of tools; what thins out is something else.

options.text: Room in the prompt for a long document
options.feedback: Nothing ties a model's tier to how much material you can hand it. The trade named in the lecture is about what the model holds and how well it thinks, not about how much you can give it.

options.text: Fluent, readable prose in the answers it writes
options.feedback: Fluency survives the drop -- small models still write clean prose, which is part of why the gap between tiers is hard to spot. The losses show up elsewhere.

options.text: Depth of world knowledge, and usually the quality of its reasoning
options.feedback: A smaller model holds less of the world in fewer numbers, so gaps in what it knows appear first, and weaker reasoning on demanding problems follows.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why did the lecture argue that finding the smallest model which can do your work correctly is the responsible default?

options.text: Smaller models hallucinate less often than larger ones do.
options.feedback: Nothing about being small makes a model more truthful -- if anything it knows less and has more room to be wrong. The argument for going small is about cost, not accuracy.

options.text: Larger models are trained on data smaller ones may not use.
options.feedback: Training data was not the issue raised here. The reason to reach for the smallest workable tier is the computation, and therefore the energy, a bigger one spends on every answer.

options.text: A larger model burns far more compute, at a real cost.
options.feedback: Every answer from a very large model is a great deal of computation, and that computation has an environmental cost. Picking the smallest tier that still gets the work right means you are not spending it for nothing.

options.text: Smaller models are the only ones that run without a network.
options.feedback: Where a model runs is a separate question from which tier you pick in a hosted picker. The responsible-default argument rests on energy use, not on connectivity.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Fable was not released as soon as it was ready. What reason did the lecture give?

options.text: It proved unusually good at hacking.
options.feedback: Along with solving hard problems and working for long stretches, that capability came with the size. It is why a model being ready did not by itself mean a model being released.

options.text: It generated tokens more slowly than the tier below it.
options.feedback: It certainly is not quick, but slowness is the expected cost of size and is true of every tier above the smallest, so it would not single Fable out. The hold-up was something the model could do, not something it was slow at.

options.text: It could not use the same tools the smaller tiers use.
options.feedback: Tooling is broadly shared across tiers, so a gap there is not the sort of thing that delays a release. The concern was what the model was unusually good at, not what it lacked.

options.text: Its answers were less accurate than the tier below it.
options.feedback: Fable was described as having capabilities not seen in earlier models, so weak answers were not the problem. Some of those new capabilities were the problem.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You move from Claude to a different vendor's product and find a completely different set of model names. What should you expect?

options.text: Every vendor offers exactly four tiers, matched one to one with Claude's.
options.feedback: What you were promised is that every major lineup is a ladder of sizes -- not that another vendor built the same number of rungs or lined them up with Claude's. The ordering is what repeats.

options.text: A vendor using different names has abandoned the size trade-off.
options.feedback: The trade-off is a consequence of building the same architecture bigger, so it does not disappear when a vendor picks different words. Only the labels are local.

options.text: The names are arbitrary, so a bigger model is not more capable.
options.feedback: Within one lineup the bigger model really is the more capable one -- that is what the extra size buys. What is arbitrary is the naming, not the ordering.

options.text: The labels differ, but the ladder from small to large is the same.
options.feedback: Every major lineup is the same idea under other words, so your judgement transfers: decide which rung the job needs, then find that vendor's name for it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The weekend exercise asks you to solve one problem with Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and Fable. What instruction was attached to Fable?

options.text: Start with it, so you have a best answer to compare the others against.
options.feedback: A best answer would make a useful yardstick, but running the largest tier first risks spending your usage before you have tried the other three. Finishing the comparison is the point.

options.text: Save it for last, because it can eat through your usage.
