options.feedback: Fable is enormous, so a single run costs far more usage than the tiers below it. Going last means the other three comparisons are already in hand if your limit runs out.

options.text: Skip it entirely unless the first three tiers all fail.
options.feedback: The exercise wants all four, not a fallback chain. You are meant to see what the top tier looks like even when a smaller one already did fine -- just not first.

options.text: Run it twice, once with thinking turned off.
options.feedback: Thinking settings are a separate dial from which tier you pick, and they were not what the Fable instruction was about. That instruction concerned the order you run the four in.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A student assumes every quiz in this course will retest all the material from earlier weeks. What is the actual policy?

options.text: Quizzes are cumulative by design, so each one covers the whole term so far.
options.feedback: That would make each quiz longer and much less focused than intended. The aim is to check the new material while you have just met it.

options.text: Each quiz is sealed off from earlier sessions and reuses nothing at all.
options.feedback: This overcorrects. A question about model size cannot avoid the ideas that size is defined in terms of, so earlier material does reappear.

options.text: Quizzes are not meant to be cumulative, though earlier ideas resurface.
options.feedback: The target is the new session, but the course is built so later ideas rest on earlier ones. When an old term shows up it is because the new material needs it, not because it is being retested.

options.text: Only the final quiz of the term reaches back across everything covered.
options.feedback: No such special final quiz was described. The design point applies to every quiz: new material first, older ideas only where they are load-bearing.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You believe a quiz question in this course was wrong. What does the course let you do about it?

options.text: File a challenge in Brightspace, and earn extra credit if it holds up.
options.feedback: Questions are drafted by a model and checked by a second one, and that process still lets errors through. A challenge that turns out to be correct is worth a point of extra credit.

options.text: Nothing -- questions are checked by a second reviewer, so they are final.
options.feedback: The second check is real, but it was described as fallible rather than final. That is exactly why a route for challenges exists and why a correct one is rewarded.

options.text: Ask for your own score to be corrected, which is all a challenge wins you.
options.feedback: You are thinking of it as a grade dispute over one attempt. It is treated as a contribution instead: a challenge that turns out to be right earns a point of extra credit on top of any correction.

options.text: Raise it in class, where a class vote decides whether it stands.
options.feedback: Nothing about question correctness is put to a vote. A challenge is judged on whether it is actually right, not on how many people agree.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: An earlier session described a model as a compressed, lossy picture of the world -- a fuzzy JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group image file). How does that idea explain the gap between a smaller tier and a larger one?

options.text: The smaller tier stores the same picture but retrieves it more slowly.
options.feedback: Speed is a real difference between tiers, but it runs the other way, and the JPEG idea is about what survives compression rather than about lookup time.

options.text: The smaller tier compresses nothing, so it holds fewer facts perfectly.
options.feedback: It is the other way round -- a smaller model compresses harder, not less. Compressing harder is exactly what makes the detail go soft.

options.text: The smaller tier keeps a separate database and consults it less often.
options.feedback: There is no database being consulted. The compression happens in the model's own numbers, which is why lost detail cannot simply be looked back up.

options.text: The smaller tier is a blurrier copy of the same picture.
options.feedback: Squeeze an image into fewer bytes and the broad shapes survive while the fine grain smears. A smaller model holds the same world in fewer numbers, keeping the general and losing the specific.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why does working with Fable burn through usage credits so much faster than working with a smaller tier?

options.text: It charges a flat fee each time you open a conversation with it.
options.feedback: Credit use tracks the work actually done, not a door charge. It is the sheer size of the model that makes each answer expensive.

options.text: It is enormous, and a model that size takes real compute.
options.feedback: Every token has to be pushed through all of that model's numbers, so one answer costs far more computation than the same answer from a smaller tier. Credits track that cost.

options.text: It always thinks at the maximum budget, whatever you set.
options.feedback: The thinking budget is a separate dial from which model you pick, and it stays yours to set. Fable is expensive because of its size, not because it is locked to a setting.

options.text: It is billed by clock time rather than by the work it does.
options.feedback: Sitting idle in a conversation costs nothing. What costs is the computation spent generating, and a model that large spends a great deal of it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: On an everyday task you cannot tell a small tier's answer from a large tier's. What does the lecture say that means?

options.text: The picker most likely routed both requests to the same model.
options.feedback: The picker sends your request to the tier you chose. Matching answers mean the task was easy enough for both, not that one was quietly substituted.

options.text: The task was too poorly specified for either model to do it well.
options.feedback: A vague prompt usually produces two different bad answers rather than two equally good ones. Matching answers point to a task that sat within reach of both.

options.text: The task did not need the extra capability the larger tier has.
options.feedback: Differences between tiers only surface when a problem is hard enough to expose them. If the small one already got it right, the extra capability had nothing to do and paying for it buys you nothing.

options.text: The difference is there but shows only in wording, not in substance.
options.feedback: Wording varies from run to run even within a single tier, so it is not the tell. On an easy task there is no substantive gap to find in the first place.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You switch from Chat to Cowork in Claude and leave the same model selected. What has changed?

options.text: The model is the same; it now has a file system, memory, and task tracking around it
options.feedback: An agent has the large language model inside it, so you can still converse with it exactly as before. What is added sits around the model -- somewhere to keep files, memory that persists, a way of tracking what it is doing, and skills -- and that is what lets it carry work out rather than only discuss it.

options.text: The model is swapped for a larger tier that can handle tools
options.feedback: Which tier you are running stays your choice in either mode, and an agent works perfectly well with a small one. The step from chat to agent is a step up in equipment, not in model size.

options.text: The model now thinks before every reply, whatever the effort setting
options.feedback: Thinking is a separate dial and it stays wherever you put it. Rolling it together with the chat-versus-agent question makes it impossible to say what an agent actually adds.

options.text: The model generates its answers in parallel rather than one token at a time
options.feedback: Generation is one token at a time wherever the model runs -- each token has to be produced and fed back in before the next. An agent changes what surrounds the model, not how a token is produced.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Asked which of two model tiers is faster and which is less capable, the class named the smaller one both times. Why is the same answer right twice?

options.text: Because the smaller tier skips stages of the pipeline that the larger one runs.
options.feedback: Both tiers run the same pipeline end to end; a tier is that architecture built bigger, not a stripped-down version of it. What differs is how big each piece is.

options.text: Because the smaller tier is given a shorter thinking budget by default.
options.feedback: The thinking budget is a separate dial you set yourself, and it is not what makes a small model quick. Size alone explains both the speed and the ceiling.

options.text: Because vendors deliberately slow the larger tier to encourage upgrades.
options.feedback: No throttling is needed. A bigger model genuinely has more numbers to push every token through, so it is really slower and really more capable.

options.text: Because both follow from size -- fewer numbers to run and to hold.
options.feedback: A tier is the same architecture built bigger, so speed and capability move together in opposite directions. One is paid for with the other.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: How should the environmental argument in the lecture change the way you pick a model?

options.text: It rules out the largest tiers entirely for any coursework.
options.feedback: Nothing was ruled out -- the weekend exercise has you use the top tier. The argument is about not reaching for it by habit when a smaller one is already correct.

options.text: It makes the smallest tier that works the sensible start.
options.feedback: Every answer from a large model costs real computation, so always reaching for the biggest one has a running cost. Start small, check the work, step up only when you must.

options.text: It applies only to models you run on your own hardware.
options.feedback: A hosted model runs on someone else's hardware, and that hardware still draws power. Where the machine sits does not change the argument.

options.text: It matters when a model is trained, not when it is used.
options.feedback: Training is expensive, but so is every single answer a very large model produces, multiplied across everyone using it. That is the cost you were asked to weigh.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why does the weekend exercise ask you to give all four tiers the same problem, rather than a different problem to each?

options.text: Because a tier can only be judged on a problem chosen to suit its size.
options.feedback: There is no per-tier problem type. Tiers differ in degree rather than kind, which is exactly why one shared problem is the right test.

options.text: Because four different problems would cost four times the usage credits.
options.feedback: Cost is a reason to run Fable last, not a reason to reuse the problem. Four different problems would simply leave you with nothing to compare.

options.text: Because holding the problem fixed shows you what size changes.
options.feedback: If the problem changes with the model, you cannot tell whether a better answer came from the tier or from an easier question. Fixing it isolates the one thing you are studying.

options.text: Because the four tiers share a cache, so a repeated problem runs faster.
options.feedback: Nothing is shared between tiers that way, and a repeat would not speed anything up. The reason for one problem is comparison, not speed.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You have a fifty-item list to alphabetize and reformat as a table, and you want it back quickly. Following the lecture's advice, which tier fits and why?

options.text: Opus 5, because reformatting work benefits from stronger reasoning.
options.feedback: Complex tasks are where Opus earns its cost, and sorting a list is not one. You would wait longer and spend more compute for capability the job never calls on.

options.text: Fable 5.1, because it is the least likely to make a mistake.
options.feedback: Fable is for the toughest problems and burns usage credits quickly. Spending it on formatting is the exact habit the responsible default is meant to break.

options.text: Sonnet 5, because the default should be used for anything structured.
options.feedback: Sonnet is a safe answer, but the default is a starting point rather than a rule. When a job is this mechanical and speed matters, the tier below it fits better.

options.text: Haiku 4.5, because the task is mechanical and small is quick.
options.feedback: The work needs no world knowledge and almost no reasoning, which is precisely the case a small tier handles as well as any other -- and faster.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A classmate wants to reduce the environmental footprint of her AI (artificial intelligence) use but still get her work done. Following the lecture, what should she do?

options.text: Try the smallest tier first and move up only when it falls short.
options.feedback: This gets both halves: the work still has to come out right, and anything above the tier that achieves that is compute spent for nothing. Testing from the bottom finds that line.

options.text: Use the largest tier so she gets it right first time and avoids retries.
options.feedback: It sounds efficient, but nothing about a larger model guarantees a first-time answer -- and the footprint tracks the size of the model that ran, not the number of tries. A big model that gets it right once has still spent a great deal of compute.

options.text: Keep her chats short, since session length is where the cost sits.
options.feedback: Chat length is not the main lever, and a short chat with an enormous model is still expensive. Which model is running is what drives the compute.

options.text: Pick whichever vendor's model name sounds smallest, whatever the work.
options.feedback: Names are labels a vendor chose, and they vary between lineups. What matters is the smallest rung that actually does your work correctly.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A classmate refuses to try Haiku for anything, saying a small model will not have access to the features he needs. What is wrong with his reasoning?

options.text: Small models actually have more features, being simpler to extend.
options.feedback: Nothing suggests smaller tiers get extra features. The point is narrower: the tooling is broadly the same, so the difference between tiers lies elsewhere.

options.text: Tooling is largely shared across tiers; knowledge is not.
options.feedback: A smaller model keeps most of the same surroundings; it just holds less of the world and reasons less well on hard problems. Whether it suits a job depends on the job.

options.text: Features depend on your subscription, so the tier makes no difference.
options.feedback: Your plan does affect what you can use, but the tiers are genuinely not interchangeable -- they differ in knowledge and reasoning. The claim to correct is the one about tooling.

options.text: He is right, so the smallest tier should be kept for casual chat.
options.feedback: That gives up too much. The real cost of a small tier is world knowledge and reasoning quality, and plenty of everyday work leans on neither.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You run the same drafting task on Sonnet and on Opus and cannot tell the two outputs apart. What is the sensible next move?

options.text: Escalate to Fable, since the comparison came out inconclusive.
options.feedback: Going up a tier when two tiers already agree spends credits answering a question you have answered. The larger models earn their place on harder problems than this.

options.text: Rerun both with a much longer prompt until a difference appears.
options.feedback: Padding a prompt does not make a task harder in the way that separates tiers. You would spend more and reach the same finding.

options.text: Keep using the smaller tier for this kind of task from now on.
options.feedback: A task both tiers handle equally is a task that does not need the larger one, so the smaller is the right long-term choice here -- faster, cheaper, and just as good.

options.text: Stay on the larger tier anyway, since more capability cannot hurt.
options.feedback: It feels like insurance, and that instinct is exactly what the responsible default is aimed at. You already have evidence the extra capability had nothing to do here, and you would pay its compute cost on every run from now on.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Your internship uses a different AI (artificial intelligence) vendor, whose model names you have never seen. How does what you learned about Claude's tiers help?

options.text: It does not -- tier reasoning is specific to one vendor's own lineup.
options.feedback: The trade-off comes from building the same architecture at different sizes, so it holds wherever that architecture is used. Only the vocabulary is vendor-specific.

options.text: Assume their default model sits at the same rung as Claude's default.
options.feedback: Anchoring on a default is tempting because it gives you a fixed point, but a default is a vendor's choice about what to hand you, not a place on the ladder. You would still have to work out how much capability the job needs.

options.text: Assume the vendor's newest model name is also its most capable one.
options.feedback: Newest and largest are different claims -- a vendor can release a small, fast model most recently. Position on the size ladder is what predicts capability.

options.text: Work out which rung of the ladder you need, then find their name.
options.feedback: Every lineup is a ladder from small and fast to large and capable, so the judgement you actually make -- how much capability this job needs -- carries over intact.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: What is a reasoning model (also called a thinking model) able to do that an ordinary large language model (LLM) does not do?

options.text: Switch into a hidden mode and write tokens to itself first
options.feedback: That is the whole of it. The model can decide your request needs more work, produce a stretch of text for its own use, and only then start the reply you see.

options.text: Search the web for current sources and cite them in the answer
options.feedback: Looking things up outside itself is a tool, and tools belong to the agent discussion rather than to reasoning. A reasoning model that pauses is producing its own text, not fetching anyone else's.

options.text: Store your earlier questions permanently so later chats start informed
options.feedback: That describes memory, which a plain chat does not have either. Thinking happens inside a single response and vanishes when it is done -- it does not carry across conversations.

options.text: Run a grammar and fact check over the finished draft before sending it
options.feedback: There is no separate checking stage bolted on at the end. Whatever checking happens is itself just more generated text, produced the same way as everything else and produced before the visible answer starts.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A reasoning model works through a hard question and finishes thinking with plenty of its budget still unspent. What ends the hidden stretch and starts the visible reply?

options.text: The thinking budget runs out and the mode closes
options.feedback: A budget really does end thinking when the model reaches it, and then you get an answer built on unfinished reasoning. This model stopped with budget to spare, so the thing that ended the mode came from its own output rather than from a ceiling.

options.text: The model generates a stop-thinking token
options.feedback: The stop-thinking token is the partner of the think token that opened the mode. Once it appears, the model turns from writing for itself to writing for you.

options.text: The user sends a follow-up message
options.feedback: Nothing you do interrupts the mode -- you are not even seeing it happen. The transition is generated by the model in the same token stream as everything else.

options.text: The decoder stack finishes its last layer
options.feedback: The decoder stack runs from top to bottom for every single token, thinking or not. Finishing it produces one more token, which tells you nothing about whether the mode has ended.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In the lecture's spoken-out-loud demonstration, the presenter said "hold on" before listing possible answers, and "stop thinking" before he replied. Inside a reasoning model, what do those two phrases correspond to?

options.text: The prompt you send and the answer you get back
options.feedback: Those are the visible ends of the exchange, and they look the same whether the model thinks or not. The demonstration was marking the two boundaries of the hidden stretch that sits in between.

options.text: Turning the thinking setting on and then off again
options.feedback: A setting is something outside the model that governs how much thinking is allowed. The demonstration was acting out something the model produces for itself, part way through generating.

options.text: The think token and the stop-thinking token
options.feedback: Both are ordinary tokens the model generates: one opens the mode where the tokens are kept back, the other closes it and the visible answer begins. Everything between them was material the model wrote for its own use.

options.text: The first and last layers of the decoder stack
options.feedback: The stack runs top to bottom for every token, thinking or not, so its layers cannot mark where a stretch of thinking starts and stops. The boundaries are tokens, not layers.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You ask a reasoning model a hard question and it sits there for fifteen seconds with nothing appearing on screen. Why is nothing showing up?

options.text: The request is queued behind other users and has not started yet
options.feedback: Queueing would look identical from your side, which is why the misreading is so easy. But the lecture's account of the pause is that work is already underway, not waiting to begin.

options.text: The model is comparing several finished drafts and choosing the best one
options.feedback: There is no bank of finished drafts to compare. The model produces a probability distribution over the next token and walks forward one token at a time, both while thinking and while answering.

options.text: The model has crashed and will time out shortly
options.feedback: This is the reading the lecture went out of its way to correct. A silent stretch is normal behaviour for a reasoning model, not a failure.

options.text: The model is generating tokens it is keeping to itself before it replies
options.feedback: Generation is happening the whole time; it is simply going into the model's own context rather than onto your screen. The visible answer starts once the model stops thinking.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The lecture summed up thinking in one idea. Which statement captures it?

options.text: The model is writing its own context before it writes to you
options.feedback: Thinking gives the model more relevant material to condition on. Every thinking token it produces is in its context when the answer begins.

options.text: The model is retrieving stored answers to similar questions it has seen
options.feedback: Nothing is being retrieved. A model does not keep a file of past questions to consult, and thinking produces new text rather than fetching old text.

options.text: The model is running its architecture at a higher precision for hard problems
options.feedback: The architecture does not change gear. The same decoder stack does the same arithmetic; only the destination of the tokens differs.

options.text: The model is checking its planned answer against its training data
options.feedback: The training data is not there to be checked against -- what training left behind are the weights. Thinking adds new tokens to the context, which is a different thing entirely.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: While a reasoning model is in its thinking mode, where do the tokens it produces go?

options.text: Into a log the vendor keeps for training the next version
options.feedback: Hidden means not displayed to you, not shipped off somewhere else. Wherever else tokens might be recorded, the reason these ones matter is that they stay where the model itself can read them as it answers.

options.text: Into the model's own context, out of your view
options.feedback: That is precisely the difference between thinking and answering: same generation, different destination. Because they land in the context, the model can build on them when it responds.

options.text: Into a scratch buffer that is cleared before the answer begins
options.feedback: If they were cleared, thinking would accomplish nothing -- the point is that the model has written itself context to answer from. They stay in the context; they are just not displayed.

options.text: Into a rewritten version of your prompt, which replaces what you typed
options.feedback: Nothing edits your prompt on the way through; it sits in the context exactly as you sent it. The thinking tokens are added after it, which is how the model ends up with more to work from than you gave it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: What changes inside the architecture when a reasoning model switches into thinking mode?

options.text: Extra decoder stacks are activated for the duration
options.feedback: The stack is fixed when the model is built; nothing is switched in or out at run time. What varies is only whether the tokens are shown to you.

options.text: An added planning layer runs ahead of the usual pipeline
options.feedback: No new layer appears. The whole point of the lecture's account is that thinking gets its power from ordinary text generation, not from new machinery.

options.text: Nothing -- the same stack produces one token at a time as always
options.feedback: Context to token encodings to embeddings to decoder stacks to probabilities to a token, over and over. Thinking is that same loop with the output withheld.

options.text: The model widens its embedding space so it can hold more meaning
options.feedback: The width of the embedding space is set before training and never moves afterwards. Thinking adds tokens to the context; it does not add dimensions to anything.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A student asks whether a reasoning model contains an extra layer of attention and MLP (multi-layer perceptron) whose job is to pick the best of several possible responses. Which description matches the lecture's answer?

options.text: The model produces a probability distribution over the next token and steps forward, nothing more
options.feedback: At the basic level that is all there is: probabilities over the vocabulary, one token taken, then forward again. Thinking looks like deliberation, but it is the same walk with the tokens hidden.

options.text: The think token switches on a selection stage that scores the response as it forms
options.feedback: The think token opens a mode of hidden generation, not a selection stage. Nothing new is switched on; the same components keep doing what they always do.

options.text: The largest models add such a stage, where the extra compute is worth spending
options.feedback: Size buys wider matrices and more layers of the same kind, not a component of a new kind. Even the largest model here is still generating one token at a time.

options.text: The model forms several candidate answers side by side and returns the highest-scoring one
options.feedback: This is a very natural picture and it is the one the lecture rejected. There are no candidate answers sitting side by side to be scored, because the model never has more than one running sequence.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You ask a reasoning model a hard question. It sits silent for about forty seconds and then produces a three-sentence answer. A classmate says the timing makes no sense for so short a reply. What explains it?

options.text: The interface held the finished answer back until the whole reply was ready
options.feedback: Buffering would mean the text already existed while you were waiting. During the silence your answer had not been started -- the model was producing other tokens first.

options.text: The question was hard, so each token of the answer took longer to produce
options.feedback: One token costs the same work whatever the question is; difficulty does not slow the pipeline down. Elapsed time tracks how many tokens were produced, and most of these were never shown to you.

options.text: The model was choosing between several answers it had drafted
options.feedback: There is no set of drafts to choose between, because the model only ever extends one sequence. Those forty seconds went into extending that single sequence out of sight.

options.text: Most of the tokens produced in those forty seconds were hidden thinking tokens
options.feedback: The length of the visible reply tells you nothing about how much was generated. Hidden tokens come out of the same pipeline one at a time, so they cost the same time each as the visible ones.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A reasoning model is part way through its hidden thinking stretch and is about to produce one more token that you will never see. Which sequence produces that token?

options.text: Context, token probabilities, token embeddings, decoder stacks, token encodings, next token
options.feedback: Probabilities cannot come second -- they are what the stack finally produces. This ordering puts the last stage near the front.

options.text: Context, token encodings, token embeddings, decoder stacks, token probabilities, next token
options.feedback: Your text becomes numbered tokens, those become positions in meaning space, the stacks work on them, and the result is a probability for every token in the vocabulary, from which one is taken.

options.text: Context, decoder stacks, token embeddings, token encodings, token probabilities, next token
options.feedback: The stacks cannot run before there are embeddings for them to run on. Encoding and embedding both have to happen first.

options.text: Context, token embeddings, token encodings, token probabilities, decoder stacks, next token
options.feedback: Encodings come before embeddings, not after -- the token id is what gets looked up to give the embedding. The stacks also sit before the probabilities, not after.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In the lecture the presenter acted out being asked a question, saying "hold on," listing several ways he might answer, rejecting one of them, and then replying. What was the point of the demonstration?

options.text: That models are conscious in the same way people are
options.feedback: The analogy is about the shape of the activity, not about inner experience. Nothing in the lecture claims a model has anything like awareness.

options.text: That people should think out loud before prompting a model
options.feedback: That is decent advice about prompting, but it was not what the demonstration illustrated. The subject of the demonstration was the model's behaviour, not yours.

options.text: That the deliberating is itself just more text being produced
options.feedback: Talking through possibilities out loud and then answering is one continuous act of generating language. That is the claim about the model too -- thinking is generation, only hidden.

options.text: That a model needs several attempts before it gets an answer right
options.feedback: The demonstration was not about retrying a failed answer. It was about producing material for yourself first, so the single answer you then give is better.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Which statement describes the difference between a reasoning model and a non-reasoning one?

options.text: The reasoning model is trained on a curated set of logic problems rather than general text
options.feedback: Nothing in the lecture ties reasoning to a special diet of logic puzzles. The distinction it drew was about what happens when you send a request, not about the training corpus.

options.text: The reasoning model applies rules of inference that were programmed into it
options.feedback: No rules are programmed into any model in this family; whatever it does with language was learned from a signal. Reasoning here means generating hidden tokens, not executing logic that someone wrote.

options.text: The reasoning model is larger, and size is what makes reasoning possible
options.feedback: Size and thinking are separate dials -- a smaller model can think and a large one can answer straight away. Confusing the two makes it impossible to reason about either.

options.text: The reasoning model can decide a request needs more work and generate tokens first
options.feedback: That decision, and the hidden stretch it opens, is the whole distinction. A non-reasoning model goes straight into the answer you can see.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why is it fair to say a reasoning model is generating text even during the stretch when your screen shows nothing?

options.text: The tokens are produced by the same process; they are simply not displayed
options.feedback: Hidden and visible tokens come out of the identical loop over the decoder stack. Concealment is a decision about what to show you, not a difference in how the tokens were made.

options.text: The model is loading its weights, which counts as preparation for generation
options.feedback: Weights are already in place before your request arrives. What is happening in the pause is real token production, not setup.

options.text: The model is translating your prompt into an internal formal language
options.feedback: There is no formal internal language being written. Thinking is ordinary generated text in the same vocabulary the model answers in.

options.text: The interface is buffering the answer and will release it all at once
options.feedback: Buffering would mean the answer already exists and is being held back. During thinking the answer has not been started -- the model is still producing material to answer from.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A classmate explains a reasoning model this way: "It writes three answers behind the scenes, grades them, and shows you the best one." Where does this go wrong?

options.text: It is right about the drafts but wrong that you never see them
options.feedback: The drafts are the invented part. There is no set of parallel answers, so there is nothing being hidden from you except the single stream of thinking tokens.

options.text: There are no parallel answers and no grader -- just one sequence of tokens
options.feedback: The model only ever holds a probability distribution over the next token and steps forward. What looks like weighing options is that single sequence, written where you cannot see it.

options.text: It grades them, but on speed rather than quality
options.feedback: Accepting the grading step is the error. Nothing in the model scores whole responses against each other, on any criterion.

options.text: It is right in outline, but the number of drafts depends on the model tier
options.feedback: Changing the count leaves the false picture intact. No tier produces multiple candidate responses and picks between them.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Before asking your question, you paste in your own rough notes working through the problem, and the answer you get back is noticeably better. Which idea from the lecture explains why that helps?

options.text: You have supplied by hand the context a reasoning model writes for itself
options.feedback: Thinking helps because the answer is generated with extra relevant material already sitting in the context. It makes no difference to the mechanism whether the model wrote that material or you did.

options.text: You have put the model into its thinking mode from the outside
options.feedback: The mode opens when the model produces a think token, and adding text to your prompt does not produce one. Your notes helped as context, which is a different route to a similar benefit.

options.text: You have given the model more time to work before it has to answer
options.feedback: Pasting text does not change how long the model may spend before responding. What changed is the material it is conditioning on, not the length of any budget.

options.text: You have narrowed the vocabulary the model draws its answer from
options.feedback: The model still has a probability for every token in its vocabulary; context shifts those probabilities rather than removing options. The gain comes from what your notes give it to condition on.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In the lecture's diagram of a reasoning model, the pipeline runs to token probabilities and then produces something in the slot where a plain next token would normally sit. What appears there?

options.text: A blank placeholder token that stands in while the model deliberates
options.feedback: There is no empty or placeholder token; every pass of the pipeline yields a real token drawn from the probability distribution. What appears here is an ordinary token that happens to open the hidden mode.

options.text: A copy of the user's prompt, re-fed into the model
options.feedback: The prompt is already in the context and does not need resending. What comes out of the pipeline is always a newly produced token.

options.text: A summary of the context so far
options.feedback: The model can certainly write a summary during its thinking, but that is many tokens of ordinary generation. The slot after the probabilities holds a single token.

options.text: A think token, opening the hidden mode
options.feedback: The diagram makes the point that thinking begins as an ordinary output of the pipeline -- one token, drawn from the probability distribution like any other.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Two people give a model the same 30,000-token thinking budget. One runs it on a laptop with no GPU (graphics processing unit) at about 5 tokens per second; the other on a specialized inference chip at about 3,000. Why is a long budget practical for one of them and not the other?

options.text: Hidden tokens are produced one at a time like any others, so the budget costs real time
options.feedback: Thirty thousand tokens is about ten seconds at three thousand per second, and roughly a hundred minutes at five. A thinking token costs exactly what a visible one costs, so how much deliberation you can afford to wait for is decided by the hardware.

options.text: The laptop cannot store a budget that large, so it discards the extra tokens
options.feedback: A budget is not something stored up in advance; it is only a ceiling on how many tokens the model may produce for itself. The laptop will happily produce all of them -- you simply wait a very long time for them.

options.text: The chip produces the thinking tokens in parallel, unlike the laptop
options.feedback: Parallel processing belongs to the initial context, which arrives all at once. Generation is sequential on any hardware: each token has to be produced and fed back in before the next one can be chosen.

options.text: The laptop is running a smaller model, which needs more tokens to reach an answer
options.feedback: Nothing here says the models differ, and a smaller model would generate faster rather than slower. What separates these two is the speed of the hardware applied to a one-at-a-time process.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why should producing tokens that you never see make the visible answer any better?

options.text: Because generating anything at all warms up the decoder stack for the real task
options.feedback: There is no warm-up effect; the stack performs identically on the first token and the thousandth. The benefit comes from what those tokens contain, not from the act of running.

options.text: Because the answer is conditioned on those tokens once they are in the context
options.feedback: Every token is produced given everything before it, so material the model wrote for itself shapes what comes next. Thinking is a way to put useful tokens in front of the answer.

options.text: Because unseen tokens are generated at a lower temperature than visible ones
options.feedback: Settings do not flip between the hidden and visible halves of a response. The advantage of thinking is the content it leaves in the context.

options.text: Because the hidden pass identifies which facts the model is missing
options.feedback: Nothing audits the model for gaps. The hidden pass simply writes text, and that text helps because the answer is generated with it in view.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Who or what decides that a particular request warrants a stretch of thinking?

options.text: The interface, which routes hard prompts to a different model
options.feedback: Routing between models is a separate matter from thinking. The mode described in the lecture opens inside the model that already has your request.

options.text: A classifier that scores the prompt for difficulty before the model sees it
options.feedback: No pre-screening stage was described. The decision shows up as a token in the model's own output, which means it happens during generation, not before it.

options.text: The model itself, by producing a think token
options.feedback: The judgement that more work is needed is expressed the only way a model can express anything -- as a generated token, which then opens the mode.

options.text: The user, who must ask for thinking in the wording of the prompt
options.feedback: You can influence how much thinking is allowed, but you are not the one who triggers the mode on a given turn. The model emits the token that starts it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A friend who has read a little about this tells you that reasoning models contain "a separate reasoning engine alongside the language part, which is why they are slower." Using the lecture's account, how would you correct the picture?

options.text: The reasoning engine is real but only runs on requests the model judges to be hard
options.feedback: Conceding the engine keeps the mistaken picture. What varies with difficulty is the number of hidden tokens, not which machinery is used.

options.text: The reasoning engine is the attention mechanism, which the model leans on more heavily while thinking
options.feedback: Attention runs for every token in every model in this family, thinking or not. It is not a component that reasoning switches to.

options.text: The reasoning engine sits after the decoder stacks and inspects the probabilities
options.feedback: Nothing sits between the probabilities and the token beyond ordinary selection. There is no inspecting stage to place there.

options.text: There is no second engine -- the same stack generates tokens the model keeps to itself
options.feedback: Slowness comes from producing more tokens, not from extra machinery. Every hidden token costs one full pass of the same pipeline, which is why thinking takes time.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In the lecture's spoken-out-loud analogy, the presenter raised a possible line of answer and then dismissed it as a bad one. What does that dismissal correspond to inside a reasoning model?

options.text: More hidden tokens, which then shape what the model generates next
options.feedback: Rejecting a line is not a special operation -- it is just more text written into the model's own context, and the answer that follows is conditioned on it.

options.text: A candidate response being deleted from a shortlist
options.feedback: There is no shortlist of responses. The model holds one running sequence of tokens, so nothing can be removed from a set that never existed.

options.text: A weight inside the model being adjusted so it avoids that answer
options.feedback: Weights are fixed by training and do not change while you are talking to the model. A rejected idea leaves its trace only as text in the context, which is what shapes the tokens that follow.

options.text: The model backing up and regenerating from an earlier point
options.feedback: Generation only moves forward, one token at a time. A rejected idea stays in the context as written text rather than being rewound and erased.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A reasoning model spends a long hidden stretch on your question and then begins its visible reply. At the moment the first visible word is produced, what is in the model's context?

options.text: Only your prompt, since the hidden stretch ended when thinking stopped
options.feedback: The stop-thinking token ends the mode, not the tokens. If those tokens vanished, the thinking would have bought the model nothing at all.

options.text: Your prompt plus everything it wrote during the hidden stretch
options.feedback: That is exactly the payoff of thinking: the model has written itself extra material and is now answering with it in view.

options.text: Only a condensed summary that the hidden stretch produced
options.feedback: No compression step runs at the end of thinking. The tokens are in the context in full, as written.

options.text: Your prompt plus a score for how promising each line of thought was
options.feedback: Nothing scores lines of thought. Whatever judgement the model expressed about them is itself text in the context, not a separate rating.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The lecture said the thinking tokens are hidden from you rather than saying they are not produced. Why does that distinction matter?

options.text: Because hidden tokens are stored for the vendor rather than the model
options.feedback: Who stores what is not the issue. The distinction is about the tokens being real generated text that the model itself uses.

options.text: Because hidden tokens are produced without consuming any of the model's capacity
options.feedback: They cost exactly what any token costs -- one full pass of the pipeline. That is why a long thinking stretch takes real time.

options.text: Because they are real tokens in the context: they cost time and shape the answer
options.feedback: Calling them hidden keeps two facts in view: the pause is generation happening, and the reply is built on what was generated. "Not produced" would lose both.

options.text: Because they are written in a different vocabulary from the visible ones
options.feedback: There is one vocabulary, and the model draws from it whether the token will be shown or not. Hidden refers to display, not to a different alphabet.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Two large language models (LLMs) are given the same hard prompt. One is a reasoning model, one is not. What difference should you expect in how the response is produced?

options.text: The reasoning model consults external sources; the other relies on what it learned
options.feedback: Consulting outside sources is a tool-use question and belongs to agents. Reasoning is entirely internal -- it is text the model writes for itself.

options.text: The reasoning model chooses among several answers; the other takes the first one it forms
options.feedback: Neither model forms several answers. Both walk forward one token at a time from a probability distribution.

options.text: The reasoning model produces its answer more slowly because each token takes longer
options.feedback: A token costs the same either way. The reasoning model is slower because it produces more tokens, most of which you never see.

options.text: The reasoning model may generate a hidden stretch first; the other answers straight away
options.feedback: That hidden stretch is the only structural difference. Both are running the same pipeline, one token at a time.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Which phrase best describes what thinking accomplishes for a reasoning model?

options.text: A way to verify its answer before committing to it
options.feedback: Verification implies a check against something authoritative, and there is nothing of the kind inside the model. Whatever it writes while thinking is more generated text, not evidence.

options.text: A way to produce useful tokens before it responds
options.feedback: That is the whole mechanism in one line. The tokens go into its own context, and the answer is generated with them present.

options.text: A way to spend more compute so the probabilities come out sharper
options.feedback: The probability distribution for a given context is what it is; extra time does not sharpen it. What thinking changes is the context those probabilities are computed from.

options.text: A way to reduce the chance of picking a low-probability token by mistake
options.feedback: How a token is chosen from the distribution is a separate control entirely. Thinking changes the material the model is working from, not the selection step.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In Claude, the effort setting puts a limit on one specific thing. What does it limit?

options.text: How varied and creative the wording of the final answer will be
options.feedback: That is what temperature does, acting on the token probabilities at the very last step. Effort is about quantity of thinking, not about which token gets picked.

options.text: How many tokens it may spend thinking before replying
options.feedback: Effort is a thinking budget: a ceiling on the tokens the model may generate for itself before it turns to your reply. The model may not use all of them, but it cannot go past them.

options.text: How many words the visible reply may contain
options.feedback: The budget covers the hidden thinking, not the answer you read. You can get a short reply after a long think, or a long reply after almost none.

options.text: How much world knowledge the model can draw on
options.feedback: World knowledge comes with the model you picked and does not move when you change a setting. Effort only changes how much work the model may do before responding.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: If you never open the effort menu in Claude, where is your conversation running?

options.text: At Low, since a conversation starts as cheaply as it can
options.feedback: Low is a setting you pick deliberately when you want an answer with very little deliberation behind it. The menu does not open at the bottom of the range; the five levels run Low, Medium, High, Extra, Max.

options.text: At High, with a generous thinking budget
options.feedback: High was named as the ceiling for the take-home work on Opus, which tells you it is a level you move up to when the problem earns it. Opening there would spend the larger budget on every trivial message you send.

options.text: At Medium, one step up from the lowest level
options.feedback: Medium is the default -- where the menu sits until you move it, which is why most people never notice the setting at all. The levels run Low, Medium, High, Extra, Max, with a separate on/off toggle for thinking beside them.

options.text: At Max, thinking for as long as it needs
options.feedback: Max does mean as long as the model needs, and the interface warns it can consume 3.5 times or more the usage of High. That is a cost you opt into, not one you inherit by leaving a menu alone.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Apart from choosing a level on the effort menu, what else can you do with thinking in Claude?

options.text: Switch thinking off altogether
options.feedback: There is an on/off toggle beside the levels, so a task that needs no deliberation can skip the thinking phase entirely. That is useful when you want a fast answer that leans on the model's world knowledge.

options.text: Carry any unused budget over into your next message
options.feedback: The budget is a ceiling for the current request, not a balance that accumulates. Unused tokens are simply tokens the model did not need this time.

options.text: Set a separate budget for each paragraph of the answer
options.feedback: The budget governs the hidden thinking that happens before the reply begins, so it is not divided up across the visible answer. There is one ceiling per request.

options.text: Type a temperature value into the same menu
options.feedback: Temperature is a different control and is not what the effort menu offers. In a chat setup the two things you are choosing are the model and the size of the thinking budget.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: What does the interface warn you about when you choose the Max effort setting?

options.text: It is capped at exactly twice the thinking tokens of High
options.feedback: Max is not described as a fixed multiple of anything -- it is presented as as long as the model needs. The warning attached to it is about usage, not about a token cap.

options.text: It quietly moves you up to a larger model tier
options.feedback: The model tier and the thinking budget are separate dials, and changing one does not change the other. A setting that silently swapped your model would defeat the point of having two controls.

options.text: It halves the speed at which tokens are generated
options.feedback: Generation speed is a property of the model and the hardware, not of the budget. A long budget takes longer overall because more tokens are produced, not because each one slows down.

options.text: It can consume 3.5 times or more the usage of High
options.feedback: Max means the model can think as long as it needs, and the interface flags that this costs 3.5x or more the usage of High. That is exactly why the take-home guidance was to stay at High or below.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A model is partway through its reasoning when it reaches the ceiling of its thinking budget. What happens next?

options.text: It starts a fresh thinking pass with a larger budget
options.feedback: Nothing raises the budget on the model's behalf -- that dial is yours. Raising it is something you do on the next attempt, after seeing what the first one produced.

options.text: It returns an error and asks you to raise the setting
options.feedback: Running out of budget is not a failure state; it is the normal way a budget ends. You still get an answer, which is why a too-small budget can be hard to notice.

options.text: It wraps up and replies using the reasoning it managed
options.feedback: The ceiling works like the clock on a timed quiz: when the time is up you hand in whatever you have worked out so far. The reply still arrives, just built on reasoning that was cut short.

options.text: It keeps thinking, since the budget is only a suggestion
options.feedback: The budget is a hard ceiling on thinking tokens, not a hint. If it were advisory there would be no way to control what a request costs you or how long you wait.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why would you not just leave a model on its largest thinking budget for everything you do?

options.text: Short, easy requests do not need thousands of thinking tokens
options.feedback: A greeting or a one-line lookup gets no better for having ten thousand tokens of deliberation spent on it, and those tokens cost you time and usage. The budget should match the size of the problem.

options.text: A large budget makes the model less accurate on every task
options.feedback: More thinking is not accuracy poison -- on a hard, well-specified problem it genuinely helps. The trouble with a large budget is waste on easy tasks and wandering on vague ones.

options.text: Budgets above Medium switch off the model's world knowledge
options.feedback: Nothing about the thinking budget turns off what the model knows; the knowledge lives in the weights of whichever model you picked. Effort only governs how many tokens it may generate before replying.

options.text: The model refuses requests it judges too simple for the budget
options.feedback: The model does not police your setting -- it will happily think hard about a trivial question. That is precisely the waste you are trying to avoid.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Which comparison did the lecture use for what happens when a model reaches the end of its thinking budget?

options.text: A fuzzy photograph of the world, losing detail as it is made smaller
options.feedback: That image is about model size -- a smaller model as a lower-quality compression of the world. It says nothing about how long a model may deliberate.

options.text: The clock on the in-class quiz, which cut thinking off
options.feedback: The class was quite literally given a budget for thinking, and when the time was up, thinking stopped and answers were handed in. A model hitting its token ceiling does the same thing.

options.text: An intern who never comes back for directions
options.feedback: That comparison is about what goes wrong when a long budget meets a badly described task, not about what a budget is. It explains a risk rather than the mechanism.

options.text: A dial that adds noise to a choice
options.feedback: That describes temperature, which nudges the model toward lower-probability tokens. Effort is about quantity of thinking, not about randomness in picking.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: At which point in the pipeline does temperature do its work?

options.text: On the token embeddings, before the decoder stacks
options.feedback: Embeddings are the model's representation of meaning going into the stacks, and temperature never touches them. Temperature comes in much later, once probabilities exist.

options.text: On the context, as it is read in
options.feedback: Reading the context is the prefill phase, and nothing there is being randomised. Temperature only has something to act on once the model has produced probabilities over the vocabulary.

options.text: On the number of tokens the model may generate
options.feedback: That is the effort setting, a budget on quantity. Temperature does not lengthen or shorten anything -- it changes which token gets picked.

options.text: On the token probabilities, at the final step
options.feedback: At the end of the pipeline the model holds a probability over every token in the vocabulary, and temperature is noise added right there. Raise it and a lower-probability token becomes a likelier pick.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why does raising temperature give you more varied or more creative output?

options.text: It gives the model a larger vocabulary of words to choose between
options.feedback: The vocabulary is fixed and every token in it already carries a probability at each step. What changes is how likely the model is to leave the top of that list, not how long the list is.

options.text: It makes tokens other than the top one likelier to be picked
options.feedback: With low temperature the model tends to take the highest-probability token every time, which reads as safe and predictable. Turning it up flattens that preference, so surprising choices get through.

options.text: It lets the model deliberate for longer before committing
options.feedback: Deliberating for longer is the effort setting, a budget on thinking tokens. Temperature acts in an instant, at the moment one token is selected.

options.text: It relaxes the grammar rules the model was trained on
options.feedback: There are no separate grammar rules to relax -- whatever the model knows about language is baked into its probabilities. Temperature only changes how those probabilities are sampled.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In an ordinary chat setup, the lecture said you are controlling two things. Which two?

options.text: The temperature and the size of the thinking budget
options.feedback: Temperature matters and was discussed at length, but it is not one of the two dials you are handed in the chat interface. The other dial is the one you pick before you type anything.

options.text: The model and the temperature
options.feedback: You do pick the model, but the second dial in the chat interface is not temperature. It is the setting that decides how much work the model may do before it starts replying.

options.text: The model and the thinking budget
options.feedback: Which model gives you raw capability, world knowledge, and reasoning quality; the budget gives you how much work it may do before answering. They interact but are not interchangeable, and a third control appears once agents enter the picture.

options.text: The temperature and the length of the reply
options.feedback: Reply length is an outcome you can ask for in the prompt, not one of the two settings the interface gives you. Neither of these is the dial you set before the conversation starts.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You move the effort setting from Medium to Max and then send a short, simple question. What does the higher setting guarantee about the model's thinking?

options.text: Only that it may think longer, not that it will
options.feedback: Effort sets a ceiling on thinking tokens rather than a quota to be filled, and on an easy question the model can stop far short of it. A budget is permission to spend, and the model spends roughly what the problem seems to need.

options.text: That the reply you read will be longer than it was at Medium
options.feedback: The budget governs the hidden thinking that happens before the reply starts, so a long think can still end in two sentences. Reply length and budget size are not tied to each other.

options.text: That every token of the budget is used before it replies
options.feedback: That would make the largest setting cost the same on every message, however trivial the message was. The ceiling limits what the model may spend; it does not instruct it to spend that much.

options.text: That the answer will be more accurate than it was at Medium
options.feedback: More room to think earns its keep on a hard, well-specified problem, but it cannot improve an answer that needed no working out. On a short question there is nothing for the extra tokens to do.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You set effort to High and then ask a one-line question. What does the model do with that budget?

options.text: It may use very little of it, because the budget is a ceiling rather than an amount to spend
options.feedback: Effort caps how many tokens the model may spend thinking; it does not oblige it to spend them. An easy request can come back almost at once even at a generous setting, which is why the ceiling only really bites on the problems large enough to reach it.

options.text: It spends the whole budget, so the reply arrives once the tokens run out
options.feedback: That would turn every setting above Low into a guaranteed wait and make the dial useless for mixed work. The budget limits thinking; it is not a quota the model has to work through.

options.text: It shortens the visible reply to make room for the thinking it was allowed
options.feedback: The budget covers the hidden thinking, not the answer you read, and the two are not drawn from one allowance. You can get a long reply after almost no thinking, or a short one after a great deal.

options.text: It raises the temperature to fill the time it was given
options.feedback: Temperature is a separate control acting on which token gets picked, and nothing links it to how much thinking is allowed. An unspent budget is simply unspent.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Temperature is often described as affecting only the style of the final answer. Why is that description too narrow for a reasoning model?

options.text: Thinking tokens are generated at a separate, higher temperature
options.feedback: There is no second temperature for the hidden phase -- the same setting is in force throughout. What matters is that the phase exists at all, so the setting has more to act on.

options.text: Temperature is applied once at the end, after the thinking has already been fixed
options.feedback: It is applied once per token, and the thinking is made of tokens too. Treating the reasoning as settled before temperature enters is exactly the misreading the question is aimed at.

options.text: It applies at every step, thinking included, so an early choice can redirect it
options.feedback: Thinking is ordinary next-token generation that happens to be hidden, so temperature is in force for all of it. One low-probability token early in the reasoning sends the model down a different path, and the answer follows that path.

options.text: Raising temperature also raises the thinking budget
options.feedback: The two dials are independent -- temperature never changes how many tokens the model may spend. What it changes is which tokens those are, at every step.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A classmate says that turning temperature up makes a model slower to answer, because picking unusual words is more work. Why is that wrong?

options.text: Producing a token costs the same whichever token it turns out to be
options.feedback: Temperature only changes which token is drawn from probabilities the model has already computed, so the same number of tokens takes about the same time. The dial that does change how long you wait is the thinking budget, because it changes how many tokens get generated at all.

options.text: Higher temperature makes the model generate fewer tokens, which cancels the cost
options.feedback: Temperature has no say in how many tokens come out; it acts at each step on which one is chosen. Nothing is being cancelled here, because nothing was added in the first place.

options.text: At high temperature the probabilities are computed less carefully
options.feedback: The model does the same work to produce a distribution over the vocabulary at every step, whatever the temperature. Temperature enters afterwards, when one token is sampled from that distribution.

options.text: Speed is fixed by the model and the hardware, so no setting can change your wait
options.feedback: Tokens per second does come from the model and the hardware, but your total wait is that rate multiplied by how many tokens are produced -- which the thinking budget controls. The claim to correct is about temperature specifically, not about every setting.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why does a large thinking budget only pay off when the task is described well?

options.text: A vague task makes the model stop thinking early and return an error instead
options.feedback: Vagueness does not stop the model; it will proceed confidently on whatever reading of your request it settled on. The failure is silent, which is what makes it costly.

options.text: A vague task lets the model spend the budget going the wrong way
options.feedback: The budget buys work, not correctness, so an unclear target just means more work aimed off to one side. That is the wandering off in the wilderness the lecture described.

options.text: Long budgets are only unlocked once a prompt is specific enough
options.feedback: The setting is yours to choose regardless of how you worded the request -- nothing inspects your prompt first. The risk is what you get for the money, not whether you can spend it.

options.text: Thinking tokens are discarded unless the prompt is specific
options.feedback: The thinking tokens become the model's own context either way and shape the answer that follows. When the task is vague, they shape it toward the wrong thing.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The lecture compared a model on a long thinking budget to a new intern who does not like coming back for directions. What point was that making?

options.text: A model needs training on your material before you can trust it with a task
options.feedback: The comparison was not about training at all -- the model already has its capability when you hand it the work. The problem being described happens after the task is handed over.

options.text: A model should be given as little context as possible
options.feedback: Less context is not the lesson; a well-described task usually needs more detail, not less. The intern goes wrong for want of direction, not from an excess of it.

options.text: A model will ask clarifying questions when your request is unclear
options.feedback: That is precisely what the intern in the comparison does not do, and it is why the analogy works. You find out about the misunderstanding only when the finished work arrives.

options.text: Given time but unclear directions, it works hard on the wrong thing
options.feedback: The long budget guarantees effort, not that the effort points where you wanted. This is why the practical move is to test with a small budget before you spend a large one.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: How does the size of the model change the risk of handing a long thinking budget to a loosely described task?

options.text: The risk disappears once the model is small enough to be fast
options.feedback: Speed only means the model reaches the wrong destination sooner. Being fast does not help you if the direction was never right.

options.text: Model size has no bearing on it
options.feedback: Reasoning quality is one of the things you give up as you go smaller, and that is exactly the faculty that keeps a long think on target. Size is part of the picture here.

options.text: Smaller models are more likely to wander off with the time
options.feedback: The wandering risk is worse with smaller models, because a weaker grip on the task compounds over a long stretch of unsupervised reasoning. Check the direction early before you buy more of it.

options.text: Only the largest models wander, since they explore more widely
options.feedback: Larger models are generally better at staying on a poorly specified task, not worse. Exploring widely is not the same as losing the thread.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You have a new task and no idea how much thinking it will need. What method did the lecture recommend?

options.text: Start with a small budget, check the direction, then raise it
options.feedback: A small budget is a cheap probe: it tells you whether the model has understood the task before you pay for a long think. Once you can see it is on the right track, raising the budget buys real work rather than confident wandering.

options.text: Start at Max so you see the best possible answer, then bring it down afterwards
options.feedback: Starting at the top spends the most usage on the attempt where you know the least about whether the task is well described. It also hides the problem, since a wrong answer arrives beautifully reasoned.

options.text: Match the budget to how long you want the answer to be
options.feedback: The budget covers hidden thinking, not the visible reply, so answer length is a poor guide to it. A short answer can need a great deal of working out.

options.text: Pick one budget and keep it for every task
options.feedback: A fixed setting is either wasteful on easy tasks or too tight on hard ones. The budget is a dial precisely because the right value depends on the problem.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You want a fast, complete answer that leans on broad world knowledge and does not really need to be worked through step by step. Which combination fits best?

options.text: A smaller model with a long thinking budget
options.feedback: That pairing suits a problem that mainly needs working through, where time can substitute for capability. Here the answer depends on what the model knows, and a smaller model knows less.

options.text: A larger model with thinking turned off
options.feedback: World knowledge is what the larger model buys you, and skipping the thinking phase keeps the reply fast. There is nothing to work through, so there is nothing for a budget to buy.

options.text: A smaller model with thinking turned off
options.feedback: This is certainly the fastest and cheapest option, but it is short on the thing the task actually depends on. Going smaller costs you world knowledge first of all.

options.text: A larger model at its maximum thinking budget
options.feedback: You would get a good answer, at several times the usage and a long wait for deliberation the task does not need. The budget only earns its cost when there is real working out to do.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A classmate says that turning the thinking budget up is just another way of moving to a bigger model. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Nothing is wrong: the budget menu is another name for the tier menu
options.feedback: These are two menus over two different things -- how capable the model is, and how much work it may do before it answers. Treat them as one control and you have a single adjustment where the interface hands you two.

options.text: The budget is the cheaper way to buy the capability a larger tier gives
options.feedback: Extra time cannot supply world knowledge that a smaller model never had, so the two are not interchangeable at any price. Time helps when a problem has to be worked through, not when it has to be known.

options.text: A larger tier does whatever a longer budget does, so the budget is redundant
options.feedback: A capable model on a short budget can still be cut off part way through a problem that has to be reasoned out. Capability and amount of work are separate things to buy, which is why there are separate dials for them.

options.text: They are separate dials, and a longer budget can lift a model past what it managed before
options.feedback: A Sonnet-sized model with a long budget may solve what the same model with a short budget could not, with no change of tier at all. The question to ask is whether the model can do the task at all or whether it just needs more time, and that split is less clean than you would expect.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You type a one-line request -- "tidy up my project" -- with effort set to Max. A long wait later you get back a careful, thoroughly reasoned piece of work aimed at something you never asked for. Which idea from the lecture explains this best?

options.text: The temperature was too high, so unlikely tokens crept in
options.feedback: High temperature produces varied or odd choices, not a coherent long effort pointed at the wrong goal. What you got was well reasoned -- just about the wrong task.

options.text: The model ran past its budget and answered with partial thinking
options.feedback: Hitting the ceiling gives you an answer built on unfinished reasoning, usually shallow rather than elaborate. Here the model had plenty of budget; the trouble was where it spent it.

options.text: A large budget on a vague request buys time to go the wrong way
options.feedback: The budget guarantees work, not that the work is aimed where you wanted -- this is the intern who never comes back for directions. Describe the task properly, or probe with a small budget first and check the direction.

options.text: The model tier was too small for a request of this kind
options.feedback: A bigger model would likely have guessed your intent better, but the root problem is that you never said what you meant. Moving up a tier is an expensive way to avoid writing a clearer request.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You are brainstorming names for a student club, and every attempt comes back with the same safe, obvious suggestions. You want stranger ones. Which control changes this, and why?

options.text: Temperature, since it lets lower-probability tokens be chosen
options.feedback: Safe and obvious is what you get when the model takes the top of the probability distribution every time. Turning temperature up flattens that preference at the moment of choice, so the odd option gets picked.

options.text: Effort, since a larger budget widens the vocabulary the model draws on
