options.feedback: The vocabulary is fixed and the budget does not touch it. More thinking may give you better-considered names, but it does not make an unlikely word likelier to be selected.

options.text: Effort, since more thinking tokens always produce more original wording
options.feedback: Longer deliberation tends to produce more thorough answers, not more surprising ones, and it can converge on the same safe options more carefully. Novelty at the point of choice is a different mechanism.

options.text: Temperature, since it lengthens the model's thinking before it answers
options.feedback: You have named the right dial for the wrong reason, which matters because it will mislead you next time. Temperature acts in a single instant on the probabilities; it does not lengthen anything.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You give a small model a carefully specified logic puzzle with the budget at Low, and the answer is wrong. No larger model is available to you. What does the lecture suggest is worth trying next?

options.text: Raise the temperature so it explores more possible answers
options.feedback: Higher temperature gives you a different answer, not a better-worked one, and on a puzzle with a single right answer that mostly adds noise. Exploration here needs reasoning steps, not randomness.

options.text: Give the same model a longer thinking budget
options.feedback: The task is well described and mainly needs working through, which is exactly the case where extra time can substitute for capability. The same model with a longer budget may solve what it could not solve at Low.

options.text: Turn thinking off so it answers straight from world knowledge
options.feedback: World knowledge is the strength you lean on when an answer needs to be recalled rather than derived. A logic puzzle is the opposite case: it has to be worked out.

options.text: Shorten the prompt so less of the budget goes on reading it
options.feedback: The thinking budget covers tokens the model generates for itself, not the tokens it reads from you. Cutting a well-specified prompt would remove the detail that keeps the reasoning on target.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: It is Saturday and you are working through the four-model comparison on Opus when you notice your usage draining fast. Following the guidance given in the lecture, what do you do?

options.text: Move to Max, so the work finishes in fewer attempts
options.feedback: Max costs 3.5x or more the usage of High, so it drains the very thing you just noticed running out. Fewer attempts at many times the price is not a saving.

options.text: Move to Extra, which is the setting recommended for take-home work
options.feedback: Extra was named alongside Max as a setting to stay away from for this assignment. Nothing in the guidance pointed you above High.

options.text: Stop for the month, since the limit will not reset before then
options.feedback: The wait is far shorter than that -- usage recovers within a day or so. Treating it as a monthly cap would cost you the weekend for no reason.

options.text: Stay at High or below, and wait for usage to come back
options.feedback: High is the ceiling recommended for this work precisely so you do not stall, and if you do run out the usage returns later in the day or the next day. Waiting costs you time, not the assignment.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You send exactly the same prompt twice to a reasoning model with temperature turned up. The two replies differ -- and so do the steps the model took to get to them. What explains the difference in the steps, not just in the wording?

options.text: The thinking budget is drawn at random for each request
options.feedback: The budget is whatever you set it to and does not vary between requests. Two runs at the same effort setting have the same ceiling.

options.text: Temperature only comes into play once the visible answer begins
options.feedback: If that were true the reasoning would be identical each time and only the phrasing would move -- which is not what you saw. Thinking is generated the same way the answer is, so the same setting applies to it.

options.text: Temperature is in force during the thinking steps as well
options.feedback: Thinking is ordinary next-token generation that happens to be hidden, so every thinking step is sampled with your temperature in force. One low-probability token early on sends the model down a different path, and the answer is built on that path.

options.text: The model was swapped for a different tier between the two requests
options.feedback: The tier is a dial you set and does not change on its own between messages. Two runs of the same model can still diverge, because the sampling is not deterministic once temperature is up.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: When you use a frontier model hosted by a company through its website, roughly how fast does it produce tokens?

options.text: About 5 tokens per second, roughly a word every second
options.feedback: That is the figure for running a model yourself on a laptop with no GPU (graphics processing unit). A hosted service runs on hardware built for the job, and that hardware is worth more than an order of magnitude.

options.text: About 60 tokens per second, sometimes closer to 100
options.feedback: This is the everyday number to carry for a hosted frontier model. Hold it as an order of magnitude rather than an exact figure, so you can place it against the ~5 on a bare laptop and the thousands on a specialized inference chip.

options.text: About 500 tokens per second
options.feedback: That falls between the two figures the lecture gave. Hosted frontier models sit in the tens per second; the thousands belong to chips built specifically for this architecture, running smaller models.

options.text: About 3,000 tokens per second
options.feedback: That speed comes from a specialized inference chip running a medium-sized model, not from a hosted frontier model. Frontier models are large, and size is exactly what those chips cannot accommodate.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You run a language model locally on a laptop that has no GPU (graphics processing unit). Roughly what generation speed should you expect?

options.text: Roughly what a hosted service gives you, around 60 tokens per second
options.feedback: A hosted service reaches that speed because of the hardware behind it. Strip the specialized hardware away and the same architecture runs more than ten times slower, which is why local models feel like watching someone type.

options.text: Thousands of tokens per second, because nothing has to travel over the network
options.feedback: Network travel is not what sets the pace -- generation is. Thousands of tokens per second is what a purpose-built inference chip achieves, and a general-purpose laptop processor is not that.

options.text: About 100 tokens per second, since laptops and servers run the same code
options.feedback: The code really is the same, and that is the point worth noticing: what differs is the hardware doing the arithmetic on enormous weight matrices. That difference costs you more than an order of magnitude.

options.text: About 5 tokens per second
options.feedback: Without a GPU the arithmetic falls to a general-purpose processor, and generation crawls at roughly a word every second or two. Running models locally is genuinely useful for privacy and cost, but this is the speed you are trading for it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Several companies are building chips specialized for the transformer architecture. On such a chip, a medium-sized model generates at a rate on the order of:

options.text: Thousands of tokens per second
options.feedback: That is roughly two orders of magnitude above a hosted frontier model. It is what makes a long stretch of generation cheap in wall-clock time, which changes what is worth building on top of a medium-sized model.

options.text: Several hundred tokens per second
options.feedback: This would only be a few times faster than a hosted frontier model, which would not change much. The whole reason these chips are interesting is that they clear the hosted rate by a much wider margin than that.

options.text: Tens of tokens per second
options.feedback: That is the range a hosted frontier model already occupies, so a chip that delivered it would offer nothing new. The specialized chips buy speed at the price of model size, and the speed gain is dramatic.

options.text: A few tokens per second
options.feedback: That is what you get on a laptop with no GPU (graphics processing unit) -- the slow end of the range, not the fast end. Purpose-built inference hardware sits at the opposite extreme.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Why does a model take noticeably longer to write out a long answer than to take in a long prompt?

options.text: The prompt is usually shorter than the answer, so there is simply less of it to process.
options.feedback: Length is not the explanation -- paste in a very long document and it is still absorbed quickly. The difference is in how the two phases run, not in how many tokens each one involves.

options.text: Taking in the prompt skips the decoder stacks, which only run during generation.
options.feedback: The decoder stacks run over the prompt too; that is how the model builds any representation of it at all. What differs is that the prompt's tokens do not have to wait for each other.

options.text: Most of the prompt is handled at once, while each token waits on the one before it.
options.feedback: The context arrives as one big collection and is processed largely in parallel. Generation cannot work that way -- each token has to be produced and fed back in before the next can be chosen, and that sequential loop is the slow part.

options.text: Generation runs slower because the model raises its accuracy while it is answering.
options.feedback: There is no separate accuracy setting that kicks in mid-answer. The slowdown is structural: generation is a one-at-a-time loop, whereas reading the context is not.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: When you first submit a large context to a model, how is that context handled?

options.text: Strictly one token at a time, in the order you typed it
options.feedback: That describes generation, not intake. Your context is already complete when it arrives, so there is nothing to wait for and the model does not have to walk it in sequence.

options.text: In chunks, with each chunk finished before the next one starts
options.feedback: Staging it that way would still make one part of your context wait on another, and that waiting is what makes generation slow. Because the whole context is present from the start, much of the work over it can go on at the same time.

options.text: Token by token, but faster than generation because nothing is written to the screen
options.feedback: Display is not the bottleneck. Generation is slow because each token depends on the one before it -- and that dependency simply does not exist for text you have already supplied.

options.text: Largely in parallel, since it arrives all at once
options.feedback: The whole context is available up front, so the work over it can be spread out rather than serialized. That is why pasting a long document costs surprisingly little time compared with waiting for a long answer.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A colleague runs a medium-sized model on a specialized inference chip at about 3,000 tokens per second, and allows it 30,000 tokens of working-out before it answers. Roughly how long does that take, and why does it matter?

options.text: About five minutes, so this kind of deliberation has to be run as an overnight batch job
options.feedback: Work the arithmetic: 30,000 divided by 3,000 is not in the minutes at all. Because it lands far below that, this stops being a batch job and becomes something you can wait through.

options.text: About ten seconds, so a heavily worked-through answer arrives almost immediately
options.feedback: Thirty thousand tokens at three thousand per second is ten seconds of wall-clock time. A year earlier that same ten seconds would only have bought a glib answer delivered quickly, and that shift is what makes the fast-chip argument interesting.

options.text: About ten minutes, which is why chips like this are used for training rather than answering
options.feedback: These chips are inference hardware -- they exist to run finished models, not to train them. And the time involved is seconds, not minutes, which is the entire point of the example.

options.text: About a tenth of a second, because tokens generated for the model itself are not produced one at a time
options.feedback: Tokens the model produces for its own use are generated exactly like visible ones, one after another. They count against the same tokens-per-second rate, so 30,000 of them takes real time.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: What is the trade-off made by the chips built specifically to run this model architecture?

options.text: They give up capacity for speed -- too small for a frontier model, but very quick on a mid-sized one.
options.feedback: Capacity is what these chips sacrifice and speed is what they buy. That is why the interesting question becomes whether a mid-sized model allowed to work at length can stand in for a very large one.

options.text: They give up speed for capacity -- any size of model fits, but it runs no faster than on a laptop.
options.feedback: This is the deal inverted. A chip that held any model but generated at laptop speed would interest nobody; the reason anyone is building them is the speed.

options.text: They give up inference for training -- they make training much quicker, but do not run finished models.
options.feedback: These are inference chips: they run finished models, which is the phase you sit and wait through. The number attached to them, thousands of tokens per second, is a generation speed.

options.text: They give up generation speed for intake speed -- prompts are absorbed faster, answers are not.
options.feedback: Taking in the prompt is already the fast phase, because much of that work happens in parallel. Speeding it up buys little; these chips attack generation, the sequential part that actually costs you time.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The lecture argued that a small model on very fast hardware might match a much larger model on some work, then said the full case could not be made yet. What was the argument, and what was missing?

options.text: A small model carries the same world knowledge as a large one; the case waits until training is covered.
options.feedback: World knowledge is exactly what a smaller model gives up -- that is the trade you make when you go smaller. The argument for small models has to come from somewhere else than pretending the gap is not there.

options.text: Speed makes each individual token more accurate; the case waits until hardware is covered in depth.
options.feedback: Running faster does not change what any single token is -- one token is one token either way. The gain from speed is that a great deal of work becomes cheap in time, not that the work becomes better per token.

options.text: Cheap speed lets a small model work at length; the full case needs agents and the harness.
options.feedback: If working through a problem costs almost nothing in time, a small model can afford a great deal of it, and on some tasks that closes the gap to a very large model. The reason the argument is incomplete is that what a model can do with all that cheap work depends on the agent and its harness, which come later in the course.

options.text: Open-weight models are consistently larger than hosted ones; the case waits on the licensing question.
options.feedback: Openly available models are generally in the small-to-medium range, which is the reason fast chips suit them. Licensing was not the gap in the argument -- the missing piece was agents.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: As a model produces the tenth token of its answer, what happens to the context it has already processed?

options.text: Every earlier token is encoded and embedded again from scratch, once per new token.
options.feedback: That would make generation vastly slower than it is, and slower still as the answer grew. The model does reinterpret the context, but it does not start the whole job over.

options.text: The earlier context is thrown away, and the model works only from the token it just wrote.
options.feedback: If that were so, the model could not stay on topic past a sentence. The earlier context is still very much in play -- what changes is that the model avoids redoing work it has already done on it.

options.text: Only a short summary of the earlier context is kept, and the individual tokens are dropped.
options.feedback: Nothing is compressed away like that; the whole context is still there for the model to work over. What gets saved between tokens is repeated computation, not the text itself.

options.text: Stored state is reused -- the KV (key/value) cache -- so the same work is not repeated.
options.feedback: There are well-known tricks for keeping state around so earlier work is not thrown away, and the KV cache is the one people name. When a vendor says their model is special because of its KV cache, this is what they are talking about.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A classmate installs a model on a laptop with no GPU (graphics processing unit) and says the answer crawls out a word at a time, while the same kind of model in a browser feels close to instant. What best explains the gap?

options.text: The local copy has fewer parameters, so it needs more time to reach the same answer.
options.feedback: Fewer parameters means less capability, not more time -- a smaller model is the faster one, all else equal. The gap here is hardware, not model size.

options.text: The hosted copy runs on hardware that produces roughly ten times more tokens per second.
options.feedback: About 5 tokens per second on a bare laptop against roughly 60 from a hosted service is more than an order of magnitude, and you feel every bit of it because generation is sequential. Same architecture, same code -- different hardware doing the arithmetic.

options.text: The browser holds the whole answer back until it is finished, so nothing is genuinely faster.
options.feedback: Hosted interfaces stream tokens as they arrive, which is why you watch text appear. The speed difference you are seeing is real, not a display trick.

options.text: The laptop has to re-encode the entire context before each token, which the server avoids.
options.feedback: Neither one starts over per token -- that is what stored state such as the KV (key/value) cache is for, and it is part of the same software in both places. The laptop is simply doing the arithmetic on slower hardware.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A student asked how a model learns, given that it is not a brain. What did the lecture say actually happens?

options.text: It predicts the next piece of the signal and is corrected -- backpropagation.
options.feedback: An architecture is designed, a capability is provided, and then the whole of training is that one instruction: predict the next piece of the signal, and be corrected. Nothing about language is stated in advance.

options.text: Linguists write the rules of grammar into the model before training begins.
options.feedback: No logic and no rules are programmed in at any point. Whatever the model represents about grammar is worked out from the signal it was asked to predict, which is a genuinely different kind of system.

options.text: It searches a stored collection of example sentences at the moment you ask it something.
options.feedback: That describes a lookup system, not a trained model. There is no collection of sentences to consult -- there are weights, and they were arrived at by repeated correction during training.

options.text: Its logic is designed by hand, then tuned by engineers across successive releases.
options.feedback: Hand-designed logic is exactly what this family of models does without. Engineers design the architecture and the training setup; the content of what the model knows comes from the training procedure.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: If nobody writes grammar into a language model, where does whatever it represents about the rules of language come from?

options.text: From a rule table that the architecture supplies before training starts.
options.feedback: The architecture supplies a capability -- a shape that can learn -- not any content. There is no table of rules anywhere in it before training runs.

options.text: From your prompt, which has to carry the rules the model needs each time.
options.feedback: Your prompt supplies the context for one exchange, not the model's grasp of language. It arrives at the model already able to handle grammar, which is why a two-word prompt still gets a fluent reply.

options.text: From the training signal itself, by guessing what comes next.
options.feedback: The instruction during training is only ever predict the next thing in this signal, and being corrected on that is the sole source of what the model represents. It is a strong claim and worth sitting with: the structure was never told to it.

options.text: From a grammar checker applied to the model's output after it is generated.
options.feedback: There is no separate corrector downstream of generation -- the output is simply the tokens the model chose. Fluency comes from the weights, which is to say from training.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The class was shown the formal pseudocode for a decoder-only transformer. In it, what do the matrices written W_e and W_p produce?

options.text: The probabilities over the vocabulary at the very end
options.feedback: Those come from the softmax on the final line, not from these matrices. W_e and W_p are near the top of the pseudocode, acting before any decoder stack has run.

options.text: The weighted average that attention computes over nearby tokens
options.feedback: That is the attention step, which appears further down as its own routine. W_e and W_p run before attention and supply the vectors that attention then works on.

options.text: The dense two-layer network inside each decoder stack
options.feedback: That network is the MLP (multi-layer perceptron), written with its own pair of matrices further down. W_e and W_p belong to the very first stage instead.

options.text: The token embeddings, position included
options.feedback: W_e is the token embedding matrix and W_p the positional one, so together they map a sequence of token IDs into the embedding space with order encoded. On the pipeline diagram you already know, this is the token embeddings stage.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In the transformer pseudocode, the line that reads MHAttention(...) stands for what, and how often does it occur in the model?

options.text: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron), appearing once for the model as a whole
options.feedback: The MLP is a separate piece written with its own weight matrices, and it is not what MHAttention names. Neither component appears just once -- both are repeated through the stack.

options.text: Multi-head attention, one per decoder stack
options.feedback: MHAttention is multi-head attention, and it recurs once in each decoder stack rather than a single time. Notice how compact it is on the slide -- attention itself runs to about five lines.

options.text: The softmax over the vocabulary, applied once at the end
options.feedback: The softmax is the final line, producing the probabilities. MHAttention sits inside the repeated block, well before any probabilities are formed.

options.text: The positional embedding, applied once per token
options.feedback: Position is handled by the embedding matrix near the top of the pseudocode. MHAttention is the mechanism that moves a token's meaning using the tokens around it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: In the transformer pseudocode, two weight matrices written W_mlp1 and W_mlp2, with a step called GELU (Gaussian error linear unit) between them, are the linear algebra for which component?

options.text: The MLP (multi-layer perceptron), a dense two-layer network
options.feedback: Those two matrices with a step between them are the whole of the MLP in symbols -- the dense two-layer network sitting inside each decoder stack. The symbols are short; what they stand for are very large matrices of learned numbers.

options.text: The multi-head attention mechanism inside each decoder stack
options.feedback: Attention appears separately, as its own routine of about five lines. It moves meaning between tokens, while this pair of matrices works on a token's representation on its own.

options.text: The tokenizer that turns your text into token IDs
options.feedback: Tokenization happens before the pseudocode begins -- its input is already a sequence of token IDs. These matrices act deep inside each decoder stack.

options.text: The softmax that yields the probabilities over the vocabulary
options.feedback: That is the return line at the very bottom of the pseudocode. W_mlp1 and W_mlp2 run much earlier, inside the repeated stack.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The last line of the transformer pseudocode returns a softmax. What does that softmax give you?

options.text: The single token that the model has settled on saying next
options.feedback: Choosing one token is a further step taken after this. What the pseudocode returns is the full distribution that the choice is then made from.

options.text: The tokens the model produced for itself before answering
options.feedback: Those are generated by running this whole pseudocode repeatedly, one token at a time. A single pass through it returns something much narrower than a stretch of text.

options.text: A probability for every token in the vocabulary
options.feedback: One pass through the model ends with a number for each token the model could possibly say next, and that is the token probabilities stage on the pipeline diagram. Everything else in the picture exists to shape that distribution.

options.text: The weights the model arrived at during training
options.feedback: The weights are the matrices in the pseudocode, fixed before you ever run it. The return value is computed fresh for your context each time.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Having shown the pseudocode, the lecture made a point about size. What is genuinely enormous about a model like Opus?

options.text: The volume of code, which runs to millions of lines
options.feedback: The striking thing about the slide is how little there is -- attention alone is roughly five lines. Size lives somewhere other than the code.

options.text: The number of distinct rules the architecture states
options.feedback: The architecture states no rules about language at all; that is what makes it different from earlier approaches. Whatever the model represents was learned, and it lives in numbers rather than statements.

options.text: The length of the attention routine, which dominates the listing
options.feedback: Attention is about five lines -- among the shortest parts of the slide, not the longest. Its compactness is exactly the surprise.

options.text: The weights -- on the order of a trillion numbers
options.feedback: The symbols in the pseudocode stand for matrices, and at this scale those matrices hold roughly a trillion values. Very little code, an unimaginable quantity of numbers, is a fair one-line summary of the whole family.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A student asks what a model's parameter count is actually counting. What is the answer?

options.text: How many separate rules are written into the architecture
options.feedback: No rules are written in anywhere, so there is nothing of that kind to count. What can be counted is the numbers, and those are what the term refers to.

options.text: How many individual numbers are stored in its weight matrices
options.feedback: Parameters are numbers, plainly -- the values filling all those matrices -- so the count is a broad measure of how much it takes to represent the model. It is a rough proxy for capability, not a precise one.

options.text: How many tokens the model can hold in its context at once
options.feedback: That is the context window, a separate quantity entirely. A model's parameters are fixed after training, while what fits in its context is about each individual conversation.

options.text: How many training documents the model was shown
options.feedback: Training data volume is a different measure and is not what the number reports. Parameter count describes the model itself once training has finished.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Which of these would raise a model's parameter count?

options.text: Adding more decoder layers to the stack
options.feedback: Each extra layer is another copy of the attention and MLP (multi-layer perceptron) matrices, so more layers means more numbers. Widening the MLP or the embedding space does the same thing by a different route.

options.text: Loading the finished model onto hardware with more memory
options.feedback: Memory determines whether a model will run, not how many numbers it contains. The count is fixed by the design before training and does not vary with the machine.

options.text: Asking it questions that are longer and more detailed
options.feedback: What you send changes the context, not the model. The weights are the same for every user and every prompt.

options.text: Keeping more of the context in the KV (key/value) cache
options.feedback: That cache holds working state from your conversation so the model does not repeat computation over the context; it is not part of what the model is. Parameters are the trained weights, and they are the same numbers before and after any conversation.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: A team is about to train a model and decides to double the width of its embedding space, changing nothing else in the design. What have they done?

options.text: Doubled how much text the finished model can hold in its context
options.feedback: Embedding width is how many dimensions each token's representation has, not how many tokens fit. Those are independent choices and this one does not touch the context window.

options.text: Made the finished model faster, since a wider space needs fewer layers
options.feedback: Width and depth are set separately -- widening one does not remove the other. A wider model has more numbers to multiply, so if anything it runs slower.

options.text: Created room for more parameters, which training then has to fill
options.feedback: Widths like this are hyperparameters, fixed before training starts, and raising one enlarges the matrices that hold the model's numbers. Those extra numbers arrive empty and only become useful once training has filled them, so the decision buys capacity, not capability.

options.text: Added knowledge to the model before any training has taken place
options.feedback: Nothing the model knows is put in by hand at any stage. Enlarging the design creates space; only training, guessing what comes next and being corrected, puts anything into it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: What does an agent have that a plain chat does not?

options.text: A bigger LLM (large language model) inside it, carrying far more parameters than chat uses
options.feedback: The same model can sit inside either one -- you can converse with an agent just as you would in chat. What is added is around the model, not a bigger model.

options.text: A longer context window, letting it take in much more of your prompt at one time
options.feedback: Context length belongs to the model, and agents do not change it by themselves. What an agent adds is places to put things other than the context window.

options.text: A dedicated inference chip, so that it produces its tokens several times more quickly
options.feedback: Speed comes from the hardware a model runs on, and that is a separate question from whether you are in chat or in an agent. An agent is not faster; it is better equipped.

options.text: A file system it can write to, memory, task tracking, and skills
options.feedback: Chat is context in and tokens out. An agent has the model inside it plus somewhere to keep files, memory that persists, a way of tracking what it is doing, and skills -- which is why it can carry out work rather than only discuss it.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: Claude now shows two modes under the prompt box, Chat and Cowork. What separates them?

options.text: Chat runs a smaller model, while Cowork always runs the largest one you have access to
options.feedback: Model choice is a separate control, and either mode can use whichever model you pick. The distinction is what surrounds the model, not which model it is.

options.text: Chat is context in and tokens out; Cowork is an agent
options.feedback: Everything covered so far -- prompt, context, next token -- is chat. Cowork wraps that same model in a file system, memory, task tracking, and skills, which is what makes it an agent.

options.text: Chat retains your history, while Cowork forgets everything between messages
options.feedback: This has it backwards: memory is one of the things an agent adds. Cowork keeps more across a piece of work, not less.

options.text: Chat runs in a browser, while Cowork is only available at the command line
options.feedback: Both appear under the prompt box in the same interface. The command-line tool is a separate thing that comes later in the course.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: The lecture said most people's picture of generative AI stops at one way of using it. Which one, and what does that leave them unaware of?

options.text: It stops at chat, so they do not know that agents exist.
options.feedback: Most people have only ever met a prompt box, so their sense of these systems ends at context in and tokens out. An agent runs the same model with a file system, memory, task tracking, and skills around it, and that is the part they never see.

options.text: It stops at the browser, so they do not know a desktop application exists.
options.feedback: Which window you use matters less than what is around the model. The desktop app is worth installing because it can be pointed at a folder on your machine, and that folder is an agent's file system -- the agent is the point, not the app.

options.text: It stops at the default model, so they do not know the tiers can be changed.
options.feedback: Choosing a model is a real control, and one of the two you have in a chat setup. But someone who switches models every day is still working in chat, which is the boundary people do not see past.

options.text: It stops at short prompts, so they do not know long documents can be pasted in.
options.feedback: Getting the right material into context is a genuine skill and the lecture keeps returning to it. Pasting in a long document is still chat, though: context in, tokens out, with nothing around the model.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You want the version of Claude that can work with files on your own computer rather than only inside a browser tab. Which of the products on Claude's apps and extensions page should you install?

options.text: Claude for Chrome, because a browser is where the agent needs to run
options.feedback: That extension works inside the browser, which is precisely the setting you are trying to leave. To reach files on your machine you want the application that installs on it.

options.text: Claude Code, the CLI (command-line interface), which is the desktop version under another name
options.feedback: Claude Code is a separate tool that runs in a terminal, and it does come up later in the semester. It is not the desktop application, and it is not what to install this weekend.

options.text: Desktop, then download the build for macOS or Windows
options.feedback: Desktop is the entry to take, and the installer is offered for either operating system. That is the version that can be pointed at a folder on your machine, which is what turns a chat window into something more useful.

options.text: Claude for Design, which is the desktop application listed under its product name
options.feedback: Claude for Design is its own separate product, not an alias for the desktop app. Take the one labelled Desktop; the others on that page do different jobs.

questions.source: Quiz 2 - Sessions 1-3: Choosing a Model and Thinking Budgets
questions.question: You have installed the desktop app and want to give an agent access to your files so it can help you write up a research project. What should you point it at?

options.text: Your whole Documents folder, so that nothing it might need is left out
options.feedback: Handing over everything is the instinct to resist. Most of what is in there has nothing to do with this project, and the aim is to get the right material in front of the agent rather than the most material.

options.text: Everything on your computer, so it can locate files wherever they happen to sit
options.feedback: This is the version of the mistake with the widest blast radius, both for privacy and for usefulness. Breadth of access is not what makes an agent good at a task.

options.text: Your Downloads folder, since that is where new material tends to arrive
options.feedback: Downloads is a pile of unrelated things, which is the opposite of a focused working space. Move what belongs to the project into its own folder first.

options.text: One subdirectory holding that project's papers and files
options.feedback: The name of the game is getting the right material into context, and a folder is just another way of doing what a good prompt does. The class survey presentation was made exactly this way: an agent given one subdirectory of survey responses and asked to make sense of them.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What is seat-minder, the app the instructor demoed at the start of session 4?

options.text: A grading tool that scores lab reports against a rubric
options.feedback: That is the grading-skill demo described later in the session, not seat-minder. Seat-minder handles check-in and cold-calling, not grading.

options.text: A scheduling tool for booking office hours
options.feedback: Office-hours booking never comes up in the notes. Seat-minder is about in-class check-in and cold-calling, not appointment scheduling.

options.text: A check-in and cold-calling web app for the class
options.feedback: Students scan a QR code and tap their seat to check in, and the app then lets the instructor see who is present, who has opted in to being called on, and pull up a photo and name before calling on someone.

options.text: A skill-editing tool for revising the lecture-notes skill
options.feedback: Editing the lecture-notes skill was a separate part of the session, a different exercise from building seat-minder.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: How do students check in with seat-minder at the start of class?

options.text: They scan a QR code and tap their seat on a chart of the room
options.feedback: That is the flow the notes describe: scan the QR code, tap the seat you are sitting in on the seating chart, and you are checked in.

options.text: They type their VUnetID into a web form
options.feedback: Typing an identifier is not part of the flow described in the notes; check-in runs through a QR scan and a seat tap instead.

options.text: They raise their hand and the instructor marks them present
options.feedback: Raising a hand belongs to the later cold-calling view, not to how the initial check-in happens.

options.text: They swipe a student ID card at the door
options.feedback: No card swipe appears in the notes; the described entry point is the QR code and the seating chart.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The seat-minder project began with a 'North Star' problem statement. What did that statement describe?

options.text: The exact database schema and table design the app would need
options.feedback: A schema is a technical detail. The North Star named the problem to be solved, and it came before any technical decision was made.

options.text: The programming languages and hosting provider the build had to use
options.feedback: Those choices came later, and the agent made them from stated requirements. The North Star itself named no technology at all.

options.text: How the app would compare with competing classroom check-in tools
options.feedback: No competitor comparison appears in the notes. The starting point was a personal account of a problem, not market research.

options.text: Knowing students' names, who will take a cold call, and their thinking
options.feedback: That is close to what was actually typed into the agent: a statement about students going unnoticed in a large class, tied to knowing names, knowing who is willing to be called on, and knowing what people are thinking before class begins.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does it matter that seat-minder began with a problem statement (the North Star) rather than a technical specification?

options.text: Technical specifications are not allowed when you are directing an agent
options.feedback: Nothing in the notes bans a technical spec. Implementation guidance, like the airline seat-reservation analogy, arrived later, layered on top of the North Star.

options.text: It fixed what the software had to accomplish before any implementation detail
options.feedback: The North Star was the thing the software actually had to do. Only after that came implementation guidance, and the agent picked the technologies from there.

options.text: It was necessary because the instructor could not have written a specification
options.feedback: Requirements and guidance were given confidently throughout the build. The point is sequencing the goal ahead of the details, not an inability to specify anything.

options.text: It guaranteed that the finished software would ship without any bugs
options.feedback: A real concurrency risk still had to be named and guarded against, so starting from a problem statement did not remove the correctness work.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What implementation guidance was added after seat-minder's North Star was stated?

options.text: Model it on an airline seat-reservation system, where a seat is kept or changed
options.feedback: That is the analogy the notes give, alongside tracking attendance so repeated absences can be followed up and making the app robust enough to survive real use.

options.text: Build it as a native mobile app distributed through the iOS and Android stores
options.feedback: The notes describe a Vercel-hosted web backend that students reach from a QR code, with no native mobile app anywhere in the picture.

options.text: Use only open-source models and open-source libraries for every part of the build
options.feedback: No open-source-only constraint appears in the notes. The guidance covered the seating analogy, attendance tracking, and robustness.

options.text: Require every student to create an individual account with a username and password
options.feedback: The described check-in is a QR scan and a seat tap, with no account creation or password step in between.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A student has now missed more than one class session in a row. Based on how seat-minder's attendance tracking is described in the notes, what should happen next?

options.text: The student is automatically dropped from the course roster
options.feedback: No automatic drop appears in the notes. The consequence described is a personal follow-up, not an administrative action.

options.text: Nothing in particular, since seat-minder only records who is present each day
options.feedback: Attendance is recorded through seat-minder precisely so a pattern like this surfaces, rather than being logged and then left alone.

options.text: The student's seat is reassigned to someone else for the rest of the semester
options.feedback: The airline-style model lets you keep your seat or pick a new one each class, so no seat is taken away over absences.

options.text: The instructor follows up with that student personally
options.feedback: The notes say a no-show over more than one class period triggers a personal follow-up, which is part of why attendance is being recorded this way this semester.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The instructor said about seat-minder: 'Yes, I used AI to help me solve that problem. Also, yes, technically I created the software. But what I was really doing was using AI to create a solution.' What distinction is this drawing?

options.text: Free consumer AI tools versus paid professional ones
options.feedback: Cost is not the contrast here. The quote is about what role a person plays in a build, not about what the tools charge.

options.text: Frontend web programming versus backend server programming
options.feedback: That split is a detail of the stack seat-minder ended up with, not the thing this quote sets against itself.

options.text: Writing the code yourself versus directing an agent to build it
options.feedback: The quote separates literal authorship of the code from what actually happened: a problem and a set of requirements were specified, and the agent did the engineering that turned them into software.

options.text: Reasoning models versus non-reasoning models on hard tasks
options.feedback: That distinction belongs to the Lab 1 debrief later in the session, not to this quote about how the software came to exist.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Which technologies did seat-minder end up using, as described in the notes?

options.text: A Ruby on Rails application backed by a MySQL database
options.feedback: Rails and MySQL appear nowhere in the notes; the stack described is JavaScript and Python over a Postgres-compatible database.

options.text: JavaScript and Python on Vercel, with a Postgres-compatible database
options.feedback: That is the stack the notes describe (Neon for the database), and the agent picked it from stated requirements rather than having it dictated up front.

options.text: A no-code drag-and-drop site builder with no database behind it
options.feedback: The notes describe a real database absorbing many simultaneous check-ins, which is exactly the work a database-free builder could not do.

options.text: A shared spreadsheet that every student in the room edits live
options.feedback: No spreadsheet approach appears in the notes; seat-minder is a hosted web backend with its own database.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Who actually chose seat-minder's technology stack (JavaScript, Python, Vercel, Neon)?

options.text: The agent, working from the requirements it was given
options.feedback: The notes credit the agent with the choice: requirements such as running on Vercel and needing a database of a particular kind were supplied, and the agent selected the technologies to satisfy them.

options.text: A committee of teaching assistants who reviewed several options
options.feedback: No committee or teaching-assistant review of the stack appears in the notes; the choice is attributed to the agent.

options.text: The instructor, from years of experience with each technology
options.feedback: The notes contrast exactly this: requirements were given rather than every technology being personally known, and that is part of why the build moved so fast.

options.text: Vanderbilt's IT department, following a mandated technology list
options.feedback: No institutional mandate is mentioned. The technologies follow from the requirements the agent was working to.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The agent building seat-minder was told things like 'it has to run on Vercel, it needs a database like this,' rather than being handed every detail of the stack. What do the notes say this approach made possible?

options.text: Testing the software was no longer necessary before it went live
options.feedback: Refinement carried on over several days and the concurrency risk got specific attention, so nothing about this approach skipped testing.

options.text: The agent was guaranteed never to make a design mistake
options.feedback: A real concurrency risk still had to be called out separately, so requirement-level direction did not head off every possible mistake.

options.text: The project could skip having a North Star problem statement
options.feedback: These requirements came after the North Star, as guidance layered on top of it rather than as a substitute for it.

options.text: Reaching a working solution faster than by knowing every technology first
options.feedback: Giving requirements instead of specifying each technology got to a solution far faster, with a first working prototype coming together in about an hour.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What specific engineering problem did seat-minder face with around 120 students potentially checking in within the same few seconds?

options.text: The QR code image failing to render correctly on some students' phones
options.feedback: No rendering failure appears in the notes. The problem described happens after students are already scanning and tapping.

options.text: Students being unable to find the check-in link on their own
options.feedback: Findability is not raised as an issue; the difficulty starts once many students are checking in at once.

options.text: A concurrency problem: two check-ins racing for the same seat or row
options.feedback: Many check-ins landing in the same few seconds can collide, with two students claiming one seat or two requests updating the same database row at the same instant.

options.text: The seating chart forgetting a student's seat between one class and the next
options.feedback: Keeping a seat or picking a new one is expected behavior in the airline-style model, not the failure the notes are describing.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why was the agent asked for 'defensive, non-blocking code' while seat-minder was being built?

options.text: To make the app look more polished and professional on screen
options.feedback: This request is about handling simultaneous check-ins correctly. Appearance came up separately, when a later model produced a prettier interface.

options.text: To survive many students checking in at nearly the same moment
options.feedback: With around 120 students arriving within the same few seconds, requests can race to claim one seat or update one database row, and this is the kind of code that keeps that from corrupting the result.

options.text: To reduce how much the Vercel hosting for the app would cost
options.feedback: Hosting cost is never offered as a motivation. The stated reason is the crush of check-ins at the start of class.

options.text: To make sure the app kept working without an internet connection
options.feedback: Offline use is not discussed anywhere in the notes; students reach a hosted web backend by scanning a QR code.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What lesson does the seat-minder build illustrate about directing an agent to write software, according to the notes?

options.text: Moving the typing to an agent does not remove the need to state requirements
options.feedback: Correctness, concurrency, and privacy still have to be asked for out loud. The seat-minder concurrency risk is the same category of bug a hand-written system would have to guard against.

options.text: An agent finds and fixes every bug in a build without being asked to
options.feedback: The notes show the opposite: defensive, non-blocking code had to be requested explicitly rather than turning up unprompted.

options.text: Agents can only build software that has no database behind it at all
options.feedback: Seat-minder runs on a Postgres-compatible database, so the notes contradict this one directly.

options.text: Directing an agent removes the need for a clear problem statement first
options.feedback: The sequence runs the other way: the North Star problem statement came first, and the agent-directed build followed from it.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What does it mean that seat-minder was built as a 'clean room' with respect to student data?

options.text: The app was tested in a sandboxed environment with no live student data
options.feedback: That is a reasonable everyday reading of 'clean room', but here the term is about the code itself rather than about a separate testing environment.

options.text: Only the instructor was allowed to view the completed app
options.feedback: The teaching view is used in class, but who is allowed to look at the app is not what 'clean room' refers to here.

options.text: The database was wiped at the end of each semester
options.feedback: Data retention is not discussed in the notes. The clean-room point is about what the code does and does not contain.

options.text: The code itself never has any student's name or photo written into it directly
options.feedback: The program is written to know that a roster and a set of images exist somewhere it can read, and to look them up at runtime, rather than carrying anyone's name or photo inside it.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does seat-minder look up student names and photos from a roster at runtime instead of hard-coding them into the program?

options.text: Hard-coding names and photos would make the app run noticeably slower
options.feedback: Speed is not the reason given. The reasoning is about privacy, and about a habit worth keeping whenever an agent handles personal data.

options.text: Runtime lookups of this kind are required by the Vercel hosting platform
options.feedback: No hosting requirement of this kind is mentioned; the practice is described as a general good habit, not a constraint of the platform.

options.text: It keeps personal data out of the code itself, by design
options.feedback: The program knows only that a roster and a set of images exist somewhere it can read, which is the same privacy-by-design pattern this course's own FERPA-safe roster tooling uses.

options.text: It lets the app work for a student not yet added to the roster
options.feedback: Missing roster entries are not discussed. The stated reason is keeping personal data out of the program rather than covering an edge case.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Suppose you are directing an agent to build a new app that will display students' photos next to their quiz scores. Based on the privacy-by-design pattern described for seat-minder, what should you ask the agent to do?

options.text: Embed a snapshot of the current roster and photos directly into the app's code so it always has the data on hand
options.feedback: This is exactly the hard-coding pattern seat-minder was built to avoid. The notes favor looking data up from a source rather than writing it into the program.

options.text: Have the app read student names, photos, and scores from a roster and gradebook source at runtime, the way seat-minder reads its roster and images
options.feedback: This mirrors the pattern the notes describe: the code should know a data source exists and look it up, rather than having personal data written into the program itself.

options.text: Store the data in a spreadsheet emailed to every student
options.feedback: Broadly distributing personal data to every student is not the privacy pattern described. The notes emphasize the program looking up data it needs, not sharing it out.

options.text: Ask the agent not to worry about privacy since it is only used by the instructor
options.feedback: The notes present privacy-by-design as a general habit to build in regardless of who else can see the interface, not something to skip because access seems limited.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: During class a student raises their hand in seat-minder, and the instructor taps that raised hand on the teaching-view seating chart. What does that show?

options.text: That student's photo and name, plus photos and names of several neighboring seats
options.feedback: The notes describe exactly this: tapping a raised hand pulls up the student's photo and name along with several neighbors, useful for calling on that student or picking someone nearby.

options.text: A running transcript of everything the student has said in class so far
options.feedback: No transcript feature is described in the teaching view. It surfaces photos, names, and neighboring seats, not a log of speech.

options.text: The student's grades on previous quizzes and labs
options.feedback: Seat-minder's teaching view is about check-in, cold-calling, and attendance, not gradebook data. No grade display is described in the notes.

options.text: A confirmation that the student has been marked absent
options.feedback: This reverses the situation described: a raised hand means the student is present and checked in, and tapping it surfaces identifying information, not an absence marking.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: How does seat-minder indicate which students are comfortable being cold-called?

options.text: By listing their names in a footer at the bottom of the screen
options.feedback: No footer list appears in the notes. The opt-in shows up on the seating chart itself, where the rest of the information already lives.

options.text: By hiding students who opted out from the seating chart entirely
options.feedback: Nobody is hidden. The chart still shows every seat; students who opt in simply get a distinct highlight on top of it.

options.text: With a distinct highlight, described as 'OK to call on,' for students who opt in
options.feedback: Students mark separately whether they are comfortable being cold-called, and that highlight is what makes it possible to choose someone confidently rather than at random.

options.text: By ranking students from most to least willing on a leaderboard
options.feedback: No ranking appears in the notes. What is described is a yes-or-no opt-in shown as a highlight, not a scored ordering.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why is it useful that tapping a raised hand also shows the photos and names of neighboring seats, not just the student whose hand is raised?

options.text: It fills otherwise empty space on the instructor's screen
options.feedback: The notes present this as a working part of cold-calling, not as a way to use up room on the display.

options.text: It lets the instructor take attendance for the whole row at once
options.feedback: Attendance comes from check-in, which has already happened by the time anyone raises a hand, so nothing about tapping a hand records it.

options.text: It shows which nearby students have opted in to being cold-called
options.feedback: The 'OK to call on' highlight is already visible on the chart for everyone who opted in, so tapping a raised hand is not what reveals it.

options.text: It supports calling on that student or on someone sitting nearby
options.feedback: Seeing the neighbors alongside the raised hand leaves you a choice: take the hand that is up, or bring in someone close by who has not spoken yet.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: How did seat-minder change the instructor's experience of cold-calling, according to the notes?

options.text: It let him call on people by name and photo, knowing who opted in
options.feedback: Check-in supplies the names and photos and the opt-in highlight supplies the willingness, so a cold call in a large room stops being a call on an unidentified student.

options.text: It let him skip cold-calling, with the app picking answers for students
options.feedback: The app helps identify and choose who to call on; it never answers on a student's behalf.

options.text: It let him grade students automatically from the answers they gave
options.feedback: Grading turns up later in the session as a separate demo with a rubric and an agent, not as anything seat-minder does.

options.text: It let him limit cold-calling to only the top-performing students
options.feedback: The opt-in is about comfort with being called on, not about performance, and no grade data feeds the seating chart at all.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In the Lab 1 debrief, what task did a student use to compare a mid-size Claude model with reasoning turned off against the same model with reasoning turned on?

options.text: Working out the day of the week for a given date
options.feedback: Getting that right turns on fiddly details such as leap years, which is what made it a useful way to see whether reasoning changes the outcome.

options.text: Summarizing a long research paper down to a few paragraphs
options.feedback: Summarization is not the comparison described in the debrief; the task chosen had a single checkable right answer.

options.text: Translating a paragraph of text from English into Spanish
options.feedback: No translation task appears in the debrief. The comparison used a calculation whose answer could be marked right or wrong.

options.text: Writing a short poem about the seat-minder check-in app
options.feedback: No creative-writing task is described. The point of the comparison was a task where a missed detail produces a clearly wrong answer.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture stresses that a reasoning model generates tokens one at a time in exactly the same way a non-reasoning model does. Where, then, does its ability to check itself before answering come from?

options.text: From post-training, very likely a form of reinforcement learning
options.feedback: Nothing about token-by-token generation changes. What post-training adds is the habit of spending some of those tokens on a private scratch space -- restating the problem, trying answers, weighing them against each other -- before committing to a reply.

options.text: From a separate verification model that checks each draft answer
options.feedback: It is tempting to picture a second model marking the first one's work, but the lecture describes one model producing one stream of tokens. The checking happens inside that stream, not in a reviewer standing beside it.

options.text: From a wider embedding space in the larger model tiers
options.feedback: Width is one of the levers that makes a model tier bigger, but the lecture keeps raw size separate from whether a model reasons. Reasoning is a behaviour training installs, not a size a model grows into.

options.text: From pre-training on a corpus made up mostly of step-by-step explanations
options.feedback: Pre-training is where a model picks up what it knows about the world. The lecture puts this capability one stage later, in the training that shapes how a model uses what it already knows.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: As explained in the Lab 1 debrief, what does a non-reasoning model do when it responds to a question?

options.text: It searches a database of previously answered questions for a match
options.feedback: That describes a lookup system. The model is still generating tokens rather than retrieving a stored answer, whether or not reasoning is switched on.

options.text: It picks a token from a probability distribution and commits right away
options.feedback: There is no stepping back and no assessing: the answer starts immediately, one token at a time, along whatever path the first choice sets.

options.text: It waits for a human to approve its draft before finalizing an answer
options.feedback: No approval step sits inside generation. The distinction being drawn is entirely about what the model does on its own before committing.

options.text: It generates several full answers and lets the user pick the best one
options.feedback: Generating and comparing candidate answers is close to what a reasoning model does privately, and it is never surfaced to you as a menu to choose from.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: According to the Lab 1 debrief, what capability does a reasoning-capable model have that a non-reasoning model lacks?

options.text: The ability to reach the internet for up-to-date information
options.feedback: External information access is a different capability. The debrief is about what happens inside the model before it commits to an answer.

options.text: The ability to generate longer and more detailed answers
options.feedback: Length is a side effect at most. A reasoning model can be brief; what changes is that it can weigh candidates before it settles.

options.text: The ability to run code in order to check its own answer
options.feedback: The checking described happens in tokens, in a private scratch space, not by handing the problem to a separate tool that executes it.

options.text: The ability to try and compare answers before committing to one
options.feedback: Those tokens build a private scratch space -- restating the problem, trying answers, checking them against each other -- and the capability comes from post-training rather than from any change in how tokens are generated.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A classmate is deciding whether to use a reasoning-enabled model or a non-reasoning model for a task that involves several small, easy-to-miss details, similar to the day-of-week calculation from Lab 1. Based on the debrief, what should they expect?

options.text: The reasoning model is more likely to succeed, since it can check answers first
options.feedback: That is the Lab 1 finding: the non-reasoning model committed immediately and got it wrong, while the reasoning model could compare candidates before settling on one.

options.text: There should be no difference, since both generate tokens the same basic way
options.feedback: Both do generate tokens the same basic way, which makes this tempting, but the extra step of checking work before committing is exactly what separated the two results.

options.text: The non-reasoning model is more likely to succeed, because it avoids overthinking
options.feedback: Speed is not accuracy here. On this task the faster model was the one that got the answer wrong, having committed with no chance to look again.

options.text: Neither model can be trusted with a task that turns on small details
options.feedback: The reasoning-enabled model handled this exact kind of fiddly-detail task, so the honest conclusion is about which mode you pick, not about giving up on both.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture offered two explanations for why even a very capable model like Opus 5 resists having its thinking turned off. What was the first explanation?

options.text: Its post-training likely leaned on reasoning traces from a strongly reasoning-oriented predecessor model.
options.feedback: This is the training-shapes-voice explanation: if a model learned its style and its standard for a good answer from another model's reasoning-heavy output, dropping reasoning can cost both the quality and the voice that training built in. The lecture offered this as the instructor's own reading, not a vendor disclosure.

options.text: Its vendor documentation reportedly forbids disabling reasoning for legal reasons.
options.feedback: No such documentation appears in the notes. Both explanations in the lecture were offered as the instructor's own reading of the situation rather than anything the model's maker had published.

options.text: Its attention mechanism probably cannot run without a reasoning step between tokens.
options.feedback: Mechanically nothing about token-by-token generation changes when reasoning is on or off -- the model still produces tokens the same way it always does. Reasoning is a mode that post-training adds, not something attention requires.

options.text: Its pre-training data apparently excluded examples of answering without reasoning.
options.feedback: This puts the explanation in the wrong stage. The lecture's point was about post-training -- what kind of reasoning traces shaped the model's later behavior -- not about what pre-training contained.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What was the lecture's second explanation for why a model like Opus 5 might resist turning off reasoning?

options.text: Without reasoning it would have no way to reach the knowledge stored in its weights.
options.feedback: Knowledge lives in the weights and is available on every pass, reasoning or not. Reasoning changes whether the model can lay out and compare candidate answers before committing, not whether it can reach what it learned.

options.text: It is built to run inside a harness as an agent on long, multi-step tasks.
options.feedback: A model meant to work as an agent for hours at a stretch benefits from having reasoning available throughout. That is a different design goal from a chat product optimized for the fastest possible reply, which would trade the other way.

options.text: Turning reasoning off would exceed the model's maximum context window.
options.feedback: The notes do not connect reasoning availability to context window size. A context window limits how much text the model can hold at once, not whether it reasons before answering.

options.text: Its weights cannot produce output without an internal looping pass.
options.feedback: This borrows the looped-transformer idea from later in the session, which is about refining a representation inside a stack. The notes never link looping to why reasoning stays on.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why might a model's post-training on a strongly reasoning-oriented predecessor's traces make the model dependent on reasoning to sound like itself?

options.text: Because reasoning traces permanently rewire which words the model's tokenizer can produce.
options.feedback: Tokenization is fixed independently of what post-training contains. The lecture's point was about the model's learned style and standard of quality, not about its vocabulary.

options.text: Because reasoning traces cost more to generate, which the model was trained to avoid.
options.feedback: Compute cost is not the mechanism the lecture described. The explanation was about what behavior the model learned to imitate, not about efficiency.

options.text: Because the model absorbed its standard for a good answer from reasoning-heavy examples.
options.feedback: The model's sense of what a good response looks like was built on reasoning-heavy output, so skipping reasoning can mean skipping the behavior it learned to reproduce well. The lecture offered this as an interpretation, not a disclosed fact.

options.text: Because a model can only imitate text it saw during pre-training, not post-training.
options.feedback: Post-training is exactly the stage that shapes how a model uses what pre-training gave it, including whether and how it reasons. That is where the lecture placed this effect.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why would a model meant to operate as an agent for long, multi-step tasks make a different trade-off about reasoning than a model built purely for fast chat replies?

options.text: Because an agent has to reason before it can generate any text at all.
options.feedback: Agents generate tokens the same way any model does. Reasoning is a mode available to them, not a precondition for producing text at all.

options.text: Because reasoning tokens do not count against an agent's context window budget.
options.feedback: Reasoning tokens occupy context like any other tokens, for agents and chat alike. The lecture's distinction was about intended use -- long multi-step work versus instant replies -- not about how tokens are counted.

options.text: Because the harness does the reasoning for the agent, on the model's behalf.
options.feedback: The harness supplies a file system, memory, task tracking, and skills; it does not think for the model. Reasoning still happens inside the model, which is why keeping it available matters for long agent work.

options.text: Because long tasks benefit from reasoning at each step, while chat trades it for speed.
options.feedback: An agent working through many linked steps benefits from having reasoning available throughout, whereas a product optimized for quick back-and-forth makes the opposite trade-off.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A student uses a top-tier reasoning model for a single quick factual question and is annoyed that it still 'thinks' for several seconds before answering, even though the question needs no multi-step work. Based on the lecture, which explanation best accounts for this?

options.text: It is built mainly to work as an agent on long tasks, so reasoning stays on.
options.feedback: A model designed to sustain multi-step agent work keeps reasoning available even when a particular request is short and simple. The lecture offered this as its own reading of the design choice, not as a documented setting.

options.text: It is deliberately slowed down so that people will not overuse it.
options.feedback: The notes describe no such throttling. The explanations given are about training and intended use, not about rate limiting.

options.text: Quick factual questions need more computation to answer than complex ones do.
options.feedback: This reverses the usual relationship, and nothing in the notes supports it. A short factual question does not inherently demand more computation than a hard one.

options.text: Looping forces every answer to pass through the decoder stack a second time.
options.feedback: Looping is a separate architectural idea about refining a representation inside a stack. The lecture never offered it as the reason reasoning cannot be turned off.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture is careful to frame both explanations for why Opus 5 keeps reasoning on as something specific. What is that framing?

options.text: A peer-reviewed finding published by an outside research lab.
options.feedback: No such publication appears in the notes. The explanations are presented as one person's reading of a model's behavior, which is a much weaker kind of evidence.

options.text: The instructor's own reading of the situation, not a disclosed vendor specification.
options.feedback: The notes say this explicitly, and it matters for how much weight to put on the two explanations: they are informed guesses about why a model behaves as it does, not confirmed technical documentation from its maker.

options.text: A confirmed detail from the model's official system card.
options.feedback: The notes deny this level of certainty. Treating an interpretation as an official disclosure is exactly the overreach the framing was guarding against.

options.text: A guess a student offered during the lab, not the instructor's.
options.feedback: The lab is where the finding came from -- students could not turn thinking off on Opus 5 -- but the two explanations for it came from the instructor.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: According to the lecture, what was the original working definition of AGI (artificial general intelligence) used across the field for decades?

options.text: Outperforming the best human expert at every possible task.
options.feedback: This is a far higher bar than the definition the lecture gave, which asked only for average human performance -- and the gap between the two bars is exactly what the moving-goalposts discussion is about.

options.text: Passing a specific, standardized written exam designed for AI systems.
options.feedback: The lecture did not define AGI by a single test. The definition was about the level and breadth of task performance, not about clearing one exam.

options.text: Performing at the level of an average human on most tasks.
options.feedback: The original bar was deliberately modest: typical human performance, across most tasks rather than all of them. Holding that definition steady is what lets you notice when it has been cleared.

options.text: Operating without human supervision for an extended period.
