options.feedback: Autonomy over time is a different property. The definition in the notes is about how well and how broadly a system performs, not about how long it runs unattended.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: By the original working definition described in the lecture, roughly when did the instructor argue the field actually crossed the AGI (artificial general intelligence) threshold?

options.text: At the moment Astra was released, during this class session.
options.feedback: The argument placed the crossing well before this release. Astra came up as the occasion for revisiting the definition, not as the moment the bar was met.

options.text: It has not been crossed yet by any released model.
options.feedback: This is the opposite of the argument made in class, which was that the line had already been passed under the older definition and simply went unremarked.

options.text: Sometime in the era of expert systems, decades ago.
options.feedback: The notes place the crossing far more recently -- about a year and a half before this lecture -- not in an earlier era of AI.

options.text: Roughly 18 months before this lecture, largely unnoticed.
options.feedback: That is the claim made in class, under the older and more modest definition of AGI. It is offered as the instructor's own reading of the timeline rather than a settled finding in the field.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does the lecture suggest the AGI (artificial general intelligence) milestone passed quietly, without much public agreement that it had happened?

options.text: The definition of AGI itself shifts each time a capability threshold is reached.
options.feedback: This is the moving-goalposts problem: the bar keeps being redrawn as models improve, so clearing the original bar never registered as a single, agreed-upon event.

options.text: The companies that build these models suppress announcements about AGI.
options.feedback: The notes describe no concealment. The explanation offered is about the definition moving over time, not about anyone hiding a result.

options.text: No model has reached average human performance on ordinary tasks.
options.feedback: This contradicts the argument in the notes, which was that average-human performance across most tasks had in fact been reached under the older definition.

options.text: AGI was redefined as a legal term with no technical meaning.
options.feedback: The shifting described in the notes happens in how the field informally talks about capability thresholds, not in law or regulation.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What problem is Google DeepMind's Levels of AGI (artificial general intelligence) framework, mentioned in the lecture, designed to address?

options.text: It provides a single yes-or-no test any model can be run through once.
options.feedback: This is the opposite of the framework's purpose. A single pass/fail threshold is precisely the thing it was built to replace, because that threshold kept being redrawn.

options.text: It replaces a single yes/no threshold with graded levels of performance and generality.
options.feedback: Grading performance and generality against what a model actually does gives you something checkable, instead of one label that gets redefined every time it is met.

options.text: It certifies which company may use the term AGI in its marketing.
options.feedback: The notes describe no certification or naming-rights function. The framework is a way of measuring capability, not of policing who may use a word.

options.text: It counts a model's parameters to decide whether it qualifies as general.
options.feedback: Parameter count is not what the framework grades. It looks at levels of performance and generality in a model's actual behavior.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A new model matches average human performance on most everyday writing and reasoning tasks, but a commentator says 'that's not real AGI (artificial general intelligence), since it still can't do X' for some newly emphasized task. Which idea from the lecture best names what is happening?

options.text: The commentator is applying the Levels of AGI framework correctly, since it defines AGI as needing to do X.
options.feedback: The Levels of AGI framework grades performance and generality against behavior rather than fixing one new required task; this scenario is not an application of that framework.

options.text: The model must not actually be reaching average human performance if a commentator disagrees.
options.feedback: Disagreement about labeling does not by itself mean the underlying performance claim is false; the lecture's point was about the definition shifting, not about the performance being disproven.

options.text: Moving the goalposts: as capability thresholds are met, the informal definition of AGI shifts to demand something more.
options.feedback: This matches the lecture's explanation for why the AGI milestone passed quietly -- each time a bar is cleared, a new, harder bar gets treated as the real definition.

options.text: This shows AGI was defined correctly from the start and has never changed.
options.feedback: This is the opposite of the lecture's argument, which was that the definition has shifted over time rather than staying fixed.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Per the lecture, what lever for making a model larger was already established in Session 3, before today's addition?

options.text: Adding more decoder stacks to the pipeline.
options.feedback: This is today's addition (depth), not the Session 3 lever. Session 3's lever was about width, not the number of stacks.

options.text: Feeding a stack's output back into itself for extra passes.
options.feedback: This describes looping, a separate architectural idea introduced today, not the Session 3 lever about model size.

options.text: Increasing the temperature setting used at output time.
options.feedback: Temperature affects sampling randomness at the final output step and is unrelated to what makes a model tier larger.

options.text: Wider MLP (multi-layer perceptron) matrices and a larger embedding space.
options.feedback: This is the lever Session 3 established: a larger model tier typically means wider MLP matrices and a bigger embedding space, both about the width of the pipeline rather than its length.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What second lever for model size did today's session add, beyond width?

options.text: More decoder stacks, making the same pipeline longer.
options.feedback: Depth is the lever added today: the same attention-then-multi-layer-perceptron block repeated more times, rather than each block being made wider.

options.text: A larger vocabulary of possible output tokens.
options.feedback: Vocabulary size sets what tokens the model can emit. It is not one of the two levers the lecture discusses for making a model tier larger.

options.text: A higher maximum context window length.
options.feedback: Context window is how much text the model can hold at once, a separate property from how many decoder stacks the pipeline contains.

options.text: Replacing the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) with a lookup database.
options.feedback: The MLP still carries what the model learned in training, and nothing gets looked up in a database. The lever the lecture adds here is the number of decoder stacks.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What did the lecture say about the number of decoder stacks in Astra specifically?

options.text: It has exactly 32 stacks, like the smaller reference model used in class.
options.feedback: The 32-stack figure was given for a smaller reference model, to make the comparison concrete. It was not offered as a count for Astra.

options.text: The exact count is not public, though the lecture indicated there are a lot.
options.feedback: The lecture was careful here: a frontier model of this size clearly has many stacks, but the actual number has not been disclosed, so any specific figure would be a guess.

options.text: It has fewer stacks than smaller models, since looping replaces depth.
options.feedback: Looping and stack count are two distinct levers in the notes, not substitutes for each other. Nothing suggests a frontier model has fewer stacks than a smaller one.

options.text: It has 16 stacks, matching the smallest model tier mentioned.
options.feedback: Sixteen came up as a plausible count for a smaller model, not as a figure for Astra, whose count the lecture says is not public.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In the pipeline diagram described in the lecture, what does the ellipsis ('...') between two decoder stacks represent?

options.text: A pause where the model stops to check its work before continuing.
options.feedback: That describes something closer to reasoning or looping, both of which are separate ideas. The ellipsis is a drawing convention, not a step the model takes.

options.text: A missing part of the diagram that was never finished.
options.feedback: The ellipsis is deliberate, not an unfinished drawing. It stands for content that is real but too repetitive to draw out.

options.text: A stand-in for however many more decoder stacks the model actually has.
options.feedback: Only two stacks fit on the slide, but a real pipeline repeats the same attention-then-MLP (multi-layer perceptron) pattern many more times than a diagram can show.

options.text: The point where image tokens are converted into word tokens.
options.feedback: No conversion between token types happens there. The ellipsis marks more repetitions of the same decoder stack pattern.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A colleague claims a new frontier model must be more capable purely because its embedding space and MLP (multi-layer perceptron) matrices got wider. Based on the lecture, what alternative explanation should you also consider?

options.text: The model might also have more decoder stacks, making the pipeline deeper rather than wider
options.feedback: Session 3 gave you width -- wider MLP (multi-layer perceptron) matrices and a bigger embedding space. Today's session adds length: the same attention-then-MLP block repeated more times. A bigger model can grow either way, so width is not the only explanation on the table.

options.text: The model might simply have a longer maximum context window, letting it hold more of the prompt at once
options.feedback: A longer window changes how much you can put in front of the model, not how much computation the model does with it. The lecture keeps window size separate from the levers that make a model tier bigger.

options.text: The model might use a smaller embedding space, which forces it to represent meaning more efficiently
options.feedback: This runs the lever backwards. A larger embedding space is one of the width increases that comes with a bigger model tier, so shrinking it is not what a step up in capability looks like.

options.text: The model might be running on faster hardware, so the same computation simply finishes sooner
options.feedback: Faster hardware gets you the same answer sooner, not a better one. Everything the lecture offers as a real difference between model tiers is about the shape of the pipeline, not the speed it runs at.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: As defined in the lecture, what does 'looping' mean in a looped transformer?

options.text: Feeding a stack's output back into that same stack for extra passes.
options.feedback: Looping re-runs a stack over its own output instead of always handing it forward to a new stack, which is what gives the representation a second pass to settle.

options.text: Running the whole model twice on two different prompts and averaging.
options.feedback: That is an ensembling trick applied across separate runs. Looping happens inside a single forward pass, on one representation.

options.text: Repeating the training process several times over the same dataset.
options.feedback: That describes training epochs. Looping is an architectural choice that acts at inference, every time the model runs.

options.text: Sending the final output token back to the very first decoder stack.
options.feedback: Looping re-runs one stack over its own output, rather than routing a finished token back to the start of the pipeline.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture used the phrase 'a second bite of the apple' to describe what?

options.text: A student getting a second attempt at a quiz question.
options.feedback: This phrase was used in the lecture about the architecture, not about quiz retakes.

options.text: A representation passing through the same decoder stack again, becoming further refined while staying stable.
options.feedback: This matches the lecture: the phrase describes looping, where sending a stack's output back through itself gives the representation another pass to become more refined without losing stability.

options.text: A model being retrained from scratch on new data.
options.feedback: Retraining from scratch is a much larger and different process than the extra inference-time pass the phrase describes.

options.text: Adding a second, completely separate model to check the first model's answer.
options.feedback: The lecture describes one stack processing the same representation again, not a second, separate model reviewing the first model's work.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does running a representation through the same decoder stack a second time tend to make it more stable, according to the lecture?

options.text: A second pass erases the first pass, so the representation starts over.
options.feedback: Looping refines what is already there rather than discarding it. Starting over would throw away the work the first pass did.

options.text: The second pass uses a different, unrelated stack with entirely fresh weights.
options.feedback: Reusing the same stack and the same weights is what makes it a loop. Routing to a different stack is just continuing forward through the pipeline.

options.text: A single pass can leave a representation unstable, and a second pass lets it settle.
options.feedback: One trip through a stack can leave a representation easily pushed around by small changes elsewhere. Running it through the same stack again lets it settle into a more solid state -- enriched, but stable.

options.text: The second pass shrinks the embedding space, which is easier to stabilize.
options.feedback: Nothing about the representation's size changes. The same-sized representation is simply run through the same stack again.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What trade-off does the lecture identify as coming with looping?

options.text: Looping leaves the model unable to generate any text.
options.feedback: Generation continues as normal. Looping only changes how much refining a representation gets before the pipeline moves on.

options.text: Looping removes the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) from the pipeline entirely.
options.feedback: Looping re-runs the same attention-then-MLP stack; it does not take a component out. The trade-off the lecture named is about what you can see, not about what is present.

options.text: Looping makes the model's embeddings incompatible with the rest of the pipeline.
options.feedback: The looped output is the same kind of representation, just more settled. The rest of the pipeline consumes it exactly as before.

options.text: Interpretability gets murkier, since some refinement happens silently in the repeated pass.
options.feedback: Work done inside an extra pass never becomes a readable token, so the visible reasoning trace covers less of what the model actually did. That is the cost paid for the added stability.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture compares a model's reasoning trace to a person explaining how they solved a math problem. What point does this comparison make?

options.text: A stated reasoning process is a good proxy for what happened, not a complete record.
options.feedback: People often describe solving a problem in a way their own errors contradict -- not lying, just without full access to their process. A model's reasoning trace has the same limit.

options.text: People and models describe their reasoning with complete accuracy.
options.feedback: The comparison was drawn to make the opposite point: a stated explanation can diverge from what actually produced the answer.

options.text: Only models give unreliable explanations of their reasoning; people are accurate.
options.feedback: People were used as the parallel case, not the contrast. The unreliability shows up on both sides.

options.text: A person who cannot explain their reasoning is lying about how they solved it.
options.feedback: The lecture rejected this reading directly. An explanation that does not match the errors made is not a lie; the person simply does not know their own process.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: An agent works through a long, multi-step coding task without losing track of earlier decisions, even though its visible reasoning trace does not show every internal adjustment it made. Which architectural idea from the lecture best explains this kind of stability?

options.text: Looping -- re-running a representation through the same stack so it settles first
options.feedback: One pass through a stack can leave a representation a little unstable. Sending it back through the same stack lets it settle into a more solid state before it moves on, which is what the lecture ties to holding a long task together -- and because that extra pass produces no new token, it never shows up in the visible trace.

options.text: A larger context window, so nothing from earlier in the task ever falls out of view
options.feedback: This is a real and tempting answer, since a long task does need earlier decisions to stay available. But a bigger window is the chat-shaped fix; the lecture's answer for holding a long task together is an agent writing things down outside itself, and the stability described here is a property of the representation, not of how much text is in view.

options.text: More decoder stacks, so the pipeline runs longer before producing each token
options.feedback: Depth and looping are two separate levers in the lecture, and it is easy to run them together. More stacks means more different blocks in sequence; looping means the same block run again on its own output, which is the one connected to settling into a stable state.

options.text: Wider MLP (multi-layer perceptron) matrices alone, with no change in passes
options.feedback: Width is the Session 3 lever, and the lecture keeps it distinct from what today added. Making each block wider does not give a representation a second pass to settle in.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The addendum describes a more recent line of work that studies looping under a specific name. What is that architecture called?

options.text: A wide-embedding architecture.
options.feedback: Width -- bigger embeddings and wider matrices -- is the Session 3 lever for model size, not the addendum's line of work on reusing one block.

options.text: A fixed-depth architecture.
options.feedback: This is close to the opposite. The architecture in the addendum is defined by unrolling a shared block to an arbitrary depth at inference, not a depth fixed in advance.

options.text: A recurrent-depth architecture.
options.feedback: The block is shared and unrolled as many times as needed at inference time, so depth becomes something you can spend more of on a hard problem instead of a fixed property of the model.

options.text: A projection-based architecture.
options.feedback: Projection describes how image understanding gets added to a model pretrained on text, discussed elsewhere in this session, not the looping work in the addendum.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: According to the addendum, a recurrent-depth model can spend extra computation at inference time. What does it avoid having to produce in order to spend it?

options.text: A final answer.
options.feedback: The answer still comes. The extra computation happens before it, refining a hidden representation rather than replacing the output.

options.text: A new set of weights.
options.feedback: The same shared block, with the same weights, is what gets unrolled again -- that reuse is the point. Nothing new is created at inference time.

options.text: A longer training run.
options.feedback: The addendum places this extra computation at inference, when the model is answering a question, not back in training.

options.text: Extra visible tokens.
options.feedback: The refinement happens in a latent representation, so the model can put more computation into a hard problem without writing out a longer reasoning trace to do it.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Two models are given the same hard problem. Model A produces a much longer written chain-of-thought before answering. Model B produces a short visible answer but, per the addendum's description, unrolls a shared recurrent block to a greater depth internally before producing that answer. Which statement best matches the addendum?

options.text: Model B spends extra computation on a hidden representation; Model A spends it on visible text.
options.feedback: These are two different ways of buying more computation at answer time: unrolling a shared block more times, or writing out a longer reasoning trace. The addendum contrasts them without ranking one above the other.

options.text: Model A must be less capable, since a long chain-of-thought signals confusion.
options.feedback: Trace length is not offered as evidence of capability anywhere in the addendum. Writing more is simply one way to spend extra computation.

options.text: Model B is not using additional computation, since its visible answer is short.
options.feedback: This is exactly the inference the addendum warns against. The extra work happens inside the repeated pass, so a short answer says nothing about how much computation went into it.

options.text: Both models use the same mechanism, just with different output lengths.
options.feedback: Refining a latent representation and emitting more tokens are two distinct mechanisms in the addendum, not one mechanism producing different amounts of text.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: GPT-style models are trained on images using self-supervised learning, the same general method Session 3 introduced for text. What does that look like when applied to images, as described in the lecture?

options.text: Images and text are folded into one shared sequence from the start, with pieces of that sequence left out for the model to predict
options.feedback: This is the native multimodal approach the lecture describes: text and images are part of the same training process from day one, treated as a shared sequence rather than two separate pipelines bolted together.

options.text: A separate model is trained only on images, then combined with the text model afterward through a projection step
options.feedback: That describes the other approach the lecture contrasts this with -- the Anthropic-style method of pretraining on text first and adding vision later. It is a real approach, just not this one.

options.text: Human labelers write captions for each image, and the model is trained to reproduce those captions
options.feedback: Writing captions for supervision is a plausible-sounding training method, but it is ordinary supervised learning with human labels, not the self-supervised, predict-the-missing-piece method the lecture describes.

options.text: An already-trained language model is simply shown static images afterward and asked to describe them, with no additional training involved
options.feedback: That describes using a finished model at inference time, not training it. Both approaches the lecture discusses involve real training on image data, whether jointly from the start or in a later step.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture describes an Anthropic-style approach to giving a model vision, distinct from GPT-style native multimodal training. Which of these best describes it?

options.text: Images and text are trained together in one self-supervised process from the very first step
options.feedback: That is the GPT-style, native multimodal approach the lecture contrasts this one with. The Anthropic-style approach adds vision in a separate, later step instead.

options.text: The model is pretrained on text first, and a separate later step maps image features into the representation space the model already learned for words
options.feedback: This is the projection-based approach: a vision encoder's features get mapped, through a projection layer, into a language model that was already fully trained on text before images ever entered the picture.

options.text: The model generates images the same way it generates words, as a sequence of sampled tokens
options.feedback: The lecture connects this image-as-tokens behavior to the native multimodal approach's strength at generation, not to the projection-based approach, which was described mainly in terms of understanding images.

options.text: The model matches an incoming image against a fixed dictionary of known images to find the closest caption
options.feedback: That describes a lookup or retrieval system, not what either approach in the lecture does. Both methods build a learned representation of the image rather than matching it against a stored dictionary.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture connects native multimodal training to a model's strength not just at understanding images, but at generating them. What is the reasoning behind that connection?

options.text: Native training gives the model a much larger vocabulary of words to draw on
options.feedback: Vocabulary size is not what the lecture points to here. The connection is about where images sit relative to words inside the model, not about how many words it knows.

options.text: Projection-based models add images through a separate generator bolted on later
options.feedback: The lecture describes projection as a way of adding image understanding after text training, and it does not explain generation quality by a bolted-on generator. The reasoning given is about where images live in the model's representation.

options.text: Images share the same semantic space as words, so a picture is produced token by token
options.feedback: Because a jointly trained model never separates image space from word space, making a picture is another case of drawing tokens from a vocabulary one at a time, with a little sampling randomness at each step -- the same process used for a sentence.

options.text: Native training makes image output deterministic rather than randomly sampled
options.feedback: The lecture says the reverse: image generation carries the same temperature-like sampling randomness as text, which is also why re-editing the same picture drifts over several rounds.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A student uses a GPT-style tool to generate an image, then asks for 'one more small tweak' ten times in a row on the same picture. By the tenth tweak, the image looks quite different from the first version. Which idea from the lecture best explains this drift?

options.text: The model's image training data goes stale after repeated edits
options.feedback: Training data does not change during a conversation. The drift the lecture describes comes from something that happens each time an image is generated, not from the training data degrading.

options.text: Each edit wipes out the model's understanding of the original image and starts over
options.feedback: If the model started over each time, there would be no continuity at all between edits, which is not what is observed. The drift is gradual, which points to something accumulating rather than resetting.

options.text: The projection layer wears down a little each time an image passes through it
options.feedback: Projection layers belong to the other, Anthropic-style approach in the lecture, and are not described as degrading with use. This mixes up the two approaches the lecture is contrasting.

options.text: Small sampling randomness in the token-by-token image generation compounds a little more with each round
options.feedback: Because a picture is produced with the same temperature-like randomness as a sentence, a small random change early in one round's token sequence can shift the result, and repeating this lets those small shifts add up into a visibly different image.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: As described in class, what is 'computer use' as an agent capability?

options.text: An agent reads a screenshot of the screen and decides where to click or type next, repeatedly
options.feedback: This is the loop the lecture describes: interpret the current screenshot, choose an action, act, then look at the new screen and go again, the way a person working a mouse and keyboard would.

options.text: An agent edits a program's underlying source code while that program is running
options.feedback: That describes a coding agent changing software, not computer use. Computer use is about operating an already-built interface visually, not rewriting the program behind it.

options.text: An agent reads a device's internal memory to find which application is open
options.feedback: This sounds technical but is not the mechanism described. The lecture's version works entirely from what is visible on the screen, not from reading internal memory.

options.text: An agent follows a written description of the screen supplied by a person
options.feedback: That would make a person the one doing the looking. In computer use the agent itself takes and interprets the screenshot at every step.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why might a very large, high-resolution monitor actually slow down a computer-use agent, according to the practical tip mentioned in class?

options.text: A bigger screen requires more physical mouse movement, which takes longer per click
options.feedback: The agent is not moving a physical mouse across real distance; it is choosing coordinates to act on. The slowdown described comes from processing the image, not from travel.

options.text: The agent has to interpret a bigger screenshot image at every step of its loop
options.feedback: The loop repeats a screenshot-then-decide cycle at every step, so a higher-resolution image simply costs more to interpret each time, and that adds up across a multi-step task.

options.text: High-resolution displays are not supported by most screenshot-taking software
options.feedback: This is a made-up compatibility issue, not the reason given in class. High-resolution screenshots work fine; they are just larger for the model to take in.

options.text: The agent has to scroll further on a large screen to reach the controls it needs
options.feedback: A larger screen usually means less scrolling, not more, and an agent can act on any coordinate it can already see. The cost that grows with screen size is interpreting a bigger image at every step.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Getting an agent to operate other applications, such as the 3D tool Blender, points toward which idea named in the lecture?

options.text: Replacing screenshots with direct access to the application's source code
options.feedback: This was not the direction of the discussion. The question was about connecting an agent to other software, not about reading or rewriting that software's code.

options.text: Training the model on a dedicated dataset built from one application
options.feedback: The lecture did not suggest training a model on a single application. What it named was a general way of connecting agents to tools, not app-specific training data.

options.text: Tool-and-connector integrations, formally MCP (Model Context Protocol)
options.feedback: The lecture named this formally as MCP (Model Context Protocol) and set it aside as material for a later session rather than explaining it in full at that point.

options.text: Giving the agent unrestricted administrator access to the operating system
options.feedback: Broad system access was not what was raised. The topic was connecting to specific applications through tools and connectors.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does the lecture call computer use 'genuinely difficult,' rather than a solved problem?

options.text: Because screenshots take up too much storage space to be practical
options.feedback: Storage is not the issue raised. The difficulty described is about completing tasks correctly, not about how much space images occupy.

options.text: Because most software is not built to be operated with a mouse and keyboard
options.feedback: Everyday software is built exactly for mouse-and-keyboard use by people, which is why an agent has to learn to click and type the way a person does. That is not the source of the difficulty.

options.text: Because the model must translate between two programming languages at each step
options.feedback: No language translation is involved. The work is interpreting an image and choosing where to click or type, which is a different kind of problem entirely.

options.text: Because even the best systems today finish only some of the tasks people find easy
options.feedback: Realistic desktop benchmarks are the evidence the lecture leans on: current systems fall well short of what a person does without thinking about it, which is what keeps this an open problem rather than a finished one.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A classmate says the research papers cited alongside the lecture's multimodal discussion prove exactly how GPT works inside. What is the best correction?

options.text: They are checkable examples of the general approach, not descriptions of GPT's internals
options.feedback: The lecture is explicit that neither cited paper reveals the internals of GPT or Claude, which are undisclosed. Each one is offered as a real, independently verifiable example of the kind of approach -- joint training, or projection -- being discussed.

options.text: They are the technical reports the model vendors published about their own systems
options.feedback: This is the misconception to repair. The cited work is independent research, and the lecture says plainly that the internals of these products are not public.

options.text: They were assigned reading earlier in the course and are unrelated to the topic
options.feedback: The papers are directly relevant, since they illustrate the two approaches under discussion. The trouble with the claim is not relevance; it is treating an example as proof of one product's internals.

options.text: They show that GPT and Claude use identical architectures underneath
options.feedback: This overstates in the other direction. The lecture treats the two styles of image handling as different approaches, and in neither case as a confirmed account of a specific product.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In the 'no pencils or pens' analogy, what is a student in that scenario forced to rely on if they cannot write anything down or use a computer?

options.text: A pocket calculator kept for exactly this situation, to store numbers and recall them
options.feedback: The analogy rules out computers as well as pencils and pens, so a calculator is out too. The point is that nothing external is available at all.

options.text: Their own memory alone -- 'in their mouth' in the analogy -- until it becomes unsustainable
options.feedback: With no external notes allowed, everything has to be carried in memory, and the lecture's point is how quickly that becomes unsustainable -- exactly the position a chat session is in.

options.text: A neighboring student who agrees to hold the information for them instead
options.feedback: The analogy does not introduce a helper. It is about one person with no external way to record anything, which maps onto a single chat session with no outside notes.

options.text: A phone camera, used to photograph the board and review the images later
options.feedback: A phone is a computer, and the analogy rules those out along with pencils and pens. Nothing external is allowed in the scenario.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: According to the lecture, which part of a plain chat session plays the role of the student's own memory in the 'no pencils or pens' analogy?

options.text: The model's training data, learned once and fixed before the conversation ever starts
options.feedback: Training data is fixed and does not change during a conversation, so it cannot play the role of something that fills up and runs out the way the analogy describes. The analogy is about the conversation itself, not what the model learned beforehand.

options.text: Notes the user happens to keep somewhere outside the chat
options.feedback: The analogy is about what the chat session itself has access to, not what the user personally keeps elsewhere. A chat session cannot read a user's outside notes on its own.

options.text: The current context window, which has to hold everything the conversation needs
options.feedback: Just as the student in the analogy can only hold what fits in memory, a chat session can only work with what fits inside its current context window -- there is no external place for it to set anything aside.

options.text: A separate file the chat automatically saves after every message
options.feedback: A plain chat session does not automatically save separate files; that kind of externalized storage is exactly what an agent adds and a chat session lacks, which is the whole point of the analogy.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: How does an agent solve the same problem the 'no pencils or pens' analogy describes for a plain chat session?

options.text: By using a much larger context window that is big enough never to fill up
options.feedback: A bigger window only delays the same problem. The fix the lecture describes is not about window size at all.

options.text: By compressing the earlier conversation so it takes less room in the window
options.feedback: Compression is not the mechanism pointed to. The fix is about having somewhere outside the conversation to put things, not about squeezing more into the same space.

options.text: By training the underlying model to memorize more facts before it is deployed
options.feedback: This confuses what the model learned in training with what happens during one task. The problem in the analogy is about a single ongoing conversation, which pretraining cannot fix.

options.text: By writing what it learns into files, memory, and task lists it can read back
options.feedback: Rather than holding everything in one memory the way the student in the analogy must, an agent puts things outside itself and picks them up again later -- even in a fresh context or a new subagent.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Beyond memory and task tracking, what 'less obvious' capability did the lecture say a harness gives an agent?

options.text: Command-line tools such as bash, run across many files
options.feedback: The lecture singles this out: a harness lets an agent compose filtering and extraction steps across many files, and it argues models have become unusually good at writing those commands. A chat session has no files to point them at.

options.text: A much bigger context window that holds more of the conversation
options.feedback: That is a property of the model and its limits, not something the surrounding harness supplies. The capability highlighted was reaching outside the conversation, to files and tools.

options.text: Direct access to the model's training data for looking facts up
options.feedback: A model does not consult its training data as a searchable store, and a harness does not give it one. What the harness adds is access to files and tools outside the model.

options.text: Faster token generation, so that long tasks finish sooner
options.feedback: Speed is not what a harness changes. The point was that an agent can reach for command-line tools and a file system, which a chat session cannot use at all.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does the lecture claim large language models have effectively become excellent bash-script authors, even though few people are fluent in bash?

options.text: Because bash commands are simpler to write than ordinary English sentences
options.feedback: This is not the reasoning given, and it does not hold up -- bash has its own unfamiliar syntax, which is exactly why the lecture notes that few people are fluent in it.

options.text: Because they compose filtering and extraction steps across many files correctly
options.feedback: The lecture's point is about composition: stringing together whittling, filtering, and extraction operations across many files is what models turn out to be very good at, and it fills a gap most people never had reason to close.

options.text: Because bash was weighted heavily in every model's post-training reward signal
options.feedback: The lecture makes no claim about a specific post-training recipe for bash. Its reasoning is about the kind of task bash scripting is, not about how the model was trained.

options.text: Because bash scripting needs memorized syntax rather than real understanding
options.feedback: This undersells what is being described. Composing correct multi-step operations over files takes more than recalling syntax.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A professor pastes a lab report into a chat session and asks it to 'grade this,' without attaching a rubric or any assignment description. The reply comes back confident and well-formatted. What does the lecture warn is the danger here?

options.text: The chat session will refuse to grade anything without more information
options.feedback: The demo shows the opposite: the session answered readily and confidently. The danger is precisely that it did not refuse, with nothing to go on.

options.text: The reply will look messy, making the missing rubric obvious right away
options.feedback: The demo's point is the reverse. The output looked polished, which is what makes the problem easy to miss rather than obvious.

options.text: The model has no idea what it is rating, and polished output can hide that
options.feedback: With no rubric or assignment description, the model is drawing only on general training about what grading looks like -- and because the result still reads well, confidence is easy to mistake for correctness.

options.text: The chat session will crash partway through generating the response
options.feedback: Nothing in the demo describes a technical failure. The danger is in the reliability of the content, not in the session failing to finish.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In the demo's second attempt, pasting the rubric helped, but grading a second student's submission in the same chat conversation introduced a new problem. What was it?

options.text: The rubric had to be pasted in again before every new submission
options.feedback: That is not the problem identified -- the rubric stayed in context. The issue was what else stayed in context alongside it, namely the first grading.

options.text: The chat session ran out of room to hold the rubric and submissions
options.feedback: Running out of space is not the failure described. The problem was the content that carried forward, not capacity.

options.text: The model forgot the rubric once it had finished the first submission
options.feedback: The rubric was still available. What also stayed available was the first submission's grade and comments, and that is what shifted the second result.

options.text: The first grading stayed in context, so the second was judged partly against it
options.feedback: Everything earlier in a chat can influence what comes next, so a submission graded right after another is no longer judged purely on its own merits -- it can come out harsher or more lenient because of what preceded it.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What mechanism does the lecture point to for why an earlier graded submission can bias the grading of a later one in the same chat conversation?

options.text: Attention -- everything said earlier in the conversation can influence what the model generates next
options.feedback: The lecture ties this directly to attention: because a model draws on everything earlier in the conversation when producing new output, an earlier grading can shift how a later submission comes out, for better or worse.

options.text: Sampling randomness -- each grade differs slightly by chance
options.feedback: Random sampling would produce small, undirected variation, not a systematic bias toward harsher or more lenient grading based on what came right before. The lecture points to context carrying forward, not chance.

options.text: Post-training -- the reinforcement-learning stage makes the model grade every submission identically
options.feedback: Post-training shapes the model once, before any conversation happens; it cannot explain why grading drifts within a single ongoing chat. The bias described comes from what is currently in the conversation, not from training.

options.text: The harness -- providing files and memory lets the agent treat every submission identically
options.feedback: This actually describes the fix, not the problem. A harness giving each submission a fresh subagent is what prevents this bias; it is not the cause of it.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The demo mentions copying and pasting each submission into a brand-new chat, one at a time, as a way to avoid the context-bleeding problem from grading in one long conversation. Why does the lecture call this 'not terrifically repeatable'?

options.text: Because each new chat costs significantly more money to run than one long conversation
options.feedback: Cost is not the reason given. The concern raised is about the practicality of the manual process itself, not about price.

options.text: Because doing this by hand for well over a hundred submissions does not scale
options.feedback: The lecture notes the course has well over a hundred submissions at a time; manually starting a fresh chat and re-pasting the rubric for each one is possible but tedious enough that it is not a realistic routine at that scale.

options.text: Because a brand-new chat cannot be given the rubric at all
options.feedback: A new chat can absolutely be given the rubric by pasting it in again -- that is exactly the manual step being described. The limitation is the effort of doing it by hand, not an inability to include the rubric.

options.text: Because the course's learning platform does not allow more than one browser tab open at a time
options.feedback: This is not a constraint mentioned anywhere in the lecture. The repeatability problem is about manual effort at scale, not a platform restriction.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What fix does the lecture propose for grading many student submissions consistently, and why does it solve the context-bleeding problem from grading in one long chat?

options.text: Use one long chat, but tell the model to ignore everything it graded earlier
options.feedback: Asking the model to ignore earlier content does not remove that content from what it is attending to. The fix described actually separates the submissions instead.

options.text: Reduce the sampling randomness so grades come out the same regardless of order
options.feedback: Lowering randomness does nothing about information carrying forward from one submission to the next. The bias comes from earlier context, not from chance variation.

options.text: Give an agent the submissions, the rubric, and a grading skill, one subagent each
options.feedback: Each submission gets its own fresh subagent, so no earlier grading is sitting in that subagent's context. Every submission is judged against the same fixed standard, with nothing carried over.

options.text: Have a human grade the first several submissions to warm the model up first
options.feedback: This is not part of the fix described, and it would make things worse rather than better -- more prior grading in context is exactly the source of the bias.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A colleague tells you, 'oh, we already do grading with AI (artificial intelligence),' and you want to ask the one question the lecture suggests actually tests whether that grading is trustworthy. What should you ask?

options.text: Which company's model are you using to produce the grades?
options.feedback: The concern raised is not about which vendor's model is involved. A confident, well-formatted grade can come from any model that is missing the right information.

options.text: How long does it take to generate each individual grade?
options.feedback: Speed says nothing about whether the model had what it needed to grade accurately. That is not the test the lecture points to.

options.text: Does the feedback come back looking professional and well formatted?
options.feedback: This is the trap the demo warns about -- polished formatting is what made the ungrounded first attempt look trustworthy. Presentation is not evidence of a sound grade.

options.text: Did the model have the rubric and assignment, or only the submission?
options.feedback: The demo's first attempt shows what happens without them: a confident grade produced with no idea what was being rated. Whether the standards were actually in front of the model is the real test.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A team already runs a strong text-only model in production and wants it to start reading charts and screenshots next quarter, without redoing its pre-training. Which of the two approaches described in the lecture fits that constraint?

options.text: Native multimodal training, since images can be folded into the same process at any point
options.feedback: Native multimodal training is defined by images and text being learned together in one self-supervised process from the very first step. Adding images afterwards is exactly what it does not do, so this route would mean starting the pre-training over.

options.text: The projection approach, which maps image features into the space the model already learned
options.feedback: That is the sequence the lecture gives: pre-train on text, then add a separate step that projects image features into the representation space the model already holds for words. The trained model is kept and vision is fitted on top of it.

options.text: Neither, because a text-only model can never be given image understanding
options.feedback: The lecture describes this being done in practice. The two approaches differ in when images enter training, not in whether a text-trained model can be given sight at all.

options.text: Either one, since the lecture treats the two approaches as interchangeable
options.feedback: The lecture is explicit that these are two genuinely different approaches with different downstream consequences, not two names for one thing. Only one of them adds vision to a model that is already trained.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture says a jointly-trained (native multimodal) model has a concept like 'royal' come with visual associations 'built in from the start.' What does 'from the start' refer to?

options.text: The start of the conversation, before the user has typed a first message
options.feedback: This is about training, not about any one conversation. The 'start' being described comes long before a user ever chats with the model.

options.text: The start of training, when images and text were learned in the same process
options.feedback: This approach never separates learning about words from learning about images, so a concept and its visual associations are there together from the first training step rather than being added later.

options.text: The start of the projection step that maps image features into the model's space
options.feedback: A projection step belongs to the other approach, where vision is added after text training is already finished -- the opposite of 'from the start'.

options.text: The start of the model's reasoning trace, just before it produces an answer
options.feedback: A reasoning trace happens inside a single response and has nothing to do with how images and words were learned. The phrase refers to training.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Per the lecture, what four things does a harness add to a raw model, using the 'no pencils or pens' fix as the frame?

options.text: A rubric, a grading skill, a subagent, and a database
options.feedback: These are specific tools used in the grading demo, not the general list of four things the lecture says a harness supplies to any model.

options.text: A bigger context window, more parameters, faster inference, and a larger vocabulary
options.feedback: These are properties of model scale and speed, not the externalized capabilities the lecture lists. A harness adds things outside the model, not changes to the model itself.

options.text: A file system, persistent memory, task tracking, and skills
options.feedback: These are the four things the lecture lists as what a harness supplies -- exactly the kind of externalized notes and tools the student in the pencils-and-pens analogy is denied.

options.text: A screenshot loop, a click function, a type function, and a wait function
options.feedback: These describe the computer-use loop specifically, not the general list of harness additions. Computer use is one capability a harness can enable, not the four things being asked about here.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does the lecture treat GPT-style and Anthropic-style image handling as two genuinely different approaches, rather than saying one is simply better across the board?

options.text: Because one approach gives a model image understanding and the other does not
options.feedback: Both approaches end up with a model that understands images. What the lecture contrasts is how each one got there.

options.text: Because the two approaches train the same way but run on different hardware
options.feedback: The difference is in the training process itself -- images learned jointly from the start versus added through a later projection step -- not in the hardware.

options.text: Because the difference shows up in training but not in what a model can do
options.feedback: This is the tempting reading, but the lecture ties the training difference to real downstream consequences rather than treating it as an implementation detail.

options.text: Because joint training and a later projection step lead to different capabilities
options.feedback: How a model learned to see shapes what it is good at afterward: the lecture links the difference to strength at generating images and at operating software visually.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Before Agent 2.0-style systems, what did a company's 'agent' product typically look like, according to the lecture?

options.text: A rigid, single-purpose pipeline hand-wired by a programmer to do one thing
options.feedback: The lecture calls this categorically different from what came later. An earlier agent had to be built by hand for one task, while an Agent 2.0 system pulls in files, skills, and subagents as it goes and can be pointed at many problems.

options.text: A general assistant that pulled in files, skills, and subagents as it went
options.feedback: That is the Agent 2.0 description, which the lecture treats as the new thing rather than the old one. Earlier products could not assemble what they needed on the fly.

options.text: A chat window with a longer context window and no other change
options.feedback: This is the 'chat with extra steps' reading the lecture rejects. Earlier agentic products were built pipelines, not a chat session with more room in it.

options.text: A model retrained from scratch for each customer's particular task
options.feedback: The rigidity described came from the hand-built pipeline around the model, not from retraining a model for every customer.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: According to the lecture, what is a skill, structurally speaking?

options.text: A single system prompt that gets appended to every conversation
options.feedback: A system prompt is one flat block of text added to every turn. A skill is the opposite: most of it, including any scripts or reference files, only loads when the task actually calls for it.

options.text: A subdirectory of instructions for an agent, often bundled with scripts and reference files
options.feedback: This is close to how the lecture put it: a skill is a subdirectory of instructions for the agent, and it can carry along scripts and reference files that get used only when the task needs them.

options.text: A separate, fine-tuned copy of the underlying model
options.feedback: Fine-tuning changes the model's weights themselves, which takes retraining. A skill changes nothing about the model -- it is just files that tell an existing model how to approach a task.

options.text: A plugin that only works if it is written in the same programming language as the harness
options.feedback: Skills are portable specifically because they are not tied to one programming language or vendor. Requiring a language match would defeat the point of a format any compatible harness can read.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Which part of a skill stays loaded in an agent's context even when the skill is not currently being used?

options.text: Its name and description
options.feedback: The name and description are what let the model recognize a matching request before anything else about the skill has loaded, so those two pieces stay resident even when the skill is idle.

options.text: The full body of its instructions
options.feedback: The instruction body is exactly the part that loads only on demand, once the skill is actually triggered by a matching request. Keeping it resident all the time is what the on-demand design avoids.

options.text: Any scripts it bundles, such as a frame-extraction script
options.feedback: Scripts are among the heaviest parts of a skill, which is why they load only when the skill actually runs, not just because the skill exists in the library.

options.text: Its reference files and output-format examples
options.feedback: Reference files and output-format examples are useful once the skill is in use, but loading them permanently for every skill in a library would recreate the exact bloat the on-demand pattern is built to prevent.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: You have dozens of skills installed, yet a conversation that uses none of them is no more crowded than before. What explains that, per the lecture?

options.text: Each skill is compressed into a much shorter summary before it is stored
options.feedback: Compression is not the mechanism. The instruction body is not shrunk at all -- it is simply left out of context until a request needs it.

options.text: The harness unloads and deletes any skill that has not been used for a while
options.feedback: Deleting unused skills was not part of the explanation given, and it would mean losing a skill rather than simply not paying its context cost yet.

options.text: Only a skill's name and description stay in context; the rest loads when it triggers
options.feedback: An idle skill costs almost nothing, because only its short name and description are resident. The body, the scripts, and the reference files enter context only once a request actually matches it.

options.text: Every skill is capped at the same fixed token length no matter what it does
options.feedback: A cap would not distinguish an idle skill from an active one. The point was about when a skill's content loads, not how long any one skill is allowed to be.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture-recording-to-lecture-notes skill bundles real Python scripts, such as one that pulls frames out of a video, rather than asking the model to extract frames on its own. Why does this design make sense?

options.text: Because Python is the language a skill's bundled code has to be written in
options.feedback: Skills are not tied to one language. Python shows up here because it fits the job of pulling frames out of a video file, not because the skill format demands it.

options.text: Because a bundled script handles the whole job, leaving the model nothing to interpret
options.feedback: The skill still needs the model to work out what a phrase like "as you can see" is pointing at. The script covers one mechanical step; it does not cover the task.

options.text: Because a script written once will not need revising as the rest of the skill changes
options.feedback: Nothing suggests a script is frozen once written. A skill's code can be revised like any other part of it, the way the class proposed revising its narrative-versus-expository instruction.

options.text: Because code does the mechanical extraction reliably, leaving the model to interpret what it means
options.feedback: Ordinary software handles the reliable, mechanical step of grabbing a frame at a given timestamp, while the model supplies the judgment about what that material means in context. Each side does the part it is actually good at.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In the lecture-notes skill, some work is done by its bundled scripts and some by the model's own judgment. Which task belongs to the scripts rather than to the model?

options.text: Pulling a frame out of an .mp4 video file at a specific timestamp
options.feedback: That is ordinary, mechanical software: give it a file and a time and it returns the same image every time. The model's share is deciding which moment matters and reading what the frame shows.

options.text: Working out what a speaker means by "look here" or "as you can see"
options.feedback: Resolving a vague phrase to the thing on screen takes judgment about context, which is the model's half of the pairing. No script can tell which slide "look here" points at.

options.text: Judging which moments in a session are worth a screenshot at all
options.feedback: Choosing what deserves a picture is an interpretive decision, so it sits on the model's side. The script only runs once a moment has been chosen for it.

options.text: Deciding whether the finished notes read as narrative or as expository prose
options.feedback: Style comes from the skill's written instructions and the model's reading of them -- that is the very instruction the class proposed rewording. Scripts do not weigh in on prose style.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why does the lecture treat a skill's name and description as unusually important to get right?

options.text: Because those two fields are the only ones a course platform shows to students
options.feedback: This is not a course-platform question. The name and description matter because of how the agent decides whether a skill applies, not because of what a student interface happens to display.

options.text: Because that short text is all the model has to judge whether a request matches
options.feedback: Only the name and description are resident before a skill loads, so that short text is the model's entire basis for matching a request to a skill. A vague or duplicated name therefore gets the wrong skill triggered, or none at all.

options.text: Because a longer name and description take the harness longer to parse each turn
options.feedback: Parsing time was not the concern raised. The worry was about matching the right request to the right skill, not about how fast the text is processed.

options.text: Because the name and description are the only parts of a skill you can share
options.feedback: Sharing a skill means passing along the whole set of files. What is special about those two fields is their role in triggering, not any limit on what can be handed to someone else.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What did the lecture recommend for writing a skill that needs real code behind it, such as the video-frame-extraction script in the lecture-notes skill?

options.text: Write it in plain chat, since a chat session writes code as well as any other tool
options.feedback: Chat is fine for a skill that is only instructions, but a skill that has to run and test Python needs a tool built for that, and chat is not one.

options.text: Ask a chat session for the code, then paste the files into the skill folder yourself
options.feedback: You can certainly get code out of chat, but nothing there runs or tests it, so you find out whether it works only when it fails inside the skill. That missing test loop is the whole reason a coding-capable agent was recommended.

options.text: Write it with a coding-capable agent such as Claude Code or Codex, which can test it
options.feedback: Those tools are built to write software and then actually run it, which is what a skill leaning on Python -- here, pulling frames out of a video -- needs behind it.

options.text: Write it by hand in a text editor, since an agent cannot be trusted with its own code
options.feedback: Hand-writing is always possible, but it was not the recommendation, and it gives up exactly the write-then-test loop that makes a coding-capable agent worth using.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: According to the lecture, which kind of skill is reasonable to write or edit directly in chat, without a coding-capable agent?

options.text: Any skill whose instructions fit on less than one printed page
options.feedback: Length was not the deciding factor. A short skill can still depend on code, and a long one may be nothing but prose instructions.

options.text: Any skill that has already been used successfully at least once
options.feedback: A track record does not change what a skill needs for editing. A code-bearing skill still wants a coding-capable agent no matter how well it has run so far.

options.text: A skill you expect to run only a handful of times before discarding it
options.feedback: How often you plan to use a skill does not decide where to write it. A throwaway skill can still need real code, and a heavily reused one can be pure instructions.

options.text: A skill that is pure writing or formatting instructions with no code behind it
options.feedback: With no code to run or test, the whole skill is prose, so it can be drafted and revised conversationally -- the way the class talked through rewording the narrative-versus-expository line.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What is Skill Creator, as described in the lecture?

options.text: A meta-skill that turns a problem you have already solved into a reusable skill
options.feedback: You solve the problem once, with a strong model and rich context -- ideally including a worked trace of yourself doing the task -- and Skill Creator packages that into something an agent can reuse.

options.text: A blank template you fill in by hand when starting a new skill from scratch
options.feedback: Skill Creator starts from work you have already done, not from an empty form. The solved problem, with the context around it, is the raw material it needs.

options.text: A certification a skill must pass before it can be shared with another user
options.feedback: Nothing describes a gatekeeping step. Skill Creator builds a skill and can help test it, but it does not stand between you and handing the skill to someone else.

options.text: Another name for the harness that supplies an agent with files, memory, and tasks
options.feedback: The harness is the surrounding layer that gives a model a file system, memory, task tracking, and skills. Skill Creator is one skill running inside that layer, not the layer itself.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Besides turning a solved problem into a new skill, what else can Skill Creator help with, per the lecture?

options.text: Automatically translating a skill into every other model provider's proprietary format
options.feedback: Skills are portable because they are just files, not because Skill Creator performs any translation between vendor formats -- no such feature was described.

options.text: Generating test cases for a skill and helping judge whether its output is good, so the skill can be improved over time
options.feedback: This is the iteration loop described: Skill Creator can generate test cases and help judge output quality, so a skill gets revised rather than written once and left alone.

options.text: Deleting any skill that has not been triggered recently
options.feedback: Removing a skill by hand was the instructor's own fix for a naming collision, and what was removed was the duplicate of another skill, not one that had gone unused. Either way, Skill Creator does not do it for you.

options.text: Merging two contradictory skills into one without any human review
options.feedback: Reconciling contradictory skills was described as something the model does its best at when it hits the conflict, not an automatic merge Skill Creator performs ahead of time.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Why are skills portable across different model providers, according to the lecture?

options.text: Because every provider agreed to a shared API (application programming interface) standard for skills
options.feedback: No shared industry API was described -- portability comes from what a skill is made of, not from a formal cross-vendor agreement.

options.text: Because a skill is compiled into a single universal binary before it runs
options.feedback: Compiling to a binary would tie a skill to one execution environment, which is the opposite of the plain-files approach the lecture described.

options.text: Because a skill is just files and instructions, not code tied to one vendor, so any harness that understands the same format can run it
options.feedback: Because a skill is just files and instructions rather than vendor-specific code, any agent whose harness understands the same skill format can run it -- which is exactly why a skill could move between model providers.

options.text: Because skills never contain any structure, only plain paragraphs of English
options.feedback: Skills do have structure -- a name, description, instructions, and often scripts and reference files -- the portability comes from that structure being format-based, not vendor-based, not from having no structure at all.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture mentioned using Astra, a different frontier model, to fix and improve some existing Claude skills over a weekend, then bringing the improved skills back to run in Claude. Which idea from the lecture does this best illustrate?

options.text: Contradictory skills, since Astra's edits might disagree with Claude's own instructions
options.feedback: Contradiction is about two different skills disagreeing when both apply to the same request. Here it is one skill, edited by a different model, which is a portability story rather than a conflict between two skills.

options.text: A naming collision, since Astra and Claude might pick the same skill for different requests
options.feedback: A naming collision is about two similarly named skills confusing which one the model picks. Nothing here involves two competing skill names -- it is the same skill file moving between models.

options.text: Context rot, since editing a skill with a second model adds more material to the context window
options.feedback: Editing a skill file with a different model does not add anything to a running conversation's context window. Context rot is about material piling up inside one conversation, not about which model touched a file.

options.text: Skill portability, since a skill is just files that any compatible harness can run
options.feedback: A skill is nothing more than files and instructions, so it does not matter which model wrote or repaired it. Any harness that reads the same format, Claude's included, can run it, which is exactly what let the improved version come back.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What specific problem was described with two similarly named skills, and how was it fixed?

options.text: Two very similarly named skills served the same purpose, with no reliable way to know which one the model would pick; the fix was to remove the duplicate
options.feedback: This matches what was described: an "AI class lecture recording to lecture notes" skill and "lecture recording to lecture notes" were similar enough that the model could not reliably tell them apart, so the duplicate was simply deleted.

options.text: Two skills used incompatible file formats, so one was rewritten from scratch in a different format
options.feedback: No format incompatibility was described -- the problem was about the model choosing between two similarly named skills, not about the skills being unable to run at all.

options.text: Two skills both tried to write to the same output file, causing a crash, so the output files were renamed
options.feedback: A file-write crash is a different kind of bug than the one described. The actual issue was ambiguous selection between two skills with near-identical names and purposes, not a technical collision while running.

options.text: Two skills produced identical output every time, so their instructions were combined into a single longer file
options.feedback: The problem was not that the two skills produced the same output -- it was that their names were similar enough that the model had no reliable way to choose between them for a given request.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: What example was given in the lecture of two skills contradicting each other?

options.text: A grading skill that grades leniently alongside one that grades harshly
options.feedback: Two grading skills with different strictness was not the example given -- the lecture's example was about a formatting choice that one skill requires and another forbids.

options.text: A formatting skill that always specifies orange, alongside a brand skill that bans orange in favor of a fixed palette
options.feedback: This is the example: a formatting skill that always specifies orange runs into a brand skill that bans orange for a fixed palette, and both are relevant to the same request.

options.text: A skill written for English output alongside one written for Spanish output
options.feedback: A language mismatch between skills is not the example from the lecture -- the conflict described was over a color choice, not over which language to output in.

options.text: A skill for summarizing video alongside one for summarizing audio, both claiming the same file type
options.feedback: Claiming the same file type is a different kind of problem than the one described. The lecture's example was two skills disagreeing on a formatting rule, not competing over what kind of file each handles.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A student has one installed skill that formats every report as bullet points and a separate skill that formats every report as full prose paragraphs. Based on the lecture, what should the student expect, and what is the better long-term fix?

options.text: The request will be silently rejected until one of the two skills is uninstalled
options.feedback: This kind of conflict was described as something the model tries to reconcile, or at least flags, not as a hard rejection of the request.

options.text: The harness will automatically average the two styles into a hybrid format
options.feedback: No automatic blending was described. The model may note the conflict and try to reconcile it, but that is a judgment call, not a guaranteed merge of two formats.

options.text: They may conflict when both apply; the fix is to scope skills so they rarely overlap
options.feedback: Contradictory skills are not a hard crash, but leaving the model to guess right every time is fragile. Keeping each skill narrowly enough scoped that two rarely apply at once removes the guess instead of relying on it.

options.text: The model will always silently pick whichever skill was installed first and ignore the other
