options.feedback: Installation order was not described as the deciding factor. The model notices the conflict and tries to reconcile it rather than mechanically preferring whichever loaded first.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In the live skill-editing discussion, which single word in the lecture-notes skill's instructions was identified as the source of the problem?

options.text: "Tutorial"
options.feedback: "Tutorial" appeared in the same phrase, but the actual problem was pinned on a different word in that instruction.

options.text: "Background"
options.feedback: "Background" was not the word singled out -- it appeared in the proposed replacement instruction, not in the diagnosis of what was wrong.

options.text: "Detailed"
options.feedback: "Detailed" describes the symptom students complained about (not enough detail), but it is not the word blamed inside the skill's own instructions.

options.text: "Narrative"
options.feedback: The problem was traced to the word "narrative" in the instruction "tutorial-style narrative prose," with the argument that the skill should ask for expository writing instead.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In the live skill-editing discussion, how was "narrative" distinguished from "expository"?

options.text: Narrative means telling a story about something; expository means explaining it directly
options.feedback: This is exactly the distinction drawn: narrative tells a story about the class, while expository explains the material directly -- and the notes needed the latter to support detailed quiz questions.

options.text: Narrative means using screenshots; expository means using text only
options.feedback: The distinction was about a mode of explanation, not about the presence or absence of screenshots -- screenshots were discussed separately as an assignment option for personalizing the skill.

options.text: Narrative means writing in the first person; expository means writing in the second person
options.feedback: Person (first versus second) is a different stylistic axis than narrative versus expository, and it was not the contrast drawn in this discussion.

options.text: Narrative means a shorter document; expository means a longer one
options.feedback: Document length was not the distinction being made -- the concern was whether the writing explains concepts directly or tells a story about them, regardless of how long it runs.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A student asked whether writing several detailed paragraphs of instruction into a skill risks the same context problems as an overloaded chat conversation. What was the answer?

options.text: Yes, so skill instructions should always be kept to one paragraph or less
options.feedback: No length limit was set. The answer turned on where instructions sit relative to the task, not on capping how many paragraphs they run to.

options.text: No, because a skill's instructions sit right next to the work they govern
options.feedback: The instructions arrive attached to the specific task at hand rather than competing for attention against a long, wandering chat history, which is what makes an overloaded conversation lose the thread in the first place.

options.text: Yes, but only for skills that also include scripts or other runnable code
options.feedback: The answer carved out no exception for code-bearing skills. Instructions sitting next to the relevant task holds whether or not the skill bundles scripts.

options.text: No, because skill instructions are processed by a completely separate model from chat
options.feedback: Nothing suggests a second model handles skill instructions. The same model reads them -- just without the competing clutter of a long conversation around them.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: In class, a rewording of the lecture-notes skill was proposed to make it expository rather than narrative, yet afterward the shipped skill still specified "tutorial-style narrative prose." What does this best illustrate?

options.text: That the harness automatically reverts any skill edit a student has not approved
options.feedback: No such automatic reversion exists. The rewording was never applied in the first place, which is a different situation from an edit being undone.

options.text: That narrative and expository produce identical output, so the wording never mattered
options.feedback: If the wording made no difference there would have been no complaint that the notes read too much like a story. The whole discussion assumes the word choice changes what comes out.

options.text: That a skill changes only when someone edits its file, not when a fix is discussed
options.feedback: The rewording was proposed but never merged, so the old instruction was still the one in force on the next run. Talking through a better instruction does not put it into the skill; editing the file does.

options.text: That a skill rewrites itself automatically after a class discussion about its output
options.feedback: Skills do not edit themselves out of a conversation about them. Someone has to change the file, which is exactly the gap this situation exposes.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A classmate keeps one long chat running all week, working three unrelated projects inside it, and finds that by Thursday the answers have gone vague and keep drifting off the task at hand. Which idea from the lecture names what is happening?

options.text: A naming collision between two similarly named skills
options.feedback: A naming collision is about the model having no reliable way to pick between two skills whose names are too alike. No skills are involved here; the trouble is in what one conversation has accumulated.

options.text: Context rot
options.feedback: Three unrelated projects in one window is exactly the condition the lecture names: too much, and too loosely related, material carried in a single context, with focus and quality falling off as a result. This is also why a skill keeps its body out of context until it is needed, and why an agent puts work into files instead of holding it all in the conversation.

options.text: A contradiction between two installed skills
options.feedback: Contradictory skills are two sets of instructions that disagree when both apply to the same request, like one demanding orange and another banning it. Nothing here is giving the model conflicting instructions.

options.text: The model's post-training wearing off over a long session
options.feedback: Post-training happens once, before the model is ever deployed, and nothing about a long conversation undoes it. What changes across a week-long chat is what the context window is carrying, not the model.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: Which of the following was a suggested direction for personalizing the lecture-notes skill?

options.text: Add self-study questions to each section, moving from easy to conceptually hard
options.feedback: Per-section questions that build from easy to conceptually difficult were one of the suggested directions. The list works because you are shaping the notes around how you actually study from them.

options.text: Remove every screenshot, since a picture cannot carry conceptual detail
options.feedback: The suggestion was to carry more screenshots or fewer, according to what you find useful. Screenshots were never described as adding nothing.

options.text: Cap every set of notes at a single page, whatever the session covered
options.feedback: No length cap was among the suggestions. They concerned grounding, style, structure, and how many screenshots to include, not squeezing a session onto one page.

options.text: Have every set of notes translated into a second language automatically
options.feedback: Translation was not among the directions listed. Every suggestion concerned how the notes explain the material, not what language they arrive in.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: The lecture argued that the best person to write a skill is someone who is an expert in it. In the context of this assignment, why does that fit?

options.text: Because only an expert is permitted to edit a working skill's instructions
options.feedback: There is no restriction on who may edit a skill. The point is about the quality of judgment behind the edit, not about permission to make it.

options.text: Because you are the expert on what you want from the notes, and can say so precisely
options.feedback: A skill is only as good as the judgment written into its instructions. A student who knows what makes notes useful to them can state that directly, where an outsider can only guess at it.

options.text: Because a skill written by an expert never needs to be revised afterward
options.feedback: Skill Creator's own loop of test cases and judged output assumes skills keep getting revised. Expertise makes a better first draft, not a permanent one.

options.text: Because expertise is needed to operate the coding agent that edits a skill file
options.feedback: Running a coding-capable agent takes no subject-matter expertise, and a purely instructional skill needs no coding agent at all, as the earlier discussion of writing skills in chat established.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A student asked whether you have to explicitly tell an agent to use a particular skill, or whether it happens automatically. What was the answer?

options.text: A skill only ever loads when it is explicitly named by its exact file path
options.feedback: Requiring an exact path would defeat the point of automatic matching. Loading turns on how closely a request matches the skill's name and description, not on typing a location.

options.text: Skills always require a human to approve loading them before every single use
options.feedback: No per-use approval step was described. Automatic matching is exactly what lets a skill trigger without that kind of gatekeeping on every request.

options.text: It should load automatically when a request matches its name and description
options.feedback: That match is the whole reason those two fields stay resident in context. You can also call a skill explicitly, often with a forward-slash command, but recognition is the normal path.

options.text: Automatic loading is impossible; every skill must be invoked with a slash command
options.feedback: Explicit invocation is available as an option, not as the only route. Automatic loading on a close match was described as how a skill is normally reached.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A student with no programming background wants to build a skill that only reformats meeting notes into a fixed template, with no code involved. Based on the lecture, can they do this, and how?

options.text: No -- every skill, whatever it does, needs at least some code behind it
options.feedback: A code-free skill, such as a pure reformatting skill, was described as needing no code at all, so a universal code requirement contradicts that directly.

options.text: Yes, but only after first completing a separate course in programming
options.feedback: No coding prerequisite was mentioned. The answer was that programming experience is simply not needed when there is no software behind the skill.

options.text: No -- only a coding-capable agent such as Claude Code or Codex can create a skill
options.feedback: A coding-capable agent is recommended when a skill needs real software behind it, such as video-frame extraction. A purely instructional skill does not call for that tool.

options.text: Yes -- a skill with no code behind it can be written and edited conversationally
options.feedback: Coding experience matters only when a skill has software to run and test. A fixed reformatting template is pure instruction, so it can be drafted and revised in an ordinary conversation.

questions.source: Quiz 3 - Sessions 1-4: Model Size, Thinking, and Skills
questions.question: A classmate's version of the lecture-notes skill produces notes that read like a story and are not detailed enough to answer quiz questions built from the same lecture. Based on how the lecture addressed this exact complaint, what should the classmate do, and how can they check whether it worked?

options.text: Switch to first-person narration and add screenshots, since detail comes from images
options.feedback: Screenshots were an optional personalization choice, not the source of the missing conceptual detail, and person is a different axis altogether from narrative versus expository.

options.text: Cut each section to a paragraph and stop checking the notes against the quiz
options.feedback: That addresses length, not the complaint, which was about missing grounding and detail. Dropping the quiz check also throws away the one diagnostic that was recommended.

options.text: Reword the skill toward grounded, expository notes, then answer a quiz from them
options.feedback: Ground the notes in the course's own content and references and explain directly rather than narrate, then check the fix by trying to answer the quiz from the notes alone. The rewording is the change; the quiz attempt is how you learn whether it worked.

options.text: Leave the wording alone, since a skill cannot control how detailed its output is
options.feedback: The entire live-editing discussion was about fixing exactly this complaint through the skill's own wording, so treating the output as beyond the instructions' reach gets it backwards.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What does tokenization do to text before a decoder transformer processes it?

options.text: Assigns a probability to each complete answer.
options.feedback: Next-token probabilities come later in the pipeline. Tokenization prepares the text for numerical processing.

options.text: Splits text into pieces with vocabulary identifiers.
options.feedback: A token can be a word or a piece of a word. Its identifier lets the model map that piece to a numerical representation.

options.text: Converts each sentence into a verified factual claim.
options.feedback: Tokenization handles the representation of text. It does not check whether a sentence is true.

options.text: Stores each paragraph as an independent learned weight.
options.feedback: Learned weights are model parameters. Input paragraphs become token sequences rather than new weights.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What is a token embedding in the pipeline studied in this course?

options.text: A text definition retrieved for each vocabulary entry.
options.feedback: An embedding is a numerical vector, not a dictionary definition retrieved as text.

options.text: A probability assigned to the next complete sentence.
options.feedback: An embedding represents a token before the output stage. Next-token probabilities are calculated after the decoder transformations.

options.text: A rule that selects which output token comes next.
options.feedback: Token selection uses the output distribution. Embeddings supply representations for the model to transform.

options.text: A numerical vector used to represent a vocabulary item.
options.feedback: A token identifier maps to a vector. The learned geometry can represent relationships between items.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which operation most directly describes attention in the decoder pipeline?

options.text: Combining information from relevant context positions.
options.feedback: Attention lets a representation incorporate information from permitted positions in the context. This helps account for how a token is being used.

options.text: Selecting one output token from its final probabilities.
options.feedback: Selecting the output token happens after the decoder blocks produce the next-token distribution.

options.text: Increasing the number of learned weights during a reply.
options.feedback: Using attention during ordinary generation applies trained weights; it does not add parameters as the reply grows.

options.text: Replacing input tokens with their vocabulary identifiers.
options.feedback: That is token encoding. Attention operates on numerical representations after the initial encoding and embedding steps.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What does an MLP (multi-layer perceptron) do inside a decoder block?

options.text: It picks the next output token from the final distribution.
options.feedback: Output selection is a later step. The multi-layer perceptron transforms representations used to compute that distribution.

options.text: It assigns a vocabulary identifier to each input fragment.
options.feedback: Vocabulary identifiers are assigned during tokenization. The multi-layer perceptron acts on representations inside the model.

options.text: It applies learned transformations at each token position.
options.feedback: The multi-layer perceptron uses trained weights to transform the representation at each position. Learned knowledge is distributed through the network.

options.text: It retrieves an exact source sentence for each requested fact.
options.feedback: The world-knowledge metaphor does not make this layer a literal database. A learned transformation can produce plausible output without finding a source sentence.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: In autoregressive generation, what happens to a token after it is selected?

options.text: It becomes part of the context for later token choices.
options.feedback: Each choice extends the sequence. The growing sequence influences which tokens are likely next.

options.text: It replaces the trained weights used for later token choices.
options.feedback: Generated text changes context, not the trained weights during ordinary inference.

options.text: It is held apart until the complete answer has been selected.
options.feedback: The answer is generated incrementally. Earlier generated tokens influence later choices before the whole answer exists.

options.text: It supplies a new independent layer for the decoder stack.
options.feedback: Adding a token grows the sequence. It does not add another learned layer to the model.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Immediately before next-token selection, what does the decoder pipeline provide?

options.text: A set of independently verified sentences to copy.
options.feedback: The decoder calculates token scores or probabilities. Their calculation is different from verifying sentences against evidence.

options.text: A replacement vocabulary trained on the latest prompt.
options.feedback: Ordinary generation uses the trained vocabulary and weights. A prompt does not train a replacement vocabulary.

options.text: A distribution assigning probabilities to vocabulary tokens.
options.feedback: The output stage gives the probabilities used to choose the next token. Selection then extends the generated sequence.

options.text: A complete response with every later token already fixed.
options.feedback: The next token is selected from the current distribution. Later distributions depend on the sequence as it develops.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which aspect of generation does the temperature setting directly adjust?

options.text: The number of independent weights in the trained network.
options.feedback: Changing temperature does not rebuild the network. Parameter count concerns the model architecture and its learned values.

options.text: The maximum amount of text that fits into the context.
options.feedback: Context capacity and temperature are separate settings. Temperature changes how token choices are distributed.

options.text: The amount of computation allowed before an answer begins.
options.feedback: That describes a thinking budget. Temperature can affect sampled paths, but it is not itself a compute budget.

options.text: The concentration of the distribution used for token sampling.
options.feedback: Lower temperature favors higher-scoring choices more strongly. Higher temperature spreads probability more broadly.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What does a model parameter count measure?

options.text: The number of tokens in the current conversation.
options.feedback: That is a measure of context length. Parameter count describes the trained model rather than the current conversation.

options.text: The number of learned numerical values in the model.
options.feedback: Parameters are learned numbers such as weights. Reusing those numbers during inference does not create additional independent parameters.

options.text: The number of intermediate steps in the current reply.
options.feedback: A reply can use more computation with the same parameter set. Steps during inference and learned values are different counts.

options.text: The number of factual statements guaranteed to be correct.
options.feedback: Parameters are not a catalog of guaranteed facts. A model can generate factual errors regardless of its parameter count.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What does a model's context window describe?

options.text: The size of the matrices learned during model training.
options.feedback: Matrix sizes help determine parameter count. The context window instead concerns the sequence available during a run.

options.text: The speed at which the model selects output tokens.
options.feedback: Generation speed measures throughput. Context capacity measures how much sequence material can be considered.

options.text: The maximum sequence material the model can consider per run.
options.feedback: Context includes supplied and generated material within the system's capacity. It is distinct from parameter count.

options.text: The count of times a recurrent block is reused per token.
options.feedback: Recurrent passes describe computation on representations. They do not define the capacity of the context window.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: In recurrent-depth processing, what is repeatedly transformed before an output token is selected?

options.text: An internal numerical representation.
options.feedback: The recurrent block refines hidden vectors. Those passes can occur without adding words to a visible reasoning trace.

options.text: A newly printed sentence in the response.
options.feedback: Printing additional text grows the output sequence. Hidden recurrence works on representations before output selection.

options.text: An updated set of training labels.
options.feedback: Training labels concern learning from examples. Recurrent-depth inference applies an already trained block to a representation.

options.text: A freshly expanded token vocabulary.
options.feedback: Reusing a computation block does not require expanding the vocabulary. It increases processing of the internal state.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why is raising temperature different from giving a model a larger thinking budget?

options.text: Temperature changes context capacity; a budget changes weights.
options.feedback: Temperature does not set context capacity, and an inference budget does not retrain weights. They concern sampling and available computation.

options.text: Temperature adds layers; a budget enlarges token embeddings.
options.feedback: These are architectural changes. Neither follows merely from adjusting a sampling setting or inference budget.

options.text: Temperature checks facts; a budget chooses more varied words.
options.feedback: Temperature is not a truth-checking mechanism. A thinking budget allocates computation rather than defining sampling variety.

options.text: Temperature reshapes sampling; a budget allocates computation.
options.feedback: The settings affect different mechanisms. Sampling can change a reasoning path and its length, but it does not directly specify a time or token budget.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: How can identical prompts produce different responses when the trained weights stay fixed?

options.text: Each response trains a different set of weights before starting.
options.feedback: Ordinary generation uses trained weights. Different samples can produce different text without an additional training step.

options.text: Sampling can choose different tokens and change later context.
options.feedback: A different early token creates a different continuation context. Later token choices can then follow another path.

options.text: Each prompt causes the model to create a different vocabulary.
options.feedback: A new vocabulary is not required for variation. Selection among the existing vocabulary can lead to different responses.

options.text: Attention randomly selects a complete response from a database.
options.feedback: Attention combines contextual information. It does not retrieve one complete answer from a response database.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can a fluent model response contain an incorrect factual claim?

options.text: A false answer shows the model failed to select its highest-probability token.
options.feedback: A high-probability continuation can itself contain an error. Selecting the most probable text does not verify its factual claims.

options.text: Sampling replaces learned probabilities with unrelated random words.
options.feedback: Sampling uses a distribution related to the model's scores. A false claim can still be a plausible continuation under that distribution.

options.text: Predicting plausible text differs from checking a claim's truth.
options.feedback: Next-token prediction can support fluent and useful answers, but fluency is not a verification step. Check important factual claims against evidence.

options.text: A false answer means the relevant fact was absent from training.
options.feedback: Learned representations can be imperfect, and generation is not a factual guarantee. An error alone does not show that the fact was missing from training.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can arithmetic on learned word vectors sometimes capture a relationship between concepts?

options.text: Relationships can be reflected in directions within the vector space.
options.feedback: A learned geometry can encode useful relationships. An analogy is an approximate pattern, not an exact identity guaranteed for every model.

options.text: Vocabulary identifiers are arranged as a ranked list of definitions.
options.feedback: Token identifiers identify vocabulary entries. Semantic geometry belongs to the learned vectors, not to a ranking of dictionary definitions.

options.text: Each vector contains a written rule for the requested word analogy.
options.feedback: Vectors are numerical representations rather than text instructions. Useful analogies can emerge from the learned arrangement.

options.text: Temperature performs concept arithmetic before embeddings are assigned.
options.feedback: Temperature affects output sampling later in the pipeline. It does not create the relationships in the embedding space.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: How should you interpret the metaphor that an MLP (multi-layer perceptron) contains world knowledge?

options.text: It means factual claims are stored as exact rows with citations.
options.feedback: The database interpretation is too literal. Learned weights transform representations and do not guarantee an exact source row for each claim.

options.text: It highlights learned patterns within a distributed representation.
options.feedback: The metaphor points to knowledge learned during training. Knowledge is distributed through the network rather than confined to a literal fact store.

options.text: It means attention contributes no learned information to the model.
options.feedback: The metaphor is not a strict partition of all knowledge. Attention and other learned components also participate in the network's behavior.

options.text: It identifies a file that is updated whenever you change the prompt.
options.feedback: A prompt changes context during ordinary inference. It does not update a world-knowledge file or retrain the model's weights.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can a recurrent block perform extra work without adding independent parameters on each pass?

options.text: Extra passes add new layers, each with separately learned weights.
options.feedback: Adding independently parameterized layers would increase the parameter count. A recurrent block instead reuses its existing weights on later passes.

options.text: The extra work comes from fitting more input tokens in the context.
options.feedback: Context capacity and recurrent computation describe different resources. The same block can process internal representations again without a larger input sequence.

options.text: Each pass learns improved weights that replace the previous values.
options.feedback: Recurrent depth here describes inference with trained weights. The numerical representation changes across passes, rather than a new training update replacing the weights.

options.text: The same learned transformation is applied to successive states.
options.feedback: Weight sharing reuses the existing numerical values. More applications can increase computation and latency without increasing the count of independent weights.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What distinguishes hidden recurrence from the autoregressive output loop?

options.text: Hidden recurrence trains weights; autoregression trains embeddings.
options.feedback: Both can describe inference with already trained weights. Their distinction concerns internal processing versus growth of the output sequence.

options.text: Hidden recurrence refines vectors; autoregression extends the sequence.
options.feedback: A recurrent pass can refine numerical representations before selection. Autoregression adds a selected token that shapes subsequent generation.

options.text: Hidden recurrence selects full answers; autoregression selects paragraphs.
options.feedback: Neither mechanism requires selecting a complete answer or paragraph at once. The generation process studied here advances by tokens.

options.text: Hidden recurrence enlarges context limits; autoregression enlarges layers.
options.feedback: Those are capacity and architecture changes. The two loops instead describe what is repeated during processing.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why is the length of a displayed reasoning explanation an incomplete measure of internal computation?

options.text: Internal vector processing need not appear as additional displayed tokens.
options.feedback: A system can perform numerical work without printing a corresponding sequence of words. The displayed explanation is therefore an incomplete measurement.

options.text: The displayed steps report new weights learned during the current reply.
options.feedback: The notes distinguish inference computation from learning parameters. A written explanation does not report a sequence of training updates during the reply.

options.text: The explanation describes context capacity rather than the work performed.
options.feedback: A written explanation is generated output, not a measure of the context limit. Its incompleteness comes from hidden processing that may not be displayed.

options.text: The displayed words record the original embeddings before model processing.
options.feedback: Embeddings are numerical representations transformed inside the model. The explanation is generated after model processing, not a printout of those initial vectors.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can supplying an extra document change an answer without changing the model's learned weights?

options.text: The document temporarily replaces the decoder with a search database.
options.feedback: A document can inform the decoder through context. Its presence does not imply the model has been replaced by a database.

options.text: The document increases the number of independently trained layers.
options.feedback: Adding context is not an architectural change. The same model can process different evidence without adding layers.

options.text: The document changes the input used by the existing transformations.
options.feedback: Ordinary inference applies trained weights to the current context. New evidence can change representations and next-token probabilities without a weight update.

options.text: The document turns its sentences into permanent model parameters.
options.feedback: Contextual use and training are different processes. Reading a document in a run does not by itself store it permanently in the weights.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why do successful recurrent-depth experiments leave the benefit of extra passes on a different model uncertain?

options.text: Matching parameter counts is enough to transfer the measured improvement.
options.feedback: Parameter count describes learned numerical values, not whether another model was trained to benefit from recurrent processing. The tested architecture and task matter.

options.text: Reusing fixed weights makes additional passes equivalent to a single pass.
options.feedback: Fixed weights can act on changing hidden representations. Reuse permits extra computation, but its benefit still needs evidence.

options.text: The length of a printed explanation determines the useful number of passes.
options.feedback: Visible text is an incomplete measure of hidden numerical computation. It cannot establish how much recurrent processing helps a different model.

options.text: The benefit depends on the model, its training, and the task.
options.feedback: The research demonstrates a trained approach, not a general improvement from adding loops to an arbitrary model. Evaluate the amount of processing that helps in the intended setting.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You compare "deposit at the bank" with "picnic on the river bank." Which mechanism helps the representation of "bank" fit these different contexts?

options.text: The temperature setting gives the token two permanent definitions.
options.feedback: Temperature affects sampling. The meaning appropriate to the input is shaped by contextual representations, not permanent definitions set by temperature.

options.text: The token identifier changes the model's trained vocabulary each time.
options.feedback: The same token can occur in different contexts. A context-sensitive representation does not require retraining the vocabulary.

options.text: Attention combines information from the surrounding permitted tokens.
options.feedback: Words such as "deposit" or "river" provide different contextual information. Attention helps the representation reflect the usage in each phrase.

options.text: The output sampler looks up both sentences in a reference database.
options.feedback: The sampler chooses from output probabilities. Contextual interpretation happens through model processing rather than a required sentence lookup.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: A token has a 30% probability in the sampling distribution, while another has 60%. The sampler chooses the 30% token. What does that show?

options.text: A sample can select an option other than the most probable one.
options.feedback: Thirty percent is a nonzero chance of selection. Sampling does not require picking the highest-probability token on every step.

options.text: The model must have changed its weights during the selection step.
options.feedback: The distribution can remain unchanged while different samples are drawn. A less probable selection is not evidence of a weight update.

options.text: The 30% token must be more factually accurate than the 60% token.
options.feedback: Sampling probability is not a guarantee or ranking of factual correctness. The selected token still contributes to a claim that may need checking.

options.text: The model has increased its maximum available context window.
options.feedback: Selecting a token does not expand the system's context capacity. It extends the current sequence within that capacity.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You run a trained recurrent block four times instead of twice, using the same weights and input. What resource change is most directly supported?

options.text: Twice as many independent weights have been learned.
options.feedback: Applying weights more times does not create additional independent parameters. Learning new weights would require a different operation.

options.text: More block computations occur without adding independent weights.
options.feedback: The shared block is applied twice more. That increases processing work even though the trained parameter set is unchanged.

options.text: The maximum number of input tokens has doubled.
options.feedback: Recurrent depth and context capacity are separate resources. More passes do not establish a larger context window.

options.text: The number of displayed reasoning tokens must double.
options.feedback: Hidden processing operates on vectors. More recurrent passes do not require a proportional increase in displayed text.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Two models have equal parameter counts but different maximum context lengths measured in tokens. Which conclusion follows from those facts?

options.text: They have different context limits with equal learned parameter counts.
options.feedback: Context capacity and learned parameter count describe different resources. These facts establish a capacity difference, not a universal quality ranking.

options.text: The larger context limit indicates a larger learned parameter set.
options.feedback: The stated parameter counts are equal. A longer context window does not by itself establish a larger parameter set.

options.text: The larger context limit establishes faster completion on comparable tasks.
options.feedback: The facts concern capacity, not latency. Processing more text can require additional work, and speed needs separate evidence.

options.text: The larger context limit establishes better answers on comparable tasks.
options.feedback: A capacity advantage does not guarantee that relevant evidence will be used correctly. Task performance needs to be assessed directly.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: A commercial model gives a better answer after spending longer on a problem. You know research models can use hidden recurrence. What can you conclude about this commercial model?

options.text: It uses the same recurrent block as the published research model.
options.feedback: Similar behavior does not establish identical internals. A published research architecture is evidence about that research system.

options.text: It added new independent parameters while working on this request.
options.feedback: More inference time does not establish a larger parameter set. Existing weights can support additional computation.

options.text: Its printed explanation fully specifies the hidden numerical process.
options.feedback: A written explanation is not a complete record of internal vector operations. It does not disclose the architecture merely by describing an answer.

options.text: Its architecture remains uncertain from that behavior alone.
options.feedback: Longer processing and a better answer are observations of behavior. They do not identify the undisclosed mechanism that produced the result.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which file holds a skill's central instructions?

options.text: SKILL.md
options.feedback: This is the central file that combines identifying metadata and the reusable procedure.

options.text: references/writing-guide.md
options.feedback: A referenced guide can provide detailed supporting instructions. It supports the central procedure rather than replacing SKILL.md.

options.text: assets/notes-template.md
options.feedback: A template provides a reusable starting structure. The central instructions explain how to use that structure.

options.text: outputs/lecture-notes.md
options.feedback: Generated notes are the result of one run. Their filename does not make them the reusable procedure for future runs.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which pair of metadata fields does SKILL.md require?

options.text: name and licensing information
options.feedback: A name is required, but licensing information is optional. The required partner is the description.

options.text: name and description
options.feedback: These fields identify the skill and explain its intended use so it can be selected.

options.text: description and compatibility
options.feedback: A description is required, while compatibility information is optional. The skill also needs a name.

options.text: compatibility and licensing
options.feedback: These can supply useful extra information, but neither replaces the required name and description.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What should a skill's description communicate?

options.text: Its folder size and creation time
options.feedback: Those details describe a saved folder, but they do not explain whether its procedure fits your task.

options.text: Its complete procedure and every example
options.feedback: The full procedure belongs in the instructions loaded after selection. The description offers a shorter basis for choosing.

options.text: Its outcome and when it applies
options.feedback: The description helps connect a requested task with an appropriate reusable procedure.

options.text: Its latest input and generated output
options.feedback: Those describe one run. The description should characterize the recurring work the skill handles.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Where would detailed writing guidance commonly belong in a skill folder?

options.text: A completed document in the output folder
options.feedback: A finished result shows what one run produced. Detailed reusable guidance is better organized as a reference.

options.text: An executable operation in scripts/
options.feedback: Scripts hold code for repeatable operations. Prose guidance about writing belongs in a referenced document.

options.text: The current transcript in the task workspace
options.feedback: The transcript is the content to process for one task, rather than reusable guidance for writing.

options.text: A linked document in references/
options.feedback: References hold detailed guidance that can be opened when the main procedure calls for it.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Where would a reusable blank notes template commonly belong?

options.text: The skill's assets/ folder
options.feedback: Assets can supply reusable inputs such as templates that support the procedure.

options.text: The skill's executable scripts/ folder
options.feedback: Scripts provide repeatable code operations. A blank document template is an asset rather than an executable routine.

options.text: The latest run's completed notes document
options.feedback: Completed notes are a task output. A template is a reusable starting structure for many outputs.

options.text: The latest run's source transcript file
options.feedback: A transcript supplies the content for a particular run. A reusable template instead supplies structure.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What is the role of a skill's scripts/ folder?

options.text: Holding prose about when to select the skill
options.feedback: Selection guidance belongs in SKILL.md and its description. Scripts provide executable operations.

options.text: Holding code for repeatable operations
options.feedback: A skill can include executable routines for operations such as extraction that recur across tasks.

options.text: Holding the finished documents from every run
options.feedback: Finished documents are outputs of particular tasks. Scripts contain code used to perform recurring operations.

options.text: Holding blank layouts for future documents
options.feedback: Blank layouts are reusable assets. Scripts instead supply executable steps.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: In a lecture-notes workflow, what role does the transcript of the current lecture play?

options.text: The reusable procedure for all future runs
options.feedback: A transcript contains lecture content, not the general instructions for turning any suitable transcript into notes.

options.text: Metadata describing when to select the skill
options.feedback: Metadata describes the skill's role. The current transcript supplies the material for one use of it.

options.text: Input for this particular run
options.feedback: The transcript provides the source content to which the reusable procedure is applied.

options.text: An output generated by the notes procedure
options.feedback: The notes are the output in this workflow. The transcript is supplied as source material.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: In a lecture-notes workflow, what role do the newly created notes play?

options.text: The procedure that replaces future instructions
options.feedback: One finished set of notes contains a particular lecture's content. It does not replace instructions for processing other lectures.

options.text: The metadata used to discover every skill
options.feedback: Discovery uses short skill descriptions. Newly created notes are the product of an already selected workflow.

options.text: The source transcript supplied before the run
options.feedback: The transcript is an input. The newly written notes are what the procedure produces from that input.

options.text: Output from this particular run
options.feedback: The notes are the result of applying a reusable procedure to the current lecture material.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What information initially helps an agent choose a relevant skill from a catalog?

options.text: The catalog names and short descriptions
options.feedback: These give the agent an initial account of each skill's purpose and applicability before loading detailed instructions.

options.text: The full procedure of every installed skill
options.feedback: The detailed procedure is loaded after a skill is selected. Requiring every complete procedure would defeat staged loading.

options.text: A ranking by when the skills were installed
options.feedback: Installation order does not establish whether a procedure fits the requested work. The description supplies relevance information.

options.text: The largest collection of bundled examples
options.feedback: Many examples may help a procedure, but their number does not identify whether its purpose matches the task.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which scope best suits a skill that follows conventions specific to one project?

options.text: Personal scope with the project conventions applied everywhere
options.feedback: Personal reuse is suitable when assumptions fit the receiving projects. Applying unusual conventions everywhere ignores that condition.

options.text: Project-local scope where those conventions apply
options.feedback: A skill tied to a project's assumptions fits project-local scope. It remains reusable across tasks in that project.

options.text: Personal scope with project-specific selection guidance removed
options.feedback: Removing the guidance makes its assumptions harder to recognize. Broader availability does not make those assumptions broadly appropriate.

options.text: Project-local scope with its reusable procedure removed
options.feedback: Local placement is useful, but removing the procedure discards the reusable expertise. Location and instructions serve different purposes.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should a lecture-notes skill keep its reusable procedure separate from one lecture's transcript?

options.text: The procedure should reproduce the same notes each time
options.feedback: Reusability means applying a method to changing inputs, not forcing every lecture to produce identical content.

options.text: The transcript must contain the skill's selection metadata
options.feedback: Selection metadata describes the skill. A transcript is source material and should not have to define the skill's identity.

options.text: The procedure must apply to different lectures
options.feedback: The skill encodes how to do recurring work; the transcript supplies the content that changes from run to run.

options.text: The transcript becomes a reusable template after one run
options.feedback: A source transcript still describes a particular lecture. Repeated use does not turn its content into a general output template.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why does a description that says only "helps with documents" give weak selection guidance?

options.text: It omits the entire step-by-step procedure
options.feedback: A description is supposed to be shorter than the full instructions. The problem is unclear scope, not the absence of every step.

options.text: It fails to include a finished document from each run
options.feedback: Selection guidance should describe recurring work. Appending finished outputs does not repair an unclear task boundary.

options.text: It lacks the names of every file in the assets folder
options.feedback: An inventory of assets does not itself explain the skill's purpose. The description needs a clear outcome and use condition.

options.text: It leaves the intended task too vague
options.feedback: A useful description indicates both the outcome and when the skill applies, so a broad label makes relevance harder to judge.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why is the number of installed skills insufficient to determine whether a skill catalog is useful?

options.text: Selection also depends on description quality, overlap, and context use.
options.feedback: The same count can describe clearly separated procedures or a confusing set of overlapping ones. The notes give no universal maximum for useful installed skills.

options.text: Selection depends on the total length of all previous generated outputs.
options.feedback: Past outputs describe particular runs, while selection begins with skill descriptions. Output volume does not establish whether the catalog offers clear, relevant guidance.

options.text: Selection improves whenever more skills cover the same recurring task.
options.feedback: Overlapping coverage can make the intended procedure harder to identify. More entries do not by themselves establish a more useful catalog.

options.text: Selection quality follows from storing the catalog in one project folder.
options.feedback: Project scope can fit local conventions, but storage location does not establish description quality or distinguish overlapping procedures. Assess how the skills fit the work.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why place a long, specialized writing guide in a reference linked from the main procedure?

options.text: Its instructions then become the input for every task
options.feedback: The guide remains reusable guidance, not the changing source content for each task.

options.text: It can be opened when that guidance is needed
options.feedback: Staged loading keeps the main procedure focused while making detailed guidance available for relevant steps.

options.text: The guide no longer needs a connection to the procedure
options.feedback: A useful reference supports the procedure. Separating it into a file does not remove the need to know when it applies.

options.text: It automatically becomes an executable writing program
options.feedback: A referenced document remains guidance. Executable operations belong to code, not prose made into a separate file.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: How should a skill's relevance be judged when a request uses different wording from its description?

options.text: Require the description's exact words before selecting the skill
options.feedback: Different wording can express the same task. The notes describe relevance-based activation rather than a mandatory magic word.

options.text: Choose the skill used most recently for any document task
options.feedback: Recent use does not establish a match to the current request. The procedure's intended outcome and conditions matter.

options.text: Compare the requested work with the skill's intended purpose
options.feedback: A semantic match can make a skill relevant even when the request uses different words from the description.

options.text: Prefer the broadest skill because it mentions more task types
options.feedback: A broad description can obscure task boundaries. Mentioning more categories does not establish the best fit for this request.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can adding many unrelated responsibilities make a skill harder to select?

options.text: Every included responsibility makes the skill equally suitable for each task
options.feedback: Listing many kinds of work does not establish equal suitability. Unrelated responsibilities can make its intended use less clear.

options.text: A broader skill can be selected without considering its description
options.feedback: The description still supplies the initial selection guidance. Breadth does not remove the need to assess relevance.

options.text: More responsibilities reduce the importance of the requested outcome
options.feedback: The requested outcome remains the basis for choosing a procedure. A broad collection of instructions cannot replace that match.

options.text: Unrelated responsibilities make the skill's intended use less distinct
options.feedback: A focused procedure is easier to match to a concrete task. Unrelated responsibilities blur the boundary of what the skill handles.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can two skills with vague, overlapping descriptions lead to poor selection?

options.text: Their descriptions fail to distinguish the intended uses
options.feedback: Selection begins with compact guidance about relevance. Similar vague descriptions can make different procedures appear interchangeable.

options.text: Their latest modification dates determine which procedure fits
options.feedback: Modification dates do not establish task fit. Clear differences in purpose and applicability are more useful selection evidence.

options.text: Their overlapping words prove the procedures are interchangeable
options.feedback: Similar wording can hide different procedures. The overlap creates ambiguity rather than proving the skills do the same work.

options.text: Their shared vocabulary makes the full instructions unnecessary
options.feedback: A description supports initial selection. Overlapping vocabulary does not replace the detailed instructions for carrying out the work.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can a small skill consist of SKILL.md alone?

options.text: Supporting folders would prevent the catalog from selecting it
options.feedback: Supporting files are compatible with progressive disclosure. They are opened when needed rather than preventing selection.

options.text: Its procedure may need no additional supporting files
options.feedback: A focused procedure can fit in the central file. References, assets, and scripts are added when they serve a useful purpose.

options.text: The central file is intended to hold metadata without a procedure
options.feedback: SKILL.md contains both identifying metadata and instructions. A one-file skill still needs its reusable procedure.

options.text: A short procedure gains executable behavior from its filename
options.feedback: Naming an instruction document does not turn it into a script. Some useful skills rely on instructions without bundled executable code.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should a personal skill's assumptions fit the projects where it is used?

options.text: Personal scope removes the need for a description
options.feedback: A personal skill still needs selection guidance. Broader availability does not replace the required description.

options.text: Each project must produce identical output content
options.feedback: Cross-project reuse concerns the method. Different inputs and purposes can still yield different task outputs.

options.text: Its reusable procedure may be applied across projects
options.feedback: Personal scope supports use beyond one project, so assumptions should suit that broader intended use.

options.text: Each project must store its transcripts inside the skill
options.feedback: Task-specific transcripts belong with their runs. Personal scope does not turn all project inputs into reusable skill content.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why does a skill instruction allowing file edits fail to establish that an agent can edit a particular file?

options.text: The instruction changes model weights before the file operation is attempted.
options.feedback: Loading a skill supplies guidance rather than retraining weights. Whether an operation can run depends on the tools and permissions in the environment.

options.text: The file becomes editable when its path is mentioned in the instructions.
options.feedback: A path identifies a possible target; mentioning it does not grant access. The operating environment must supply a permitted way to edit that target.

options.text: The instruction transfers the skill author's file access to the current agent.
options.feedback: Sharing a procedure does not transfer the author's permissions. Access must be available in the environment carrying out this run.

options.text: The operating environment must supply the necessary tool and permission.
options.feedback: A skill describes intended behavior, but instructions do not grant access or create a secure sandbox. The harness operates under the current environment's execution constraints.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You are building a notes skill for repeated use. You have one lecture transcript and instructions for processing any lecture. How should you organize them?

options.text: Keep the procedure in SKILL.md and the transcript with its task
options.feedback: The procedure is reusable expertise, while the transcript is the changing input for a particular run.

options.text: Put the transcript in SKILL.md and the procedure in the output notes
options.feedback: This reverses the roles: source content would replace the reusable instructions, while the method would be buried in one result.

options.text: Put both in the description so selection also supplies every detail
options.feedback: The description should summarize outcome and applicability. Full instructions and current source material belong in their own roles.

options.text: Put both in assets as blank templates for all future lecture tasks
options.feedback: A transcript is a completed source, not a blank template, and procedural instructions belong in the main skill file.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Your skill needs a blank notes layout and a program that repeatedly extracts text. How should you organize these supporting files?

options.text: Place the layout in scripts/ and the program in references/
options.feedback: This treats a template as code and executable code as detailed guidance. The file roles point to assets and scripts respectively.

options.text: Place the layout in assets/ and the program in scripts/
options.feedback: The layout is a reusable template, while the extraction program performs an executable operation.

options.text: Place both in the description so they determine the skill's name
options.feedback: The description communicates purpose and applicability. It is not where templates and executable routines take the place of supporting files.

options.text: Place both among finished outputs for the most recent task run
options.feedback: These files support future runs. Treating them as one run's outputs confuses reusable resources with generated results.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Two skills are both described as "turn text into useful documents," but one makes lecture notes and the other makes meeting summaries. What edit most directly clarifies selection?

options.text: Give both skills the same shorter name and description
options.feedback: Making their identifying guidance even more alike preserves the ambiguity instead of explaining their different uses.

options.text: Move both complete procedures into a single shared description
options.feedback: More procedural detail is not the same as a clear boundary. The description should distinguish purposes without absorbing both full procedures.

options.text: Describe each output and the kind of source it handles
options.feedback: Specific outcomes and use conditions distinguish the two procedures when an agent matches a request to a skill.

options.text: Add the latest generated document to each scripts folder
options.feedback: Generated documents are outputs, not executable routines, and moving them does not clarify when each skill applies.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You have a writing procedure that depends on one project's unusual document conventions. You want it available where those conventions apply. Which arrangement fits best?

options.text: Make it personal and describe it as suitable for every project
options.feedback: That broad claim would hide its specific assumptions. Personal reuse requires assumptions appropriate to the other projects.

options.text: Replace its instructions with the latest finished project document
options.feedback: An example output does not replace the reusable method that applies the project's conventions.

options.text: Remove its description and rely on a distinctive template filename
options.feedback: A template filename does not supply the required description or clearly explain when the skill should be selected.

options.text: Keep it as a project-local skill
options.feedback: The procedure's assumptions are tied to that project, which is the use case for project-local scope.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You request a particular notes skill by name. The task matches its purpose, but your request lacks the keyword used in its description. How should that affect selection?

options.text: The explicit request can still activate the relevant skill
options.feedback: The notes allow users to request a skill directly. Activation is based on relevance rather than a mandatory magic word.

options.text: The skill must be ignored until the keyword appears exactly
options.feedback: This treats activation as a rigid text match. An explicit request for a relevant skill is another way to select it.

options.text: Every available skill must be activated to resolve the wording
options.feedback: An explicit request and a matching purpose already identify the relevant procedure. Loading unrelated skills does not resolve a keyword issue.

options.text: The skill's current outputs must replace its detailed instructions
options.feedback: Naming a skill selects its procedure; it does not change prior outputs into the instructions needed for this run.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What role does the harness play when an agent requests a file operation?

options.text: It invokes an available tool and returns its result.
options.feedback: The harness connects a supported request to an available tool. Returning the result lets the model use evidence from the operation.

options.text: It treats the generated request as a completed operation.
options.feedback: A request expresses an operation to attempt. Execution and checking the outcome still have to happen.

options.text: It stores the learned weights that select the next token.
options.feedback: Learned parameters belong to the model. The harness provides the operating environment that executes supported tool requests.

options.text: It makes a successful tool call count as a verified outcome.
options.feedback: Executing a tool supplies a result to inspect. You still need to check whether that result meets the task requirement.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What is the language model doing when it generates a request to read a file?

options.text: Opening the file directly without an intervening tool.
options.feedback: Generating text is different from performing a file operation. The harness invokes a tool to carry out a supported request.

options.text: Producing a request for the harness to execute.
options.feedback: The model can choose and express an operation. The harness handles execution and supplies the result for a later model step.

options.text: Verifying that the file contains the expected final content.
options.feedback: A request to read is not yet evidence about the contents. Verification requires receiving and checking the actual result.

options.text: Adding every file in the project to the current context.
options.feedback: A file request can target one relevant source. Access to a project does not mean all its files enter the model input.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which sequence distinguishes the stages of completing an agent operation?

options.text: Request the operation, announce success, then execute it.
options.feedback: Announcing success before execution reports an outcome that has not been established. The result needs to be checked after the operation.

options.text: Execute the operation, request it, then infer success.
options.feedback: The request precedes execution in the agent loop. Inferring success also leaves out checking the resulting state.

options.text: Request the operation, execute it, then verify it.
options.feedback: These are separate events: a request proposes an action, execution attempts it, and verification checks whether the result meets the requirement.

options.text: Verify the planned wording, request it, then announce success.
options.feedback: Checking wording can improve a request but cannot establish what happened in the environment. Completion requires evidence from the affected result.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What is the purpose of a project manifest in organizing agent work?

options.text: To copy the entire project into each model input.
options.feedback: A manifest helps locate relevant material. It does not imply that the contents of every listed file have been loaded.

options.text: To guarantee that every published file is accurate.
options.feedback: Organization helps you find files, but accuracy still requires checking the contents against the task.

options.text: To replace the source evidence after a summary is made.
options.feedback: A manifest can point to sources, but it cannot substitute for their evidence. Keep important originals available to reopen.

options.text: To help locate relevant project material.
options.feedback: A useful manifest works with filenames and folders to guide retrieval. The agent can then read the material needed for its current step.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What does conversation compaction do during a long task?

options.text: Summarizes earlier conversation for a smaller active context.
options.feedback: Compaction makes it possible to continue with less conversation in the active input. The summary can omit details, so important original evidence should remain available.

options.text: Copies every available project file into the next model input.
options.feedback: Compaction reduces the active conversation through summarization. Reading all project files would instead add material to the input.

options.text: Preserves every original detail in a shorter lossless transcript.
options.feedback: A summary is selective and can omit details that later matter. You should retain access to the original evidence.

options.text: Turns the current project record into a permanent personal preference.
options.feedback: Compaction summarizes task history. Changing project facts and recurring personal preferences have different roles.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which information belongs in a compact working record for an unfinished project?

options.text: The preferred output style and unrelated personal examples.
options.feedback: A recurring style preference can be useful, but it does not tell you what happened in this project or what remains to do.

options.text: Goals, decisions, progress, issues, sources, and next steps.
options.feedback: These details allow work to resume with its purpose and current state intact. Source locations also support reopening evidence when the summary is insufficient.

options.text: The complete contents of every file that the agent can access.
options.feedback: A working record preserves useful state rather than duplicating an entire project. Relevant originals can be retrieved when needed.

options.text: The intended final answer with every unfinished check omitted.
options.feedback: A desired outcome is not a record of progress. Unresolved checks matter because they distinguish unfinished work from verified completion.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What is a suitable task for a fresh subagent in a long project?

options.text: Infer a missing acceptance decision from the project title.
options.feedback: A title helps identify a project but does not supply its decisions. Give the subagent relevant decision evidence for its bounded question.

options.text: Expand a document check into completing the remaining project.
options.feedback: A fresh subagent is useful for a bounded question. Expanding the assignment adds scope beyond the focused check it was meant to perform.

options.text: Investigate a bounded question with relevant context.
options.feedback: A focused task lets a subagent work with the information it needs and return a concise finding. Fresh context does not remove the need to check the answer.

options.text: Certify a proposed repair from its description before it runs.
options.feedback: A proposed repair describes an intended action, not an observed outcome. A subagent still needs evidence and its finding still needs checking.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: How should a bounded technical-support workflow handle an unfamiliar problem?

options.text: Apply the closest familiar repair and inspect only if challenged.
options.feedback: Similar symptoms do not establish that a known repair fits. An unfamiliar case belongs at the escalation boundary.

options.text: Try a newly generated repair because it includes an undo plan.
options.feedback: Reversal information can help manage a change, but it does not make an unfamiliar repair a known, authorized procedure. The bounded workflow escalates unfamiliar cases.

options.text: Treat a familiar phrase in the report as proof of a known case.
options.feedback: Matching a phrase is weaker than inspecting the current state and comparing it with a documented case. Ambiguous cases should be escalated.

options.text: Escalate the case with the evidence collected.
options.feedback: The workflow is bounded by known, authorized repairs. Escalation preserves useful evidence while handling uncertainty explicitly.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What should a support workflow check after applying a repair?

options.text: The affected object and its requested behavior.
options.feedback: Read back what changed and check the behavior the user needed. This establishes more than the fact that an operation was attempted.

options.text: The wording of the original repair request alone.
options.feedback: The request identifies the desired result but does not show the current state. Verification requires observing the affected object.

options.text: The confidence of the agent that proposed the repair.
options.feedback: Confidence is generated output, not evidence of the repair. Check the actual saved result and behavior.

options.text: The success record of the same repair on a prior case.
options.feedback: A documented case helps select a procedure, but its past success does not establish the current result. Read back the object changed in this run.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What should the final response in a bounded support workflow communicate?

options.text: An attempted repair to every available course contact.
options.feedback: An attempt is not a verified result, and broad delivery can misdirect the message. Check success and use the intended recipient.

options.text: The verified result and the responder's automated identity.
options.feedback: The response should go to the intended recipient after validation. Identifying the automated responder makes the nature of that communication clear.

options.text: A planned repair described as completed by a human operator.
options.feedback: A plan does not establish completion, and describing an automated responder as human obscures who acted. Report the verified result accurately.

options.text: The original report with the verification outcome left unstated.
options.feedback: Repeating the report does not tell the recipient what happened. The workflow calls for communicating the result that has actually been checked.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can two interfaces using the same language model support different actions?

options.text: Their product labels specify which file operations the model can perform.
options.feedback: A product label is insufficient evidence of available actions. Inspect the actual tools and permissions supplied by the environment.

options.text: Their models execute file operations directly after describing them.
options.feedback: A model generates a request; execution happens through the harness and an available tool. A description alone does not perform the operation.

options.text: Their harnesses can supply different tools and execution permissions.
options.feedback: Sharing a model does not imply sharing its operating environment. The harness and tools determine which supported requests can actually run.

options.text: Their project names determine the operations built into the model weights.
options.feedback: Project selection gives the agent relevant context and a place to work. It does not change model weights to provide file operations.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why is a plausible document title insufficient evidence that a repaired link is correct?

options.text: The saved title is sufficient evidence that the link has the intended target.
options.feedback: A plausible label can point to the wrong document. Reading the destination checks its identity rather than relying on the displayed label.

options.text: The agent's completion claim establishes that the destination was inspected.
options.feedback: A completion sentence is not evidence that inspection occurred. Check the destination content and the actual action evidence.

options.text: Opening a document establishes that the link now reaches the intended reading.
options.feedback: A successful click establishes that a destination opens. You still need to inspect whether that destination contains the intended reading.

options.text: Different documents can appear under the same convincing title.
options.feedback: A label can look appropriate even when the destination is wrong. Open the saved link and confirm that the document itself is the intended one.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why does an action log separate a proposal, an attempt, and a verified result?

options.text: They establish different amounts of completion evidence.
options.feedback: A proposal describes intent, an attempt shows that an operation was tried, and a verified result shows the checked outcome. Keeping them distinct prevents an attempt from being reported as success.

options.text: Each is an interchangeable description of a completed operation.
