options.feedback: These stages are not equivalent. A proposed or attempted repair can still fail to produce the required result.

options.text: A detailed proposal guarantees that the operation will execute properly.
options.feedback: A well-specified proposal can guide execution but cannot guarantee its result. The environment still has to be observed after acting.

options.text: Recording an attempted operation removes the need for later inspection.
options.feedback: A log of an attempt documents activity, not necessarily success. Verification needs evidence about the resulting object or behavior.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can an agent work with a large project without reading every file into its current context?

options.text: Accessible files are already fully represented in every model input.
options.feedback: Access means material can be retrieved, not that its contents have already been loaded. The current input may contain only a small selection.

options.text: It can search for and read material relevant to the current step.
options.feedback: Useful organization and file tools support selective retrieval. This keeps the current context focused while retaining access to other sources.

options.text: Filenames contain enough detail to replace the original source evidence.
options.feedback: Names help locate material but do not prove its contents. The agent still needs to open the relevant sources.

options.text: A long conversation automatically copies every project file into memory.
options.feedback: Conversation history and available files are different sources of information. File contents need to be retrieved through available tools.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should important original evidence remain available after conversation compaction?

options.text: The summary guarantees that every source will be reopened automatically.
options.feedback: A summary does not guarantee later retrieval. Keeping source locations and originals available makes reopening possible when a detail is needed.

options.text: The summary turns earlier tentative claims into verified project facts.
options.feedback: Summarizing a claim does not validate it. Original evidence may be needed to check whether a tentative statement was established.

options.text: The summary can omit details that later become relevant.
options.feedback: Compaction selects what to preserve in a shorter account. Original evidence lets you recover a detail that the summary did not retain.

options.text: The summary requires all originals to be pasted into every later request.
options.feedback: Sources can remain accessible without being included in every input. Reopen the evidence needed for the next step.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should a preferred writing style be distinguished from a record of which file was published?

options.text: The writing style is a project fact that expires when a file is published.
options.feedback: A style preference can recur across tasks. Publishing a file changes project state without necessarily changing that preference.

options.text: The publication record is a preference for what should happen on the next task.
options.feedback: A publication record tracks what happened in this project. A recurring preference guides later choices rather than establishing completed operations.

options.text: Both records describe stable choices that can be reused without updating.
options.feedback: Preferences may recur, but a project record tracks changing facts. Reusing stale publication state can misrepresent what has actually been completed.

options.text: One can recur across tasks; the other tracks changing project facts.
options.feedback: A preference may guide many tasks, while project state records current decisions and operations. Maintaining both appropriately helps prevent stale assumptions.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should you correct a remembered preference that came from a role-play example?

options.text: The example may not represent your actual preference.
options.feedback: A system can mistake an imagined role for a fact about you. Inspecting and correcting that memory prevents later work from inheriting the mistaken preference.

options.text: A preference mentioned in role-play is evidence of a lasting personal choice.
options.feedback: An example can describe an imagined role rather than you. Its appearance in conversation does not establish a recurring personal preference.

options.text: The stored version should take priority because it came from an earlier message.
options.feedback: Earlier context can be misinterpreted. Inspecting and correcting the memory helps it represent your actual preference.

options.text: The remembered preference can be treated as a record of completed project work.
options.feedback: A preference guides recurring choices; project state tracks changing facts and operations. Neither role turns a fictional example into a fact about you.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why does a fresh subagent need both a focused assignment and relevant background?

options.text: Fresh context automatically includes every decision from the main conversation.
options.feedback: Fresh context should not be assumed to contain unsupplied facts. Relevant background has to be provided or made accessible.

options.text: A narrow task still depends on facts it may not have received.
options.feedback: Focus limits the question, but it does not supply missing evidence. Give the subagent enough context and check its returned finding.

options.text: A bounded assignment guarantees that the returned finding needs no checking.
options.feedback: Narrow scope can help manage context, but it does not guarantee accuracy. The resulting answer still needs verification.

options.text: Loading unrelated history is a substitute for supplying the relevant evidence.
options.feedback: A larger input does not necessarily contain the evidence the question requires. Select the background that supports the bounded assignment.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why must a course-support workflow resolve the intended section before applying a familiar repair?

options.text: A familiar symptom proves that every section has the same current problem.
options.feedback: Sections can have different current states. The workflow needs evidence about the intended target, not only a familiar symptom.

options.text: The section can be inferred from whichever course object is easiest to edit.
options.feedback: Convenience does not identify the intended target. Resolve the course and section from the report and available evidence.

options.text: The same repair could otherwise change the wrong course area.
options.feedback: A repair can be technically familiar yet affect the wrong target. Section identification is part of establishing that the authorized procedure fits.

options.text: Checking the section after a response gives the recipient stronger evidence.
options.feedback: A later check cannot justify an earlier claim about the target. Resolve the section before changing anything and verify before responding.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should a support repair record include what changed and information needed for reversal?

options.text: Recording a change makes every attempted repair automatically reversible.
options.feedback: A record supports reversal where possible but does not guarantee it. The workflow must preserve information relevant to the actual change.

options.text: A change record replaces the need to inspect the repaired object.
options.feedback: Logging and verification serve different purposes. The record documents the action; inspecting the object checks whether it worked.

options.text: The record lets the agent apply unfamiliar repairs without escalation.
options.feedback: Documentation does not turn an unknown procedure into a known repair. Unfamiliar or ambiguous cases still need escalation.

options.text: It supports tracing and undoing the repair where possible.
options.feedback: Recording the change and relevant prior information makes the intervention easier to inspect and reverse. It also preserves useful project state beyond the conversation.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You ask an agent to fix a reading link. The new link opens a document with the expected title, but two documents share that title. What should you check next?

options.text: Read the destination and compare it with the intended reading.
options.feedback: The title is ambiguous, so content readback is the evidence that can identify the intended document. A successful click alone does not settle the issue.

options.text: Accept the repair because a successful click establishes the right content.
options.feedback: A successful click shows that something opened. It does not distinguish between two documents with the same title.

options.text: Check the operation log for a completed update and accept that as verification.
options.feedback: A log showing an update establishes that an operation was attempted or executed. It does not establish that the saved link reaches the intended content.

options.text: Compare the displayed title again and omit reading either document itself.
options.feedback: Repeating an ambiguous title check cannot resolve which document is linked. The content must be inspected.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: After a long conversation is summarized, you need to resume a project, but the summary omits whether a saved file passed its final check. What should you do?

options.text: Assume the check passed because the summary says the file was saved.
options.feedback: Saving and verifying are separate events. A missing check should remain unresolved until you recover or obtain evidence.

options.text: Reopen the project record and evidence to establish the check status.
options.feedback: Explicit state and accessible originals help recover details omitted by compaction. Use them to determine what remains before claiming completion.

options.text: Use the earlier plan to validate the file as evidence that validation happened.
options.feedback: A plan records an intended check, not its execution or result. Recover the check evidence or inspect the artifact before claiming completion.

options.text: Ask the agent for a confident completion statement based on the summary.
options.feedback: The summary omits the needed evidence. Another generated statement cannot establish whether the file passed its check.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You want a fresh subagent to determine which of two project files contains the accepted revision. How should you prepare its assignment?

options.text: Provide only the project name and assume it knows the acceptance decision.
options.feedback: A fresh subagent may not have the decision history. It needs the relevant file locations and evidence of what was accepted.

options.text: Ask it to complete every remaining project task before comparing the files.
options.feedback: Expanding the task adds unrelated scope. The immediate need is a bounded comparison grounded in the acceptance evidence.

options.text: Provide both file locations and the acceptance evidence for comparison.
options.feedback: This supplies the focused context needed for the question. Check the concise result against the sources before using it as project state.

options.text: Tell it to choose the newest-looking filename without opening either file.
options.feedback: A filename can guide retrieval but does not establish accepted content. The subagent needs to read and compare relevant evidence.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: A support report describes a familiar broken link, but you cannot establish which of two course sections the sender means. What should the workflow do?

options.text: Repair both sections so that one of the changes will reach the intended target.
options.feedback: Changing both expands the intervention without resolving the target. The workflow first needs to establish the intended section.

options.text: Repair the first section listed because the symptom matches a known case.
options.feedback: A known symptom does not identify the correct course area. Acting on list order risks changing the wrong target.

options.text: Choose the section with the most familiar title and report a verified repair.
options.feedback: A plausible title is not sufficient target evidence. Reporting verification would also be premature before checking the affected result.

options.text: Resolve the section or escalate the ambiguity before repairing.
options.feedback: The repair boundary includes a known target as well as a known procedure. Preserve the collected evidence and escalate if the section remains uncertain.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: A known, authorized repair has been applied to the intended course section. The agent has not read back the object and has two possible recipient addresses. What should happen before a success message is sent?

options.text: Verify the repaired behavior and establish the intended recipient.
options.feedback: An applied operation is not yet a verified outcome, and recipient ambiguity remains unresolved. Check both before communicating success and identify the automated responder.

options.text: Use the first address and describe the attempted change as a verified result.
options.feedback: List order does not establish the intended recipient. The claimed result also needs evidence from the affected object.

options.text: Send the same success message to both addresses to cover the uncertainty.
options.feedback: Broad delivery does not resolve who should receive the result. The workflow restricts the recipient and validates the repair before responding.

options.text: Ask the agent to confirm its confidence and reuse the most plausible address.
options.feedback: Confidence cannot substitute for inspecting the repaired behavior. A plausible address also needs to be established as the intended destination.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: When you improve a skill with artificial intelligence assistance, what does human expertise contribute?

options.text: A guarantee that the first draft will work reliably
options.feedback: Expert guidance improves the requirements, but the procedure still needs testing on actual tasks.

options.text: Proof that the agent executed every requested step
options.feedback: A person can specify the steps, but you need evidence of execution to establish that they happened.

options.text: Requirements about important errors and quality
options.feedback: Your experience identifies misunderstandings, costly mistakes, and standards that the agent may fail to infer.

options.text: Automatic installation in every compatible environment
options.feedback: Human expertise shapes the procedure; installation and environment compatibility require separate checks.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: How can you directly change the behavior specified by an existing skill?

options.text: Edit its instructions and test the revised procedure
options.feedback: You can revise the document yourself, then inspect results to see whether the change helped.

options.text: Retrain the model before changing the procedure
options.feedback: A skill is editable guidance. Changing its instructions does not require changing the model through training.

options.text: Rename the output without changing the instructions
options.feedback: Changing an output name does not revise the procedure that produces it.

options.text: Correct one generated answer without updating the saved skill
options.feedback: Repairing one output can improve that artifact, but it does not change the reusable instructions that govern later runs.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What evidence supports a claim that the requested Skill Creator procedure was actually used?

options.text: A final message that prominently names Skill Creator
options.feedback: Naming a procedure in generated text does not establish that its instructions were loaded or its steps performed.

options.text: A skill folder with a polished title and complete instructions
options.feedback: A finished document can exist without the requested authoring procedure having been followed.

options.text: A record showing that the agent read the short catalog description
options.feedback: The description helps select a skill. Evidence of selection alone does not establish that the detailed instructions were loaded and their required steps completed.

options.text: Records of loaded instructions and completed required steps
options.feedback: Check evidence that the procedure was loaded and that its required work actually occurred, including relevant evaluation artifacts.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What must you establish after saving a skill folder before relying on it in the intended host?

options.text: That the folder has been copied into several unrelated projects
options.feedback: Extra copies do not establish that the intended host has discovered and enabled the skill.

options.text: That the host has discovered and enabled the skill
options.feedback: Saving files and making them available for use in a host are distinct events. Check the destination environment.

options.text: That the agent reports successful installation in its final message
options.feedback: A completion claim is generated text. Inspect whether the destination actually discovered and enabled the skill.

options.text: That its text is identical to the version on a different machine
options.feedback: Matching text can help preserve a procedure, but does not establish that the destination can use it.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What comparison is central to evaluating whether a skill improves task performance?

options.text: Matched tasks with and without the skill
options.feedback: Keeping inputs and relevant settings comparable helps you interpret differences in the resulting artifacts.

options.text: Different tasks using unrelated models and instructions
options.feedback: Several factors change at once, so the resulting difference gives weak evidence about the skill itself.

options.text: The lengths of the skill file and the generated answer
options.feedback: Length does not measure whether the output meets the task requirements.

options.text: The confidence of the author before and after editing
options.feedback: Confidence can change without performance improving. Evaluate actual outputs against defined criteria.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: When should you define the required qualities of an output in a skill evaluation?

options.text: After choosing the output that looks most impressive
options.feedback: Choosing standards after seeing a preferred result can reward appearance instead of the intended task requirements.

options.text: After the skill has been running unattended for several weeks
options.feedback: You need success criteria during development, before relying on repeated unattended operation.

options.text: Before judging the outputs from the evaluation
options.feedback: Advance criteria give you a stable basis for inspecting results and deciding whether the skill helps.

options.text: After a user reports a failure in the deployed procedure
options.feedback: Reported failures can improve later tests, but initial evaluation also needs explicit success criteria.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What kinds of inputs should you include in a small initial skill evaluation?

options.text: A varied set of easy examples with short, clearly written sources
options.feedback: Variety among easy cases can show some behavior, but difficult inputs are needed to expose weaknesses those cases miss.

options.text: Representative examples plus at least one difficult case
options.feedback: Typical inputs show ordinary behavior, while a difficult case can reveal weaknesses that easy examples hide.

options.text: Repeated runs of the example used to develop the first draft
options.feedback: Repeating one example can show behavior on that input, but provides narrow evidence about variation across intended tasks.

options.text: A collection of the examples that produced the best-looking outputs
options.feedback: Selecting favorable results can conceal weaknesses. Include representative inputs and a difficult case before judging performance.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What cost-conscious model strategy do the notes propose for developing and running a skill?

options.text: Choose the cheapest model and assume instructions remove quality differences
options.feedback: A skill does not guarantee adequate execution on a less expensive model. Test actual performance.

options.text: Use the most capable model for every run without examining its cost
options.feedback: A capable model can help develop the procedure, but cost and required quality still deserve comparison.

options.text: Choose a model by the length of its explanations rather than its results
options.feedback: Explanation length does not establish task success or whether the operating cost is justified.

options.text: Develop with a capable model and test cheaper execution
options.feedback: A stronger authoring model may help refine a procedure that a cheaper model can execute adequately, but you must evaluate that tradeoff.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Which set of checks most directly tests whether a transferred skill can execute its intended operations?

options.text: Tools, libraries, file access, and actual output
options.feedback: A compatible format is only part of portability. The destination must support the operations, and you should inspect a representative result.

options.text: Matching folder names, valid formatting, and clear prose
options.feedback: These checks help preserve readable instructions, but they do not establish that the destination has the programs and access needed to execute them.

options.text: A successful original run and an identical destination copy
options.feedback: Matching the original preserves the procedure, but the new host may lack its dependencies or access. Test the destination environment itself.

options.text: File existence, a discoverable catalog entry, and an enabled skill
options.feedback: These checks establish availability in the host, but do not establish that required programs and access are present or that actual outputs meet requirements.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What execution resource does a persistent automatic agent need?

options.text: A phone connection to a local computer that may be sleeping
options.feedback: Remote control does not make an unavailable local machine an always-on service.

options.text: An available host on which its operations can run
options.feedback: Persistent operation depends on an execution environment being available when work is triggered.

options.text: A saved skill folder on a laptop that is disconnected during scheduled runs
options.feedback: Saved instructions remain available as files, but scheduled operations still need a running, available execution environment.

options.text: A working installation on a computer used during the initial demonstration
options.feedback: An earlier demonstration shows past availability. Persistent work needs the execution host available when later work is triggered.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should you review a skill even when an artificial intelligence author produces polished instructions?

options.text: Fluent wording is the main evidence that every required step ran
options.feedback: Readable instructions describe work; they do not establish execution. Inspect tool and artifact evidence for completed steps.

options.text: Human review should judge wording before deciding the output requirements
options.feedback: Your expertise should make important requirements explicit before you judge the results, rather than letting polished wording determine success.

options.text: Clear prose can still omit task-specific quality requirements
options.feedback: An author can organize the instructions well while missing errors or standards that your experience tells you matter.

options.text: A procedure written by a capable model needs checking only for formatting
options.feedback: A capable author can still miss task-specific requirements. Review the substance and inspect actual results, as well as readability.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why is a saved skill file insufficient evidence that Skill Creator was used?

options.text: The same artifact could be written through a different process
options.feedback: You need execution and file evidence of the requested process, not just an artifact that could have another origin.

options.text: The file confirms the procedure was loaded, but not that testing finished
options.feedback: A file can be written without loading the requested procedure. Check both loaded instructions and completed required work rather than inferring either from the artifact.

options.text: A saved file proves the procedure ran but conceals its evaluation score
options.feedback: The file establishes an artifact exists, not that the named process or an evaluation ran.

options.text: Saving instructions automatically substitutes for comparative evaluation
options.feedback: Writing a procedure and testing its effects are different activities. One cannot establish the other.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should you keep inputs and relevant settings similar in runs with and without a skill?

options.text: To ensure that both runs produce exactly the same wording
options.feedback: The purpose is to compare performance, not force identical text. Different wording can meet the same quality criteria.

options.text: To replace a comparison of quality with a comparison of answer length
options.feedback: Similar conditions help you interpret performance, but output length does not replace defined task-specific quality criteria.

options.text: To let successful installation serve as evidence that the skill improves quality
options.feedback: Installation makes the skill available. Comparable runs still require inspecting actual outputs to evaluate improvement.

options.text: To make differences more informative about the skill
options.feedback: When the task and conditions are comparable, observed changes provide better evidence about the added guidance.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why would a transcript containing an important promise near its end be useful for testing a notes skill?

options.text: It lets you use a longer generated answer as evidence of better coverage
options.feedback: Length does not establish that the important promise was captured. Inspect the output against the relevant source requirement.

options.text: It tests whether the procedure preserves an easily missed requirement
options.feedback: A difficult case can expose omissions that a straightforward transcript would fail to reveal.

options.text: It makes repeated runs of this transcript sufficient to assess varied inputs
options.feedback: Repeated success on this case provides evidence for that case. Representative inputs are still needed to assess other challenges.

options.text: It lets you judge completeness from the output without reopening the transcript
options.feedback: An output can sound complete while omitting a promise. Compare it with the source to check the relevant requirement.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: What conclusion is supported by three successful tests of a newly edited skill?

options.text: The procedure has enough evidence to begin unattended operation without failure tests
options.feedback: Three successful examples leave failure behavior untested. Persistent operation needs explicit operating conditions and failure testing.

options.text: The procedure has enough evidence to skip a representative test after transfer
options.feedback: A new host can differ in tools, dependencies, and permissions. Success in the original environment does not establish performance there.

options.text: The procedure improved performance even though no run without it was compared
options.feedback: Successful outputs show that the tested runs met requirements. A matched comparison with and without the skill is needed to assess its added value.

options.text: The revision worked on those examples and merits further testing
options.feedback: A small set of successes can guide iteration and build limited confidence without proving broad reliability.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why do positive results for curated skills in a benchmark leave the value of your new skill uncertain?

options.text: The benchmark makes polished instructions sufficient evidence of a useful new skill
options.feedback: A polished file does not establish performance. The benchmark supports evaluating guidance rather than judging it by appearance.

options.text: The benchmark lets you infer your skill's value from who helped write it
options.feedback: The notes treat skill quality as an evaluation question. Human authorship or artificial intelligence assistance does not establish your procedure's performance.

options.text: Your procedure and task still require their own evaluation
options.feedback: Evidence from tested curated skills does not establish that every new skill improves results.

options.text: The benchmark lets you select a cheaper execution model without testing your task
options.feedback: A cheaper model may execute a well-developed skill adequately, but you must evaluate the cost-quality tradeoff on your requirements.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why must you evaluate a cheaper execution model even if a more capable model helped write the skill?

options.text: Authoring quality does not establish execution quality
options.feedback: A well-developed procedure may help a cheaper model, but only tested results show whether it meets your requirements.

options.text: The cheaper model should be rejected because another model wrote its instructions
options.feedback: The proposed strategy may work. Evaluation determines adequacy rather than assuming failure from model differences.

options.text: A stronger authoring model automatically installs all execution dependencies
options.feedback: Developing instructions does not establish that required software or access exists in the execution environment.

options.text: The authoring model permanently transfers its own abilities into the cheaper model
options.feedback: A skill supplies guidance; it does not transfer the authoring model's underlying capabilities into another model.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why should you reserve some development time and usage budget after a skill has been drafted?

options.text: A longer drafting session guarantees that later errors cannot occur
options.feedback: More drafting alone does not establish reliability. Evaluation can reveal problems the draft did not anticipate.

options.text: Checking outputs can be replaced by choosing the most capable authoring model
options.feedback: A capable model can help develop the procedure, but its involvement does not establish that outputs satisfy your requirements.

options.text: Checking outputs can reveal changes the procedure still needs
options.feedback: Useful development includes testing and revision, so spending the entire budget on the first draft leaves important work undone.

options.text: Installing the finished folder makes all further verification unnecessary
options.feedback: Installation makes a skill available but does not prove that its outputs meet the task requirements.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why can a skill written in a portable instruction format still fail after being copied to another host?

options.text: The copied instructions retrain the destination model with different weights
options.feedback: A skill supplies task guidance; loading its instructions does not retrain the model. Check the destination environment and performance.

options.text: The destination may lack required programs or permissions
options.feedback: Portable instructions do not ensure portable executable dependencies or access. Inspect the new environment and run a representative task.

options.text: The copied folder moves the original computer's permissions to the new host
options.feedback: Permissions belong to the operating environment. Copying instructions does not transfer or grant the access required in another host.

options.text: The destination uses the original run's output in place of the new task input
options.feedback: The reusable procedure, each run's input, and its output have different roles. Transferring a skill does not make an earlier output the new input.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Why does turning a one-time skill into a persistent process require additional failure testing?

options.text: Repeated execution repairs errors by retrying the unchanged procedure
options.feedback: Repetition can reproduce the same error, so define failure behavior and test it before relying on unattended runs.

options.text: Saved progress eliminates the need to check whether required inputs are present
options.feedback: Saved state supports continuity, but later runs can still encounter missing inputs or access.

options.text: An available execution host establishes that every requested action is appropriate
options.feedback: Host availability enables operations; allowed actions and verification criteria still need to be defined.

options.text: An unattended process can repeat the same error across runs
options.feedback: Persistent operation adds opportunities for recurring mistakes. Test failure cases and define when the process should stop.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: Your notes skill produces readable summaries but repeatedly omits challenging study questions. You know those questions are essential. What is the best next step?

options.text: Specify the missing requirement and evaluate revised outputs
options.feedback: Your expertise identifies the needed quality criterion. Make it explicit, then test whether the revision changes the artifacts as intended.

options.text: Assume the polished summaries show that the original skill meets the need
options.feedback: Readable prose is only one quality dimension. The repeated omission shows an important requirement is unmet.

options.text: Switch to unattended operation so repeated runs eventually include the questions
options.feedback: Repeated operation does not reliably repair an omitted requirement and can keep producing the same inadequate output.

options.text: Replace the test transcripts with easier ones before comparing the summaries
options.feedback: Easier inputs can conceal the problem. Evaluate whether the revised procedure meets the actual requirement on useful examples.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You test a new skill on an easy source using a stronger model, then test without the skill on a difficult source using a cheaper model. The first output is better. What should you do next?

options.text: Conclude that the skill caused the improvement because its output was better
options.feedback: Task difficulty and model choice changed too, so the observed difference cannot be attributed clearly to the skill.

options.text: Repeat with matched sources and comparable model settings
options.feedback: A matched comparison reduces competing explanations and lets you examine whether the skill improves the results.

options.text: Conclude that the stronger model caused every observed difference between outputs
options.feedback: The model is one possible influence, but the task and skill also changed. This comparison cannot isolate any one cause.

options.text: Average the output lengths to estimate how much quality the skill added
options.feedback: Length is not a substitute for task-specific quality criteria, and averaging it does not remove the mismatched conditions.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: A copied skill is enabled on a second computer, but its extraction step reports that a required library is missing. What should you address first?

options.text: Rewrite the output requirements so that extraction is no longer evaluated
options.feedback: The reported failure concerns an execution dependency. Removing a quality check would conceal rather than fix it.

options.text: Treat the first computer's successful run as proof that the second run worked
options.feedback: Success on the original host does not establish success where the required library is absent.

options.text: Rename the installed skill so that the host treats it as a new procedure
options.feedback: A different name does not supply the missing library that the extraction operation requires.

options.text: Resolve the library dependency, then rerun and inspect the output
options.feedback: The error identifies an environment requirement. After resolving it, verify the procedure on an actual input in that host.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: You receive an unfamiliar shared skill that includes executable scripts and asks for file access. What should you do before running it?

options.text: Grant the requested access because shared instructions provide a secure sandbox
options.feedback: Instructions do not create a secure sandbox. Review the source, scripts, and requested access before use.

options.text: Read only the output examples because successful examples establish code safety
options.feedback: Examples illustrate possible results but do not establish what included code does or where it came from.

options.text: Review its source, script behavior, and requested access
options.feedback: A skill can include ordinary executable code. Understanding its origin and operations helps you assess what you are installing.

options.text: Assume the scripts are harmless because their folder uses a compatible format
options.feedback: Format compatibility concerns organization, not the behavior of executable code or the trustworthiness of its source.

questions.source: Quiz 4 - Sessions 1-5: Building and Improving Agent Skills
questions.question: A daily document-processing skill succeeds in a manual trial. You want it to run unattended. Which preparation best addresses the added demands?

options.text: Define triggers, saved progress, checks, and stopping rules
options.feedback: Also establish required inputs, allowed actions, missing-access behavior, and an available host. Test failure cases before relying on repeated runs.

options.text: Rely on the single success and repeat the same command continuously
options.feedback: A successful trial leaves failure behavior and repeated-run effects untested. Persistent operation needs explicit operating conditions.

options.text: Keep the host online and let each run start without knowledge of prior work
options.feedback: Availability is necessary, but saved progress helps later runs resume without duplicating changes.

options.text: Create a daily trigger and assume missing inputs will resolve themselves
options.feedback: A trigger schedules work but does not define what to do when inputs or access are absent. Specify failure and stopping behavior.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What is an agent harness?

options.text: Software coordinating the model's work and tools
options.feedback: The harness surrounds the model and manages its work, context, tools, and permissions.

options.text: The learned numerical parameters inside a model
options.feedback: Parameters belong to the trained model. The harness is surrounding software that organizes how the model works with tools and context.

options.text: The vocabulary used to identify tokens in a prompt
options.feedback: Vocabulary entries identify tokens for model processing. They do not manage external actions or the surrounding workflow.

options.text: The dataset used to adjust a model during training
options.feedback: Training data help determine learned parameters. A harness instead manages the system around a model as it works.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: In the lecture's README example, what does the model produce before any file is read?

options.text: An updated version of its learned weights
options.feedback: Producing a tool request is part of inference. Reading a file does not require retraining the model.

options.text: A request describing a file-reading action
options.feedback: The model proposes the action. A tool still needs to carry it out through the harness.

options.text: The verified contents of the requested file
options.feedback: The contents become available after a successful file-reading operation. A request does not supply that evidence.

options.text: A permission change for the working folder
options.feedback: Writing a request does not grant access. The harness handles the request within the permissions available.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which part of an agent system carries out an allowed file-reading operation?

options.text: A reusable skill describing the procedure
options.feedback: A skill supplies instructions about reading the file. It does not itself carry out the external operation.

options.text: The trained model producing a request
options.feedback: The model can propose the action. A separate tool must actually access the file.

options.text: A file-reading tool routed by the harness
options.feedback: The harness checks and routes the request; the file-reading tool performs the allowed operation.

options.text: The generated command displayed in chat
options.feedback: A command can describe the intended operation while remaining text. It needs an executor before the file is read.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Where does a successful tool result go so the model can use it?

options.text: Into the vocabulary as a newly defined token
options.feedback: A tool result supplies task information. It does not require a vocabulary entry for the entire observation.

options.text: Into the weights as an immediate training update
options.feedback: A model can use the returned evidence during inference without updating its learned parameters.

options.text: Into the skill as an automatic procedure revision
options.feedback: A tool observation is information for the task. Revising reusable instructions is a separate action, not an automatic consequence of receiving a result.

options.text: Into the context used for the next decision
options.feedback: The result becomes an observation the model can use when deciding its next step.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What happens when the harness blocks a proposed tool operation?

options.text: The external action remains unperformed
options.feedback: The harness can return a blocked status while the model continues generating text. The requested operation has not run.

options.text: The model becomes unable to explain the result
options.feedback: Blocking an external action does not prevent the model from generating a textual explanation of the denial.

options.text: The action runs when the model explains its value
options.feedback: A persuasive explanation is still text. It does not supply the permission needed to execute the denied operation.

options.text: The skill supplies permission for the blocked step
options.feedback: A skill describes what to do. It cannot grant access denied by the surrounding controls.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which item supplies reusable guidance rather than external access?

options.text: An available file-reading tool
options.feedback: A tool provides an action that can be invoked. Reusable procedural guidance has a different role.

options.text: A skill with task instructions
options.feedback: A skill describes how to approach the work. Tools and permissions are still needed to execute its action steps.

options.text: A granted file-reading permission
options.feedback: Permission authorizes access to a resource. It does not itself provide the procedure for doing the task.

options.text: A connector to an outside service
options.feedback: A connector exposes an integration. Guidance for using it can be supplied by a skill.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which sequence describes the agent loop after the model requests an action?

options.text: Tool acts, harness checks, observation returns
options.feedback: This puts execution before the permission check. The harness must check and route a request before the allowed tool operation.

options.text: Harness checks, model guesses, tool result is omitted
options.feedback: Checking a request does not supply its outcome. The tool must execute, and its observation returns to the model.

options.text: Harness checks, tool acts, observation returns
options.feedback: The harness checks and routes the request. The resulting observation informs the model's next decision.

options.text: Model reports success, tool acts, harness checks
options.feedback: A success statement does not establish execution. The request must pass through the harness before the allowed operation runs.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does a connector contribute to an agent system?

options.text: A replacement for the model's learned parameters
options.feedback: An integration gives access to a resource; it does not replace the numerical parameters of the model.

options.text: A preferred answer learned during post-training
options.feedback: Post-training shapes behavior. A connector supplies a route to an external service or resource.

options.text: A self-contained set of grading criteria
options.feedback: Criteria belong in the task or reusable instructions. A connector provides an integration rather than those criteria.

options.text: An integration with a service or resource
options.feedback: A connector exposes an integration that an agent can use when the surrounding system permits it.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What is the model's role in the agent system described in the lecture?

options.text: Interpreting context and proposing next steps
options.feedback: The model contributes language understanding and decisions. The harness routes its proposed actions, and tools execute permitted operations.

options.text: Authorizing access to the project's resources
options.feedback: Permission checks belong to the surrounding controls. The model's judgment that access would help does not grant it.

options.text: Executing the requested external file operations
options.feedback: The model proposes operations. Tools carry out those external actions when the harness allows and routes them.

options.text: Supplying the connection to an external service
options.feedback: A connector exposes an integration with a service or resource. The model can use available capabilities as it decides what to do.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which statement best explains why an agent's usefulness depends on the whole system?

options.text: The model's language ability determines whether file actions are available
options.feedback: A capable model can propose useful actions, but the surrounding system must provide tools and access to carry them out.

options.text: The model, tools, and guidance work within the harness
options.feedback: The lecture describes capability as a property of the parts working together. The surrounding environment affects what the model can accomplish.

options.text: A detailed skill supplies both a procedure and the access it requires
options.feedback: A skill supplies guidance. Tools and permissions must also exist for its steps to execute.

options.text: A connector supplies both service access and the complete task procedure
options.feedback: A connector exposes an integration. The instructions for using it toward your goal are a separate part of the system.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can a powerful model still fail to read a local file?

options.text: Its training must have included that exact file
options.feedback: A file-reading tool can supply current contents to context. The file need not have been present in the model's training data.

options.text: Its skill must copy the file into permanent weights
options.feedback: The file can be read into current context. A skill supplies guidance without permanently teaching the file through weight updates.

options.text: Its environment may lack the necessary access
options.feedback: The model's capability cannot replace an unavailable tool or missing permission for the file.

options.text: Its prompt must phrase the read as a confident command
options.feedback: A clearer request can describe what you want, but wording cannot create a missing tool or grant file access.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why does writing a command in chat fail to prove that the command ran?

options.text: Displaying valid syntax is enough to establish execution
options.feedback: A syntactically valid command still needs an executor. Its appearance in chat does not establish that it ran.

options.text: A relevant skill automatically executes its written steps
options.feedback: A skill can guide a procedure but does not itself provide a tool or permission to perform the action.

options.text: A detailed description counts as the operation's result
options.feedback: Describing the intended work is different from receiving an observation produced by performing it.

options.text: Command text still needs an executor
options.feedback: The model can produce a textual command without running it. A tool or other executor must carry out the operation.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can a denied tool request be followed by a normal-looking written answer?

options.text: Text generation can continue after a denial
options.feedback: The requested external operation can remain blocked while the model generates an explanation or other textual response.

options.text: A fluent answer establishes that the action succeeded
options.feedback: Fluency is a property of generated text. It does not prove that an external operation occurred.

options.text: The model performs the action internally after denial
options.feedback: The model can reason about the denied action, but generating text does not carry out the blocked external operation.

options.text: The skill supplies temporary access after the denial
options.feedback: A skill's instructions do not grant a missing permission or override the surrounding access controls.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why does adding a procedure to a skill fail to guarantee that its steps can run?

options.text: The model must discover the procedure in its pre-training data
options.feedback: The procedure can be loaded from the skill into context. It need not have appeared during pre-training.

options.text: The system also needs the required tools and permissions
options.feedback: The procedure explains what to do. Actual execution depends on capabilities and access supplied by the surrounding system.

options.text: A skill must replace the harness before it can be useful
options.feedback: Skills guide the agent within its environment. They need not replace the software that runs tools.

options.text: A skill must be converted into learned parameters first
options.feedback: The course uses skills as instructions and resources during a run, without retraining the model.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why should a file operation return its result to the model?

options.text: The returned text serves as proof that the full task is finished
options.feedback: A tool result reports one operation. The model may need further steps, and the final work still needs checking against the task.

options.text: The result grants permission for the next requested operation
options.feedback: An observation supplies information. Permission for another action remains a matter for the surrounding controls.

options.text: The next decision should reflect the actual outcome
options.feedback: The observation lets the model adapt its next step to what happened rather than continue from an unverified expectation.

options.text: The returned text permanently revises the model's knowledge
options.feedback: The model can use a tool result in its current context. This is different from changing learned weights through training.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is a well-aligned answer insufficient evidence for granting unrestricted tool access?

options.text: One good answer establishes reliable choices on later tasks
options.feedback: A useful response does not demonstrate how the model will behave in every later context. Access still needs to fit the task.

options.text: A helpful explanation establishes that broad access is needed
options.feedback: Helpfulness describes a response. It does not show that the requested work requires unrestricted tools or resources.

options.text: Aligned responses make tool results reliable without inspection
options.feedback: Behavioral training does not remove the need to inspect whether an operation and its result satisfy the task.

options.text: Good behavior does not establish the need for broad access
options.feedback: Alignment addresses the model's choices, while permissions constrain executable actions. A good answer does not establish that unrestricted authority is appropriate.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why do access controls fail to guarantee that a model's written answer is accurate?

options.text: They constrain actions without checking each claim
options.feedback: The harness can limit what the system executes while the model can still generate a mistaken statement. Output verification addresses a separate concern.

options.text: They make permitted sources automatically trustworthy
options.feedback: Permission to access a source is not a judgment that its content or the resulting answer is accurate.

options.text: They turn successful tool use into proof of correctness
options.feedback: An operation can be allowed and successfully executed while the resulting answer is incomplete or incorrect.

options.text: They supply missing evidence through the permission decision
options.feedback: A permission decision determines whether an action may run. It does not itself supply the task evidence the model needs.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can two agents using the same model perform differently on the same task?

options.text: The same model requires the same tools in each environment
options.feedback: Tools belong to the surrounding system. Two agents can expose different actions while using the same underlying model.

options.text: Their tools, context, and procedures may differ
options.feedback: The model is one component of the agent. Its surroundings affect the information and actions available for the task.

options.text: The same model brings its folder permissions to each environment
options.feedback: File permissions are supplied by the environment. They are not a capability the model carries into every deployment.

options.text: The same model guarantees the same evidence enters each context
options.feedback: An agent needs access to relevant evidence. Different tools and working contexts can provide different information to the same model.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is the label "sandbox" insufficient evidence that a deployment is safe?

options.text: The label establishes that every file operation is blocked
options.feedback: The name alone does not establish which actions the actual controls restrict. Their implementation and behavior must be checked.

options.text: The label establishes that generated statements are accurate
options.feedback: Access controls address executable actions. They do not guarantee that every written claim is true.

options.text: Its controls still need implementation and testing
options.feedback: Calling an environment a sandbox does not establish that its intended restrictions exist or work. Inspect and test the actual controls.

options.text: The label establishes that broader access is appropriate
options.feedback: A label does not determine the authority needed for a task. The tools and working area should be chosen deliberately.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What makes verification different from permission checking?

options.text: Verification authorizes actions; permissions judge completed results
options.feedback: This reverses their roles. Permissions constrain what may execute, while verification checks whether results satisfy the task.

options.text: Verification checks fluency; permissions check factual accuracy
options.feedback: Fluent text can still be wrong or incomplete. Permissions govern executable actions rather than factual accuracy.

options.text: Verification checks model size; permissions check the task instructions
options.feedback: Model size is not the definition of result verification. Access controls govern allowed operations, and results must be checked against the task.

options.text: Verification assesses results; permissions govern allowed actions
options.feedback: An action can be permitted and still produce an incorrect or incomplete result. These checks therefore serve different purposes.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You ask an agent to summarize a README. It displays a file-reading command, but no tool result appears. What should you check next?

options.text: Whether the harness actually ran the file-reading tool
options.feedback: You need evidence that the requested file was read before treating the summary as grounded in its contents.

options.text: Whether the command was phrased with enough confidence
options.feedback: More confident language does not establish that the operation was executed.

options.text: Whether the answer contains a sufficiently large word count
options.feedback: Length does not show that the agent obtained the source material.

options.text: Whether the model knows the general purpose of README files
options.feedback: General knowledge may help interpret a file, but it does not establish access to this particular file.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: An agent can read your project but lacks permission to modify it. It proposes a useful edit. What follows?

options.text: The read permission also permits the proposed modification
options.feedback: Reading and changing files require the relevant access. The scenario explicitly says the agent lacks permission to modify the project.

options.text: The suggestion does not change the project file
options.feedback: A model can describe a useful edit without executing it. Reading access and a proposal do not establish a completed modification.

options.text: The value of the edit supplies the missing permission
options.feedback: A model's judgment that an action is useful does not grant write access. The surrounding controls determine permitted execution.

options.text: The skill can write the edit using its instructions
options.feedback: The skill can guide an editing procedure. Its instructions do not perform the file operation or supply the missing write permission.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Your skill says "upload the final report," but the agent has no upload tool. What is the immediate limitation?

options.text: The skill's wording determines whether an upload tool exists
options.feedback: An instruction can name an action without providing the capability to execute it. Tools must be available in the environment.

options.text: The model's confidence determines whether an upload can run
options.feedback: Confidence is a feature of the response. It does not replace an unavailable upload tool.

options.text: The environment lacks a required action capability
options.feedback: The skill gives guidance, while tools provide actions. An upload step requires a tool or integration that can carry it out.

options.text: The report's completeness determines whether it was uploaded
options.feedback: A complete local artifact and a successful external upload are separate outcomes. The task still needs an available upload capability.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: A file-reading tool returns "file not found." What information should guide the agent's next step?

options.text: An assumed summary of what the file probably contains
options.feedback: An expectation about contents is not evidence that the missing file was read.

options.text: The model's confidence before the request was made
options.feedback: The actual tool outcome is more relevant than the earlier expectation of success.

options.text: An automatic increase in permissions for every folder
options.feedback: A missing file does not justify blanket access. The next action should fit the task and available controls.

options.text: The observed failure and the task's intended source
options.feedback: The returned observation should shape the next decision. The agent should not act as though the requested contents were received.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You are deploying an agent to work on a project folder. Which setup follows the lecture's guidance?

options.text: Give task-appropriate access and check important results
options.feedback: The tools and working area should fit the task. Inspecting important results checks whether the work actually satisfies the goal.

options.text: Grant broad access after the model gives one reassuring answer
options.feedback: A reassuring response does not demonstrate reliable behavior across tasks or justify unnecessary authority.

options.text: Rely on a detailed skill to create any permissions it needs
options.feedback: Instructions describe a procedure. They do not create access that the surrounding environment has not granted.

options.text: Choose the largest model and trust its report that actions succeeded
options.feedback: Model size and a success statement do not replace checking tool outcomes and finished artifacts.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does a token ID identify?

options.text: An entry in the model's vocabulary
options.feedback: The ID selects a vocabulary entry and its starting embedding. Meaning is represented by numerical vectors, not by the ID itself.

options.text: A coordinate describing the token's meaning
options.feedback: This confuses an index with a representation. The token ID selects an embedding; it is not itself a semantic coordinate.

options.text: A weight changed during the current response
options.feedback: Weights are learned parameters. The ID identifies the token, and ordinary response generation does not update the model's weights.

options.text: A score for the next possible token
options.feedback: Scores for possible next tokens are produced near the output. An ID identifies a vocabulary entry before that scoring step.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What is an embedding in the model described in the notes?

options.text: A vocabulary number serving as an index
options.feedback: The vocabulary index is the token ID. It selects an initial embedding, which is a vector rather than just that index.

options.text: A numerical vector representing a token
options.feedback: An embedding supplies a numerical representation. That representation can then be transformed as the token passes through the model.

options.text: A written definition retrieved for a token
options.feedback: The model processes numerical representations rather than retrieving a dictionary definition as the embedding.

options.text: A numerical score for a possible next token
options.feedback: Scores are produced near the output to support next-token selection. The embedding is the numerical representation processed before that output stage.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What passes from attention to the feed-forward network inside a transformer block?

options.text: New vocabulary entries for each token
options.feedback: Changing a representation does not create a new vocabulary entry. The same token can have successive internal representations.

options.text: Written rules describing each token
options.feedback: The block operates on numerical arrays using learned parameters. It does not pass a set of written meaning rules between its parts.

options.text: Updated numerical representations
options.feedback: The intermediate material is numerical. Attention and the feed-forward network transform representations before the model chooses an output token.

options.text: Completed sentences ready for display
options.feedback: Sentences are the visible result of generation. Inside the block, the model is still transforming numerical representations.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What role does attention play in interpreting a token?

options.text: It chooses the displayed token before any blocks run
options.feedback: Next-token selection occurs near the end of the model's processing. Attention works on representations inside the blocks.

options.text: It replaces the vocabulary index with a new index
options.feedback: The representation changes during attention. That change is not a reassignment of the token's vocabulary ID.

options.text: It saves the conversation by updating model weights
options.feedback: Using context during ordinary inference changes current representations, not the learned weights.

options.text: It incorporates relevant information from context
options.feedback: Attention lets the token's representation draw on surrounding information. This can shift its interpretation as more relevant context is considered.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) contribute within a transformer block?

options.text: It transforms representations using learned parameters
options.feedback: The feed-forward network applies transformations learned during training. Its contribution helps the interpretation develop through the model.

options.text: It executes file commands outside the model
options.feedback: External commands require a harness and tools. The MLP is part of the model's internal numerical processing.

options.text: It assigns a fresh vocabulary ID to each interpretation
options.feedback: The MLP changes the representation of a token. Successive interpretations do not require new vocabulary entries.

options.text: It displays a finished word after each block
options.feedback: Intermediate blocks transform numerical representations. Choosing a token for output happens near the end.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: In the teaching diagram, what do cat-star and cat-star-star represent?

options.text: Replacements for the model's training parameters
options.feedback: Representations change as input is processed. The diagram does not show weight updates during training.

options.text: Later representations of the same token
options.feedback: The labels mark stages in processing the token. They help you picture a changing representation without implying a different vocabulary entry.

options.text: Additional entries added to the vocabulary
options.feedback: The star labels are explanatory labels for internal stages. The model does not add those labels to its vocabulary during the example.

options.text: Separate words printed in the final answer
options.feedback: The diagram describes internal processing. Its star labels are not successive words the model must output.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What is the role of the output projection described in the notes?

options.text: It executes a tool request through its permissions
options.feedback: Tool execution belongs to the surrounding harness and tools. Output projection produces token scores inside the model.

options.text: It changes learned weights using the current prompt
options.feedback: Producing token scores is part of inference. It does not itself train new weights on the prompt.

options.text: It maps the final representation to token scores
options.feedback: After the blocks transform representations, the output stage produces scores for possible next tokens. A token can then be selected.

options.text: It retrieves an initial embedding from a token ID
options.feedback: Initial lookup happens before the transformer blocks. Output projection acts on the representation after processing.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What do the learned parameter arrays contain?

options.text: Written definitions for each vocabulary entry
options.feedback: A token ID selects a numerical representation. The model does not represent its learned parameters as dictionary definitions.

options.text: Complete conversations from earlier model runs
options.feedback: A conversation supplies context for a run. Learned parameter arrays instead contain numbers determined through training.

options.text: Hand-written instructions for particular answers
options.feedback: The program specifies operations, but a particular learned answer need not have a matching written rule.

options.text: Numerical values determined through training
options.feedback: Training determines many values stored in parameter arrays. The model program specifies operations that use those learned numbers.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does the model program specify in the lecture's distinction between code and learned parameters?

options.text: Operations applied to numerical representations
options.feedback: The program specifies the computation. Training determines many of the numerical parameter values used in that computation.

options.text: A written rule for each answer the model may give
options.feedback: A particular answer can arise from learned parameters interacting with context. It need not have a corresponding hand-written rule.

options.text: The correct factual answer to each possible prompt
options.feedback: The computation can generate mistaken claims. Inspectable software does not imply a programmed correct answer for every prompt.

options.text: A record of the text used to train the model
options.feedback: The notes distinguish the program from the data and learned numbers. The program describes operations rather than serving as a transcript of training text.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What determines many of the values stored in a model's parameter arrays?

options.text: The written explanation produced after an answer
options.feedback: An explanation is generated output. Parameter values are learned during training, not established by that explanation.

options.text: The learning process during training
options.feedback: Training determines learned parameter values. The program specifies how operations use those arrays.

options.text: The conversation added during ordinary inference
options.feedback: Conversation context can change current representations. Ordinary inference does not use that growing context to update the learned weights.

options.text: The file permissions of the agent harness
options.feedback: Permissions constrain external actions. They do not determine the model's learned numerical parameters.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why should you avoid treating a token ID as the token's meaning?

options.text: It changes into a written definition when attention runs
options.feedback: Attention transforms numerical representations. It does not turn the index into dictionary text.

options.text: It is learned again whenever the token enters a prompt
options.feedback: Processing a prompt uses the token ID to select a representation. Ordinary inference does not relearn the model's weights on every token.

options.text: It indexes an entry with a numerical representation
options.feedback: The index performs a lookup role. The selected numerical representation, and its later transformations, support interpretation.

options.text: It contains the final representation after all blocks run
options.feedback: The ID is used at the start to select an embedding. It is not the final result of the model's processing.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can the phrase about a cruel trainer angering a cat change how you interpret cat?

options.text: The vocabulary needs a new entry for an angry cat
options.feedback: A token's representation can shift with context while its vocabulary ID stays the same. A separate entry is not needed for each interpretation.

options.text: The prompt immediately retrains the model's parameters
options.feedback: Using the sentence as context can change its interpretation during inference. That is different from updating weights through training.

options.text: The model has already selected the final answer word
options.feedback: The example concerns how representations develop inside the blocks. Token selection happens after those transformations.

options.text: The surrounding words shape the representation
options.feedback: Attention brings relevant context into the token's representation. The trainer and anger context can make a large, angry animal more plausible.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is circus a possible association with the trainer-and-cat sentence rather than a fact established by it?

options.text: Learned associations suggest an unstated setting
options.feedback: Learned associations can suggest a setting, but the sentence does not identify one. You should distinguish supplied evidence from an added interpretation.

options.text: The token ID for cat explicitly names a circus setting
options.feedback: An ID identifies a vocabulary entry. It does not encode a stated location, and the sentence itself leaves the setting open.

options.text: Attention verifies that each suggested setting happened
options.feedback: Attention uses information from context. It does not independently verify that a background association describes a real event.

options.text: A changed representation proves that the setting is true
options.feedback: A representation can incorporate plausible associations. The change itself does not supply evidence for an unstated fact.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is it misleading to describe the MLP (multi-layer perceptron) as the model's searchable fact database?

options.text: It assigns vocabulary IDs instead of transforming representations
options.feedback: Token lookup and representation transformation have different roles. The MLP participates in the latter.

options.text: Learned information is distributed across the network
options.feedback: The MLP applies learned transformations, but knowledge is not confined to that component. A database lookup is too literal a picture of this processing.
