options.text: It operates on finished English sentences rather than numbers
options.feedback: The MLP transforms numerical representations. Treating it as an English-sentence processor adds another misleading picture.

options.text: It stores the current prompt by retraining on every word
options.feedback: Current context influences representations during inference. That does not mean the MLP updates its weights on each prompt word.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can adding relevant material to context improve an answer without further training?

options.text: The material becomes a new vocabulary entry before generation
options.feedback: Providing a document supplies tokens in context. It does not require adding a vocabulary entry for the document.

options.text: The material converts internal representations into written rules
options.feedback: The internal computation still transforms numerical representations. Context provides evidence without changing that process into rule text.

options.text: The model can use that evidence with its existing weights
options.feedback: Context gives the model information to use in the current generation. Improved performance does not by itself imply changed parameters.

options.text: The material replaces the parameter arrays for that response
options.feedback: The arrays still supply learned parameters. New context influences the representations processed using those parameters.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: How can two models follow the same broad computation pattern yet differ greatly?

options.text: The processing pattern determines the same learned values
options.feedback: The program specifies operations. Training can produce different values even when the broad computation pattern is similar.

options.text: The processing pattern lists each model's possible answers
options.feedback: A broad algorithm is not a catalogue of responses. Learned values and context also affect the model's behavior.

options.text: The processing pattern gives a complete account of capability
options.feedback: Knowing the operations does not specify the parameter arrays or explain every learned behavior. Similar steps can underlie very different models.

options.text: The parameter arrays differ in size or learned values
options.feedback: The same broad operations can use different collections of learned numbers. Knowing the processing pattern does not specify the full model.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why might an unwanted model answer have no single hand-written rule you can edit?

options.text: Learned values interact with the current context
options.feedback: The program specifies computation, while learned parameter values help determine behavior. A particular answer need not correspond to a single written rule.

options.text: Training stores a separate source-code rule for each answer
options.feedback: Training updates numerical parameters. It does not establish that each resulting answer has a separate hand-written rule.

options.text: Understanding the program identifies each answer's cause directly
options.feedback: You can inspect the software, but the algorithm alone does not explain every behavior arising from learned parameters and context.

options.text: The written explanation supplies the rule that generated the answer
options.feedback: An explanation is generated output. It does not establish that the model has a matching hand-written source-code rule for the answer.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why does understanding a model's algorithm leave questions about its learned behavior?

options.text: The program becomes inaccessible once training has finished
options.feedback: The notes say software remains inspectable. The difficulty is explaining learned behavior from the algorithm and parameters, not the disappearance of the program.

options.text: Learned values also affect the resulting behavior
options.feedback: The program describes how computation proceeds. The interaction of many learned parameters with context can still make a particular behavior hard to explain.

options.text: The algorithm is replaced by English instructions at inference
options.feedback: The numerical computation still runs during inference. Understanding it is useful even though it does not fully explain every learned behavior.

options.text: The vocabulary indices specify each complete answer in advance
options.feedback: Vocabulary indices identify tokens. They do not provide a list of complete answers explaining the model's behavior.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is literally averaging English words a misleading description of attention?

options.text: Attention combines final answers after the model selects them
options.feedback: Attention operates inside the transformer blocks. It helps shape representations before next-token selection near the output.

options.text: Attention combines source-code rules written for each meaning
options.feedback: The relevant inputs are numerical representations. There need not be a hand-written rule for each interpretation a model develops.

options.text: Attention combines transformed numerical representations
options.feedback: The words help you picture the process, but the mechanism works on numerical representations. The notes describe weighted combinations of those transformed representations.

options.text: Attention combines written definitions retrieved from a database
options.feedback: This replaces one literal word-based picture with another. The computation operates on representations, not retrieved dictionary prose.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why does a large context capacity still require you to choose useful material?

options.text: Capacity determines which prompt facts become permanent weights
options.feedback: Context capacity concerns what can be supplied for a run. It does not determine permanent learning of prompt facts during ordinary inference.

options.text: Capacity makes each document a verified source of factual truth
options.feedback: The ability to include a document does not verify its content or the answer. You still need relevant evidence and inspection of its use.

options.text: Capacity selects the next token before representations change
options.feedback: Context capacity is not the token-selection step. Representations are still processed through the model before output scoring.

options.text: Capacity holds material; useful evidence helps the task
options.feedback: A large context can hold more material, but you still need information that bears on the task and must verify how the model uses it.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You need an answer based on a policy document the model has not been given. Which step best follows the lecture's advice?

options.text: Supply the relevant text or a way to retrieve it
options.feedback: The task depends on evidence from this document. Put the relevant material in context or provide access so the model can use it with existing weights.

options.text: Ask the model to reconstruct it from similar policies
options.feedback: Learned associations can suggest plausible contents without establishing what this particular document says.

options.text: Provide its filename and assume that supplies its contents
options.feedback: Naming a source identifies the material you want. Its relevant contents still need to enter context or be available through retrieval.

options.text: Request a detailed answer before checking the source
options.feedback: More detail does not supply the missing evidence. Source access should support the answer, followed by checking how the evidence was used.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You compare cat in a sentence about a sunny windowsill with cat in a sentence about an angry trainer. What should you expect inside the model?

options.text: Each block must print a different replacement word for cat
options.feedback: Blocks transform numerical representations. They do not print intermediate replacement words as a required part of interpretation.

options.text: The same token can have different contextual representations
options.feedback: The initial token identity does not force one interpretation. Attention can bring different surrounding information into its representation.

options.text: The vocabulary must contain a separate ID for each sentence
options.feedback: The cat-star diagram describes changing representations of the same token. Contextual interpretation does not require a new vocabulary entry for every sentence.

options.text: The two sentences must update different permanent weight values
options.feedback: Processing different contexts changes current representations. Ordinary inference does not update permanent weights for each sentence.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You see two model implementations with similar processing steps, but one uses much larger parameter arrays. What conclusion is supported?

options.text: Larger parameter arrays must contain more hand-written answer rules
options.feedback: Parameters are learned numerical values. Their larger size does not mean programmers wrote a separate rule for every possible answer.

options.text: Larger parameter arrays make context unnecessary for interpretation
options.feedback: Context still influences representations through attention. Parameter size does not remove the value of relevant task information.

options.text: Similar operations can work with very different learned models
options.feedback: The notes separate the broad algorithm from parameter size and values. Similar processing steps do not make the models identical.

options.text: Similar processing steps require the same parameter values
options.feedback: The algorithm specifies operations, while training determines many values. Matching broad steps does not establish identical learned numbers.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: A teammate wants to stop a model inventing a detail in future responses and says, "Find the line that tells it to invent that detail, then delete it." What is the best explanation of why this code search may fail?

options.text: That detail must be stored in the vocabulary ID for its main word
options.feedback: Vocabulary IDs identify tokens. They do not each store an instruction to make a particular claim.

options.text: That detail shows the model rewrote its program during the reply
options.feedback: An unwanted output does not establish that the program changed. Ordinary inference runs computation using existing weights and current context.

options.text: Deleting the detail from this answer also changes the learned behavior
options.feedback: Editing visible output repairs that artifact. It does not establish that the underlying parameters or behavior in future responses have changed.

options.text: The detail may emerge from learned values and context
options.feedback: The notes explain why a specific answer need not have a corresponding hand-written rule. You can inspect the software without assuming that one line controls that behavior.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: While tracing one response, you observe a token's numerical representation changing across several blocks while learned weights stay fixed. How should you interpret this?

options.text: The blocks are processing context with the trained model
options.feedback: Changing intermediate representations is expected during inference. The weights can remain fixed while attention and feed-forward transformations alter those representations.

options.text: Each changed representation is a newly created vocabulary entry
options.feedback: The cat-star example uses multiple stages for the same token. A changed vector is not evidence of an expanded vocabulary.

options.text: Each block has completed a fresh round of model training
options.feedback: Training updates parameters. Your observation describes changing representations with fixed weights, which fits ordinary inference.

options.text: The trace is showing finished answer words between the blocks
options.feedback: The values moving through blocks are numerical representations. Finished output tokens are selected near the end of the processing.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does an agent skill provide for your work?

options.text: Reusable guidance and supporting resources
options.feedback: A skill packages instructions and resources so you can reuse and revise a procedure across tasks.

options.text: A trained model with replacement parameters
options.feedback: This confuses changing a procedure with changing the model. You can revise a skill without training a replacement model.

options.text: A finished report containing the task results
options.feedback: A report can be an output of using a skill. The skill supplies the reusable guidance that helps produce that output.

options.text: A conversation recording the agent's decisions
options.feedback: A conversation records an interaction. A skill is a reusable package that you can inspect and edit for later work.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which file should you ask the agent to locate when you want to inspect a skill's main instructions?

options.text: The newest output report
options.feedback: A report shows what a run produced. To inspect the procedure that guided the run, ask for the skill's instruction file.

options.text: The skill's SKILL.md file
options.feedback: SKILL.md contains the skill's instructions. Open it and inspect the supporting files to understand the procedure you are using.

options.text: The current conversation export
options.feedback: The conversation can describe a run, but the notes direct you to inspect the reusable instructions themselves in SKILL.md.

options.text: The model's parameter file
options.feedback: Parameters belong to the trained model. Editing a skill means inspecting its instructions, rather than inspecting learned model numbers.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: How should you save a skill instruction file after editing it?

options.text: As rich text with visible Markdown headings
options.feedback: Markdown-looking headings do not determine the saved format. Rich-text formatting can prevent the file from functioning as intended.

options.text: As an image with the instruction text visible
options.feedback: Visible instructions are useful to a reader, but the demonstrated workflow saves the editable instruction file as plain-text Markdown.

options.text: As plain-text Markdown with the right name
options.feedback: Check both the actual text format and the filename. An added .txt extension or rich-text format can interfere with the intended skill file.

options.text: As a formatted document with a .md label
options.feedback: Renaming a formatted document does not establish that its contents are plain text. The saved format and the filename both matter.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What should you inspect alongside a skill's main procedure to understand the package?

options.text: The model's learned parameter arrays
options.feedback: Those arrays concern the model's training. The skill-inspection workflow focuses on the instructions and supporting files you can revise.

options.text: The agent's latest completion message
options.feedback: A completion message describes what the agent says it did. It does not replace reading the resources that belong to the skill.

options.text: The editor's document appearance settings
options.feedback: Appearance can help you read a file, but understanding the skill requires looking at its procedure and supporting materials.

options.text: The procedure's supporting files
options.feedback: A skill includes instructions and supporting resources. Read both, then compare the package with your intended task and criteria.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which information helps Claude Code decide which skill to load for your task?

options.text: The skill's name and description
options.feedback: The name and description help identify a relevant skill. Detailed instructions are loaded when needed.

options.text: The full text of every available skill
options.feedback: The notes say that the name and description help decide what to load, with detailed instructions loaded when needed. Reading all skill instructions first reverses that distinction.

options.text: The output from the most recent skill run
options.feedback: A past output can help you evaluate a procedure, but the notes identify the skill name and description as information used for discovery.

options.text: The model's size and training objective
options.feedback: These describe the model, rather than which skill matches your task. A skill's name and description help with that selection.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What information should you give an agent when asking it to assemble your work into a file?

options.text: The model size and preferred editor
options.feedback: Those choices do not tell the agent what belongs in the deliverable. Specify the required contents and the output format.

options.text: The needed contents and file format
options.feedback: These instructions define what the packaged work must contain and how it should be delivered. You still need to inspect the resulting file.

options.text: The completion wording and reply length
options.feedback: These shape the agent's message about its work. They do not specify the contents of the artifact you need.

options.text: The skill title and conversation length
options.feedback: A skill title can identify guidance, but it does not replace telling the agent which materials to gather and what file format to produce.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: After saving a specific change to a skill, what is the next step in the demonstrated workflow?

options.text: Package the previous output as the final result
options.feedback: A previous output does not show what the changed skill does. Test the revised version before treating the work as complete.

options.text: Treat the saved instructions as proof of success
options.feedback: Saving confirms that you changed the procedure. The next check is whether using it produces the intended result.

options.text: Run a test and examine the resulting output
options.feedback: Testing connects the written revision to its effect. Inspect the output against the task instead of relying on the agent's success claim.

options.text: Change the model before trying the procedure
options.feedback: The skill workflow lets you revise and test instructions without training or replacing the model first.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which feature of an agent working environment is emphasized when you want help editing skill files?

options.text: A larger set of learned parameters
options.feedback: Model size is different from the working environment. The relevant distinction is whether the environment can work with your files and tools.

options.text: A more detailed written completion claim
options.feedback: A detailed claim remains a description. File-editing work depends on the environment's ability to use files and tools.

options.text: A more polished conversation display
options.feedback: Display polish does not establish file-working capability. Choose an environment with the tools and context that fit the work.

options.text: Access to the needed files and tools
options.feedback: The demonstration distinguished a conversation-centered interaction from an agent environment that can work with files and tools.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why should you deliberately choose a project or local folder before asking an agent to revise a skill?

options.text: It helps identify which materials belong to the work
options.feedback: Choosing the working area helps establish the task's relevant materials. The same model can be more useful when its tools and context fit the work.

options.text: It trains the model on every file in that location
options.feedback: Choosing a working area establishes relevant materials; it does not turn skill editing into model training.

options.text: It confirms the skill already meets the task criteria
options.feedback: A folder identifies materials, not their quality. You still need to compare the procedure and its output with the task criteria.

options.text: It proves the final file was saved in that location
options.feedback: Selecting a folder is preparation for the work. Completion still requires checking that the intended artifact actually exists in the correct place.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can revising a skill change the agent's later work without training a new model?

options.text: The revision replaces a set of learned model weights
options.feedback: This describes a change to the model rather than a change to its reusable guidance. Editing a skill ordinarily leaves the model weights unchanged.

options.text: The revision changes guidance used during the work
options.feedback: A skill supplies reusable instructions and resources. Changing that package can guide later runs without changing the underlying learned parameters.

options.text: The revision turns previous reports into model parameters
options.feedback: Reports are artifacts you can inspect or package. Editing the skill does not convert those files into trained model weights.

options.text: The revision makes the file location the task objective
options.feedback: The working location helps identify relevant materials. The procedure's instructions and the intended task still determine what the agent should do.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is seeing Markdown-style headings in an editor insufficient to confirm that a skill file was saved properly?

options.text: Typing Markdown headings automatically changes the saved format
options.feedback: Visible heading syntax does not establish the actual file format. A document can look like Markdown while still being saved as rich text.

options.text: Changing the filename also converts rich text into plain text
options.feedback: The filename and saved format are separate checks. A .md name does not by itself convert rich-text contents.

options.text: The saved format or filename may still be wrong
options.feedback: Appearance does not establish the saved file type. Check for plain-text Markdown and the intended filename before testing the skill.

options.text: Opening a file in an editor establishes that the agent can use it
options.feedback: An editor can display a document without proving it is saved as the intended skill file. Check the format and name, then test the result.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why should you compare a skill's test output with your original task criteria?

options.text: The test output establishes what the task should have been
options.feedback: This reverses the comparison. Your intended task and criteria provide the standard for deciding whether the produced output is useful.

options.text: The criteria determine which model parameters were changed
options.feedback: Skill testing checks the result of reusable instructions. It does not require treating an instruction edit as a model-weight update.

options.text: The criteria replace the need to open the output artifact
options.feedback: Criteria tell you what to look for, but you still need to inspect the actual output to see whether it meets them.

options.text: A finished run may still omit required work
options.feedback: Completing a run and satisfying the task are different checks. Evaluate the actual output against what you asked the skill to accomplish.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why should an automated grading procedure be compared with the rubric even when its score seems plausible?

options.text: A plausible score can hide a mismatch in the procedure
options.feedback: The notes treat the grading skill as a draft procedure. Compare its rules with the rubric and the requested work; the instructor remains responsible for the final grade.

options.text: A plausible score makes the procedure the grading standard
options.feedback: The procedure must be checked against the rubric and task. Its output does not replace those criteria or establish that its rules are appropriate.

options.text: A reproducible score shows that every legitimate approach is covered
options.feedback: A procedure can repeatedly apply a rule that misses a legitimate approach. Consistency does not establish that its criteria match the assignment.

options.text: A detailed explanation transfers grading responsibility to the skill
options.feedback: An automated first pass supplies evidence to review. The instructor remains responsible for the final grade even when the explanation is detailed.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why should you ask the agent to identify the actual skill file instead of assuming a folder location?

options.text: The skill's location determines whether the model was trained
options.feedback: Location concerns where the reusable package is stored. It does not turn editing instructions into training a model.

options.text: The location can differ across products and installations
options.feedback: The notes describe project and personal skill directories and warn that locations depend on the setup. Identifying the actual file avoids relying on a guessed path.

options.text: The latest report contains the authoritative skill procedure
options.feedback: A report is a result, while the skill file holds the procedure. Locate that actual instruction file and its supporting resources.

options.text: The file must be renamed each time its instructions are edited
options.feedback: The editing workflow calls for saving with the intended filename. The reason to locate the file is variation in where skills are stored.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why does an agent's message saying it created a complete file provide weaker evidence than inspecting the file?

options.text: The message changes the task requirements after execution
options.feedback: A completion message describes claimed success. The issue is whether the actual artifact satisfies the existing requirements, rather than whether the message creates new ones.

options.text: The message determines the output format more reliably
options.feedback: A message may describe a format, but opening the output lets you verify the artifact itself rather than relying on that description.

options.text: The message reports success without showing the full artifact
options.feedback: A success claim does not establish that the complete artifact exists in the correct place. Inspect its contents and verify the intended version and location.

options.text: The message confirms that every packaged component is the intended version
options.feedback: A claim of completion does not verify which versions are in the artifact. Open the file and inspect the included materials.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why should you check which skill version is included when an agent packages your work?

options.text: A skill version establishes whether the model has more parameters
options.feedback: Skill versions concern changes to instructions and resources. They are not versions of the model's learned parameter arrays.

options.text: A skill version determines whether the output needs inspection
options.feedback: The verification habit applies to the actual output regardless of the version label. A label cannot substitute for checking its contents.

options.text: A skill version replaces the need to state required contents
options.feedback: A version can identify intended guidance, but the agent still needs the required contents and output format when assembling the deliverable.

options.text: A readable package may include an outdated procedure
options.feedback: Readability does not establish that the intended materials were gathered. The notes specifically call for checking explanations, results, and intended skill versions.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You test a report-writing skill and find that it discusses two designs separately, although your task requires a comparison. What should you do next?

options.text: Add the comparison requirement and inspect a new run
options.feedback: Turn the missing task criterion into a specific instruction, then test whether the revised procedure produces the required comparison.

options.text: Edit the current report and treat the skill as repaired
options.feedback: That can improve this report, but it does not revise the reusable procedure or show that a later run will make the comparison.

options.text: Keep the skill unchanged and wait for a better result
options.feedback: Another run might differ, but this leaves the identified instruction mismatch in place. Make the requirement explicit and test it.

options.text: Remove the comparison criterion to match the output
options.feedback: The intended task supplies the evaluation standard. An incomplete result is a reason to repair the procedure, not redefine success around the omission.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Your edited instructions look right in a text editor, but the saved file is named SKILL.md.txt. What is the best next step?

options.text: Remove the extra extension and assume the file is ready
options.feedback: Fixing the name addresses one concern. The notes also call for confirming plain-text format and testing the intended skill.

options.text: Check the name and plain-text format, then test
options.feedback: The actual file must have the intended name and format. A test then checks whether the edited instructions function as intended.

options.text: Save it as rich text while giving it the intended name
options.feedback: The correct name does not make rich-text contents plain-text Markdown. Both the name and the format matter.

options.text: Confirm the instructions look right and accept the saved copy
options.feedback: Visual inspection of the wording does not resolve the extra extension or establish the saved format. Check the actual file and test it.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: An agent says it assembled your report, results, and revised skill into one file. You open it and find the revised skill is missing. How should you evaluate the work?

options.text: As complete because the message lists the required components
options.feedback: Listing materials in a message does not establish that they appear in the artifact. Your inspection reveals a missing requirement.

options.text: As complete because the existing report is readable
options.feedback: Readability is useful, but the required contents also matter. The requested package must include the revised skill.

options.text: As incomplete because required material is missing
options.feedback: Evaluate the artifact against the task. Ask for the omitted skill to be included, then inspect the repaired package.

options.text: As complete because the skill exists elsewhere in the project
options.feedback: An available source file is not the same as its inclusion in the requested package. Verify the actual deliverable contains the intended materials.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You want a skill to give feedback that explains how to improve a result, but its instructions ask for a short verdict. Which revision best addresses the mismatch?

options.text: Require a longer verdict and keep the current criteria
options.feedback: Extra length does not necessarily explain how to improve. State the specific kind of feedback you need, then inspect whether it appears.

options.text: Require a friendlier tone and keep the current criteria
options.feedback: Tone can make feedback easier to receive while leaving out improvement guidance. Revise the requested substance as well.

options.text: Require a restatement of the score before each verdict
options.feedback: Repeating the score describes the evaluation but does not explain a path to improvement. Make that explanation an explicit requirement.

options.text: Require improvement guidance and test the feedback
options.feedback: Clarifying the desired feedback changes the procedure meaningfully. Testing lets you judge whether its explanation meets the intended criterion.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does ordinary inference do?

options.text: Uses existing weights to generate an output
options.feedback: Inference runs the trained model forward. Its current representations can change without updating its learned weights.

options.text: Adjusts learned weights using prediction errors
options.feedback: Adjusting parameters from a learning objective belongs to training. Generating the current answer ordinarily uses weights that have already been learned.

options.text: Fits a reward model to human comparisons
options.feedback: A reward model can be trained from preferences during post-training. That is a learning stage, rather than ordinary generation.

options.text: Learns desired answers from demonstrations
options.feedback: Learning from example responses describes supervised fine-tuning. Inference uses the resulting trained model.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which change characterizes model training?

options.text: Transforming representations for the current input
options.feedback: Intermediate representations change as a model processes input during inference too. Training is distinguished by updates to learned parameters.

options.text: Updating learned parameter values
options.feedback: Training uses a learning objective and updates parameters. These weight changes distinguish it from an ordinary forward run.

options.text: Extending the current conversation history
options.feedback: A conversation can grow during inference. More history is not by itself evidence that the model weights changed.

options.text: Producing the next response for the user
options.feedback: Producing a response is an inference activity. Training additionally uses a learning process to change parameters.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: In next-token pre-training, where does the prediction target come from?

options.text: A person who ranks several assistant replies
options.feedback: Ranking replies is a preference-feedback example from post-training. Next-token pre-training obtains its target from the training text.

options.text: The reply preferred by a trained reward model
options.feedback: A reward model can supply a signal in a classic human-feedback pipeline. The next-token target instead comes directly from the text.

options.text: The next token already found in the text
options.feedback: The text supplies both the preceding context and the token that follows it. This provides a learning target without hand-labeling every continuation.

options.text: A person who labels each possible continuation
options.feedback: People need not label each continuation in this example. The next token in the existing text supplies the target.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What is pre-training in the text-model example?

options.text: Behavioral learning by comparing preferred assistant responses
options.feedback: Response comparisons are used in preference-based post-training. They build on a base model rather than describe the foundational prediction stage.

options.text: Response generation by running a model with fixed weights
options.feedback: Running an already-trained model describes ordinary inference. Pre-training changes weights through a learning process.

options.text: Instruction learning by imitating example assistant responses
options.feedback: Example responses are used in supervised fine-tuning. The foundational text-model example instead predicts the next token from existing text.

options.text: Foundational learning by predicting tokens in text
options.feedback: The model learns broad language patterns and associations through prediction over large datasets. Later training can shape how it responds as an assistant.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Which description best fits a base model after next-token pre-training?

options.text: A model with text patterns but uncertain assistant behavior
options.feedback: Prediction can build language patterns and world associations. It does not by itself guarantee reliable conversational helpfulness.

options.text: A model whose helpful conversational responses are already assured
options.feedback: Prediction training provides a foundation, but it does not guarantee helpful assistant behavior. Further training can shape that behavior, while suitable patterns can also elicit answers from a base model.

options.text: A model whose learned statements have already been checked for truth
options.feedback: Learning to predict likely text does not verify each learned claim. A base model can acquire associations without guaranteeing their accuracy.

options.text: A model whose replies are selected directly by human evaluators
options.feedback: People may provide examples or preferences during post-training. A base model produces text using its learned parameters, rather than having humans choose each reply.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What is the role of example responses in supervised fine-tuning?

options.text: They measure how often a response appears in the original text
options.feedback: The notes describe desired-answer demonstrations, not counting occurrences in pre-training text. Fine-tuning learns from those examples of behavior.

options.text: They demonstrate the responses the model should learn to produce
options.feedback: Supervised fine-tuning trains on demonstrations of desired responses. This shapes behavior beyond foundational next-token pre-training.

options.text: They provide pairs of replies for people to rank by preference
options.feedback: Ranking alternatives supplies preference information. Demonstrations instead show the desired response itself.

options.text: They supply a fixed conversation for an inference run to complete
options.feedback: Examples can be placed in context, but supervised fine-tuning uses them for training. That process changes learned parameters.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: In the classic reinforcement learning from human feedback pipeline, what does a reward model learn from?

options.text: The current conversation without any parameter updates
options.feedback: Using a conversation to generate a response is ordinary inference. The reward model is trained using human comparisons.

options.text: Example answers demonstrating desired assistant responses
options.feedback: Demonstrations show desired responses for supervised fine-tuning. The reward model in the classic pipeline instead learns from comparisons of alternative outputs.

options.text: Human comparisons of alternative outputs
options.feedback: People compare outputs, and the reward model learns from those comparisons. Its learned signal is then used to optimize the assistant.

options.text: Human selection of the next token in every training sentence
options.feedback: Hand-labeling every next token is not the described source of preference feedback. People compare outputs in the classic pipeline.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What follows reward-model training in the classic reinforcement learning from human feedback pipeline?

options.text: Training the reward model again on example assistant responses
options.feedback: Example assistant responses provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning. After learning a reward signal from comparisons, the described pipeline uses that signal to optimize the assistant.

options.text: Training the assistant to predict the next tokens in raw text
options.feedback: This is the foundational text-model training example. The stage after reward-model learning instead uses the learned preference signal for further assistant optimization.

options.text: Training the assistant to copy reward scores as desired replies
options.feedback: This confuses an evaluation signal with a demonstration answer. A reward signal guides optimization; it is not the response the assistant is being taught to produce.

options.text: Training the assistant using the learned reward signal
options.feedback: The reward model learns from human comparisons, and reinforcement learning uses that signal to optimize the assistant. These are distinct stages.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does alignment work aim to improve?

options.text: The match between system responses and the behavior people intend
options.feedback: Alignment aims to make behavior fit intended goals and constraints reliably. Training can encourage that fit without guaranteeing it in every context.

options.text: The enforcement of limits on which external actions tools can execute
options.feedback: This describes harness permissions and access controls. They constrain execution, whereas alignment addresses the behavior the model chooses.

options.text: The accuracy of a prediction about the next token in existing text
options.feedback: This describes the foundational text-model prediction objective. Strong prediction alone does not establish that responses fit the behavior people intend.

options.text: The confirmation that a completed artifact contains the requested work
options.feedback: This describes verification of a result. Alignment instead concerns improving the system behavior that produces responses and proposes actions.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: What does post-training build on?

options.text: A reward model that has replaced foundational language training
options.feedback: A reward model can guide a later learning stage. It does not replace the base model and its foundational training.

options.text: A base model that has already undergone foundational training
options.feedback: Post-training starts from a base model and further shapes its behavior and capabilities. Demonstrations and preferences can supply learning signals.

options.text: A conversation history that has replaced the learned parameters
options.feedback: Conversation history is context, not a replacement for weights. Post-training updates a previously trained model.

options.text: A collection of preferred responses used without a trained model
options.feedback: Preferred responses can provide training information, but the process builds on a base model. The examples do not substitute for the model itself.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can a model produce different responses to different inputs while its learned weights remain fixed?

options.text: Its weights and intermediate representations refer to the same numbers
options.feedback: The notes distinguish learned weights from the representations produced during processing. Confusing them makes an ordinary inference change look like training.

options.text: The new input acts as a human preference comparison during training
options.feedback: Receiving input is not the same as training on human comparisons. An ordinary response can change through input-dependent processing without a learning update.

options.text: Its intermediate representations depend on the input being processed
options.feedback: Inference uses existing weights while processing the current input. Changing representations are different from changes to the weights themselves.

options.text: Each new input supplies an error signal that updates learned parameters
options.feedback: This confuses ordinary input-dependent processing with training. Training uses a learning process to update parameters; a new input alone does not establish such an update.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is next-token prediction called self-supervised learning in the notes?

options.text: The model can train without any target or performance objective
options.feedback: Self-supervision still supplies a learning target. The distinction is that the target comes from the data rather than a separate human label for every continuation.

options.text: The model certifies the factual accuracy of its own predictions
options.feedback: Self-supervision describes how targets are obtained. It does not establish the truth of the learned claims.

options.text: A reward model supplies the target from human response rankings
options.feedback: This describes a signal in the classic human-feedback pipeline. The next-token example is self-supervised because the existing text itself supplies the prediction target.

options.text: Existing text supplies the context and prediction target
options.feedback: A passage can supply a context and its next token. This creates a training example without requiring a person to label every continuation.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why can strong next-token prediction coexist with inaccurate claims?

options.text: Learning likely text does not verify its associations
options.feedback: Prediction can build useful language and world patterns. The objective does not turn every association learned from text into a true statement.

options.text: Prediction quality measures how many claims humans have verified
options.feedback: The described prediction objective concerns the next token, not a count of fact-checked claims. Good prediction is therefore not a truth guarantee.

options.text: Inaccurate claims indicate that inference must have changed the weights
options.feedback: An inaccurate output can arise while using existing weights. Weight updates are not needed for a model to generate a mistaken claim.

options.text: Extensive training removes language patterns and keeps verified facts
options.feedback: Pre-training learns patterns and associations from extensive text. The notes do not describe a filtering process that leaves a store of verified facts.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why might a base model continue a request as part of a document instead of answering helpfully?

options.text: A base model has already optimized each reply for a user preference score
options.feedback: Optimizing with a reward signal is part of a classic post-training pipeline. It does not describe a base model after foundational prediction training.

options.text: Its objective teaches continuation, not reliable assistance
options.feedback: Predicting what text comes next can support document continuation. Further training helps shape reliable assistant-style responses.

options.text: Its foundational objective teaches refusal instead of language prediction
options.feedback: Refusal of harmful requests is an example of preferred behavior encouraged later. The foundational text-model objective is prediction.

options.text: A base model lacks learned patterns needed to produce connected text
options.feedback: Pre-training can build extensive language patterns. The issue is the style and purpose of the continuation, not an absence of language learning.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why does training measure performance against an objective before updating model parameters?

options.text: The measurement determines which tool permissions the model needs
options.feedback: Tool permissions constrain external operations. Training measurements instead support learning updates to the model's parameters.

options.text: The measurement certifies the truth of future generated claims
options.feedback: A learning objective guides training, but success at prediction does not verify every learned association or guarantee future accuracy.

options.text: The measured error helps guide parameter adjustments
options.feedback: Training measures performance and computes how parameters affect the error. Those results support updates to learned weights.

options.text: The measurement replaces the need to change any learned values
options.feedback: Evaluating performance supplies information for learning. Training also uses that information to update parameters; evaluation alone is not that update.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: How do demonstrations and preference comparisons supply different training information?

options.text: Demonstrations rank alternatives; comparisons provide the full desired answer
options.feedback: This reverses the roles described in the notes. Demonstrations supply example responses, while comparisons identify a preferred alternative.

options.text: Demonstrations measure truth; comparisons guarantee future helpful behavior
options.feedback: Neither training input guarantees those outcomes. The notes distinguish example responses from relative preferences and emphasize the limits of behavioral training.

options.text: Demonstrations change conversation history; comparisons leave parameters fixed
options.feedback: These are sources of training information in this question. Using them in training differs from adding material to a current inference context.

options.text: Demonstrations give examples; comparisons express relative preference
options.feedback: An example answer illustrates what to produce. Comparing alternatives expresses relative preference, which can train a reward model in the classic pipeline.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why are reward-model training and assistant optimization separate stages in the classic human-feedback pipeline?

options.text: One learns a preference signal; the other trains the assistant with it
options.feedback: The reward model first learns a signal from human comparisons. Reinforcement learning then uses that signal to optimize the assistant.

options.text: One learns a preference signal; the other copies it as an example reply
options.feedback: A learned reward is a signal for optimization, rather than a demonstration response to imitate. Example replies serve a different role in supervised fine-tuning.

options.text: One learns a preference signal; the other runs the assistant without updates
options.feedback: Running the assistant with unchanged weights describes inference. In the training pipeline, the learned reward signal guides further optimization of the assistant.

options.text: One learns demonstration answers; the other ranks responses with people
options.feedback: Demonstrations and human comparisons are inputs to different training stages. The question concerns learning a reward signal from comparisons and then using it to train the assistant.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: How can two post-training procedures differ even when both use human preferences?

options.text: A preferred output is a demonstration, so comparisons cannot guide learning
options.feedback: Comparisons can identify a preferred output without supplying the same training information as a demonstration. The notes explicitly include preferences as a learning source.

options.text: Preferences can guide training through several different methods
options.feedback: The notes identify alternatives to the classic reinforcement-learning pipeline. The common role of preference information does not make the procedures identical.

options.text: Preference information describes inference rather than further model training
options.feedback: Preferences can supply learning information during post-training. Their use is not limited to the current inference response.

options.text: Every preference method requires humans to write a target for each next token
options.feedback: That requirement confuses different learning signals. The notes distinguish text-derived next-token targets, demonstrations, and comparisons of outputs.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why does training a model to refuse a harmful request leave behavioral reliability as an ongoing concern?

options.text: A refusal during training guarantees matching responses during deployment
options.feedback: This treats an encouraged behavior as an inviolable rule. The notes explicitly distinguish improved behavior from a guarantee across contexts.

options.text: A refusal shows that learned parameters no longer influence model behavior
options.feedback: Refusals can be shaped through post-training, which affects the model. They do not indicate that learned weights have stopped influencing responses.

options.text: A favored response in training may not hold under unfamiliar framing
options.feedback: Post-training can encourage a refusal, but that response is not an unbreakable rule for every context. Reliability must extend beyond the situations represented in training.

options.text: A refusal changes external permissions each time the model generates it
options.feedback: This confuses the model choosing a response with external enforcement. Training encourages behavior; harness permissions separately constrain which actions can execute.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: Why is possible future use of a conversation for training different from learning during the current response?

options.text: Saving a conversation for future use performs a current parameter update
options.feedback: Data retention and parameter updates are different events. Saving information does not establish that the current response is updating weights.

options.text: Processing a conversation with fixed weights rules out later training use
options.feedback: Current inference does not establish a provider's future data-use policy. The notes say later collection and training depend on the service and settings.

options.text: Adding a conversation to context is the same learning process as later training
options.feedback: Context and intermediate representations can change during inference. Training adds a separate learning process that updates learned parameters.

options.text: Updating parameters later is separate from generating the current response
options.feedback: A provider may separately collect data for future training. Ordinary inference can use existing weights even if a later training process occurs.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You add a paragraph to a conversation, and the model uses it to improve an explanation. The system reports that no parameters changed. What best explains the improvement?

options.text: Inference used the new context with existing learned weights
options.feedback: Supplying relevant material can change performance during inference. The model can use the paragraph without changing its underlying weights.

options.text: Pre-training learned a new set of weights from the paragraph
options.feedback: The scenario states that parameters did not change. The improvement is explained by using relevant context, rather than a foundational learning update.

options.text: Supervised fine-tuning trained the model on a desired answer
options.feedback: The paragraph was supplied in the conversation, and there was no weight update. That differs from training on demonstrations of desired responses.

options.text: Reward-model training learned which explanation people prefer
options.feedback: The scenario provides contextual information, not human comparisons used to train a reward model. Better performance alone does not establish such training.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: A training program takes a sentence, hides its final token, and trains a model to predict that token from the earlier text. Which idea does this illustrate?

options.text: Ordinary inference using weights without a learning update
options.feedback: The scenario explicitly trains the model on a target. Ordinary inference generates outputs without that parameter-update process.

options.text: Self-supervised learning using a target supplied by the text
options.feedback: The token already in the sentence supplies the answer for the learning objective. No person needs to label that continuation separately.

options.text: Preference learning using human rankings of several responses
options.feedback: There are no ranked alternative responses in this scenario. The learning target is a token drawn from the existing text.

options.text: Assistant fine-tuning using demonstrations of helpful replies
options.feedback: This example does not provide a desired assistant reply. It uses the next token from text as a prediction target.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: You want to shape a base model into a tutor. You train it on examples pairing student questions with clear, helpful answers. Which stage does this most directly illustrate?

options.text: Foundational pre-training on unlabeled text continuations
options.feedback: The examples are selected as demonstrations of helpful tutoring responses. This is further behavioral training on top of the base model.

options.text: Ordinary inference on a growing conversation history
options.feedback: The scenario says the model is being trained on example pairs. That is a learning process, rather than merely generating the current response.

options.text: Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations
options.feedback: The supplied answers demonstrate the behavior the model should learn. This is different from asking people to rank several competing answers.

options.text: Reward-model training on preference comparisons
options.feedback: The scenario supplies example answers rather than rankings of alternatives. Comparisons would provide the signal used to train a reward model in the classic pipeline.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: People compare two explanations of photosynthesis and prefer the one suited to a young learner. What information does this comparison provide for post-training?

options.text: A guarantee that the model will explain every topic appropriately
options.feedback: One preferred response provides useful training information, not a guarantee across topics and contexts. Behavioral reliability still needs attention.

options.text: The next token that originally followed a passage in the training text
options.feedback: That would be a self-supervised prediction target. This comparison instead expresses a judgment about alternative responses.

options.text: Evidence that the current comparison has already updated the assistant weights
options.feedback: A human judgment can supply information for training. The judgment alone does not demonstrate that the subsequent training update has occurred.

options.text: A preference about which response better fits the intended audience
options.feedback: The comparison identifies a response that better serves the task. Preferences can guide behavioral training, including reward-model learning in the classic pipeline.

questions.source: Quiz 5 - Sessions 1-6: Model Training, Alignment, and the Agent Harness
questions.question: A model trained to favor refusals of harmful requests usually declines them, but a misleadingly framed version receives a harmful answer. Which conclusion best follows from the notes?

options.text: Training has encouraged a behavior that remains unreliable in some contexts
options.feedback: A preferred refusal can be learned without becoming an inviolable rule. The changed framing exposes a limit in behavioral reliability.

options.text: The initial refusals prove the later answer must be harmless in effect
options.feedback: Earlier refusals do not establish the safety of a different response. The notes emphasize that behavior may change with framing.

options.text: The changed wording proves that the model updated its weights during the request
options.feedback: Different inputs can lead to different outputs using existing weights. A behavioral change under new framing is not evidence of a training update.

options.text: The later answer proves that post-training cannot influence model behavior
options.feedback: An imperfect result does not show that training has no influence. Post-training can encourage preferred responses while leaving reliability gaps.
